questions.prompt: Your extraction service supports a multi-turn correction chat: users point out extraction mistakes and the model revises. Users report the model "forgets" corrections from two turns earlier. The service sends each API request with only the latest user message. What is the fix?

choices.text: Send the complete conversation history in every API request.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the model to remember all prior corrections.
Cache the model's last response client-side and re-send it with each new message.
Store corrections in a database and have the model query them through a tool.

questions.explanation: The API is stateless: conversational coherence requires passing the complete conversation history in every request. Sending only the latest message *is* the bug. B instructs the model to remember context it was never sent. C restores one turn of history — corrections from two turns back stay lost. D rebuilds conversation memory as external infrastructure.

questions.prompt: Each extraction is enriched via a vendor-lookup MCP tool that returns 40+ fields per call, of which your workflow uses 5. Long enrichment sessions degrade noticeably and sometimes overflow context. What is the right fix?

choices.text: Call the vendor-lookup tool less often by batching several vendors per call.
Move to a model with a larger context window to absorb the verbose results.
Summarize the conversation with /compact after every ten enrichments.
Trim the tool output to the relevant fields before it accumulates in context.

questions.explanation: Verbose tool outputs consume context disproportionately to their relevance; trimming to the relevant fields before results accumulate (tool-side or via a PostToolUse transformation) fixes the accumulation at the source. A changes call frequency, not per-call bloat. B delays the overflow and doesn't address degradation. C summarizes after the tokens are already spent, repeatedly.

questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. questions.prompt: A nightly job must cross-reference 20 related documents in a single request (they reference each other, so they can't be processed separately). Fields sourced from documents in the middle of the concatenated input show markedly higher miss rates than those near the start and end. What is the best mitigation?

choices.text: Randomize document order nightly so no document is always in the middle.
Duplicate the middle documents at the end of the input so they appear twice.
Add a key-facts summary at the beginning and organize the documents under labeled section headers.
Instruct the model: "Documents in the middle are equally important; do not skip them."

questions.explanation: This is the lost-in-the-middle effect. Since splitting the request isn't possible, apply the position mitigations: a key-facts summary at the beginning and explicit, labeled section headers organizing the detail. A rotates which fields get missed. B doubles input size and still buries other documents. D — position effects are not fixed by exhortation. --- *End of Practice Exam 7.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)

The model should be prompted to never emit text and tool calls together, making the check safe.
The loop should wait for two consecutive text-bearing responses before terminating.
Text is not a completion signal — the loop must inspect `stop_reason` and continue on `"tool_use"`.

One pass over the 10 riskiest files, ignoring the rest.

Set `tool_choice: "any"` so a tool is always called first.
List `extract_metadata` first in the tools array, since order implies priority.
Add few-shot examples demonstrating metadata-first ordering.

Mark everything optional to maximize extraction flexibility.
Require only fields genuinely present in every document; make possibly-absent fields optional/nullable.
Mark required whatever downstream systems need, regardless of the documents.

Just the validation error, to keep the retry cheap.
The original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation errors together.
The failed extraction with an instruction to "fix the errors."

questions.prompt: Documents arrive continuously and your contract guarantees results within 30 hours. Batch processing can take up to 24 hours. Which submission schedule guarantees the SLA while minimizing submission overhead?

choices.text: One batch daily — 24-hour accumulation plus 24-hour processing stays under two days.
Every 12 hours with a priority flag on older documents.
Every 8 hours — the tighter cadence usually leaves several hours of margin in practice.
Submit a batch every 4 hours.

questions.explanation: Worst case must fit the SLA: a document arriving just after a submission waits the full interval plus processing. Every 4 hours: 4 + 24 = 28 ≤ 30, with margin. A's worst case is 48 hours; B's is 36; C's is 32 — over the line, and "usually leaves margin" isn't a guarantee.

A makes the biased check mandatory. B gives the biased check a checklist. D calibrates a signal produced by the same blind process.

The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues, with custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: Gift-card purchases are non-refundable by policy; the agent should route those customers to a goodwill-credit workflow instead. The rule lives in the system prompt today, and violations still occur monthly. What is the correct mechanism?

choices.text: Add gift-card examples to the few-shot section of the prompt.
Add a second model that reviews each refund decision before execution.
Move the gift-card rule into the `process_refund` tool description.
Intercept `process_refund` with a hook that blocks gift-card refunds and redirects to goodwill credit.

questions.explanation: A monthly-violated financial policy needs interception: a hook that blocks gift-card refunds at the tool-call level and redirects to the goodwill workflow. A adds probabilistic reinforcement to an already-failing prompt approach. B doubles inference cost for a still-probabilistic check. C relocates prompt text; descriptions guide selection, they don't enforce.

questions.prompt: Account email changes must be preceded by a completed identity verification in the same conversation. Reviewing incidents, you find the agent occasionally performs the change when a persuasive customer insists verification "already happened last week." What prevents this?

choices.text: A system prompt instruction to never trust customer claims about prior verification.
Few-shot examples of the agent politely refusing unverified email changes.
A prerequisite gate: `update_email` stays blocked until verification has actually completed in the current session.
A daily audit report of email changes for the fraud team.

questions.explanation: The gate must check what actually happened in the session, not what the conversation claims: block `update_email` until a verification step has completed. Social engineering defeats prompt rules (A, B) precisely because the model weighs persuasive context. D detects fraud after the account is compromised.

questions.prompt: A billing dispute arrives with symptoms that don't match any known pattern — the charge exists in one system but not another. There is no established runbook. How should the agent approach the investigation?

choices.text: Follow the standard billing-dispute script, which handles the majority of disputes correctly.
Use an adaptive investigation plan: form a hypothesis, run a lookup, and let each finding set the next step.
Escalate immediately, since no runbook exists for this symptom pattern.
Run every available lookup tool once, then decide from the combined results.

questions.explanation: No-runbook, unknown-cause investigations call for adaptive plans: hypothesize, look up, let findings drive the next step. A applies a script to a case that explicitly doesn't fit it — the script's coverage of ordinary disputes is what makes it tempting. C escalates work the agent can meaningfully progress. D burns calls without a hypothesis connecting them.

questions.prompt: A support case is reopened the next morning through a new chat. Yesterday's session contains extensive tool results (order status, refund state) that may have changed overnight, plus the negotiated resolution details. How should the agent be initialized?

choices.text: Start a new session injecting a structured case summary, re-running lookups for time-sensitive data.
Resume yesterday's session unchanged — continuity matters most.
Resume yesterday's session and instruct the agent to distrust any tool results.
Start fresh with no context and let the customer re-explain the situation.

questions.explanation: Overnight, tool results go stale while the negotiated resolution stays valid — exactly the split a structured case summary preserves: start fresh, inject the durable facts, re-look-up the time-sensitive ones. B trusts stale state. C carries the stale context along while distrusting it — the worst of both. D throws away the resolution details and burns customer goodwill.

questions.prompt: You maintain four agent behavior requirements. Three are enforced with hooks. Which one is appropriately left to system-prompt guidance alone?

choices.text: Refunds above $500 must be approved by a human.
Identity must be verified before account mutations.
Responses should acknowledge the customer's frustration before presenting solutions.
Refunds must go only to the original payment method.

questions.explanation: Tone and empathy are behavioral guidance where occasional imperfection is tolerable — the appropriate domain of prompt instructions. A, B, and D are compliance rules with financial or security consequences, which is why they're hooked: any violation is unacceptable, so enforcement must be deterministic.

questions.prompt: The agent calls `lookup_order` with the date "next Tuesday" in a field expecting `YYYY-MM-DD`. How should the tool respond so the agent can recover in one step?

choices.text: `isError` with a generic "invalid request" so the agent tries something else.
Silently interpret "next Tuesday" server-side using the current date.
A transient-category error so the agent retries the same call.
A validation error naming the field, stating the expected format (`YYYY-MM-DD`), and marked correctable.

questions.explanation: A malformed input is a validation error: name the field, state the expected format, and mark it correctable so the agent fixes the argument and re-calls in one step. A gives no correction path. B silently guesses intent inside the tool — hidden behavior that will misfire. C triggers retries of an input that will fail identically every time.

Rename `process_refund` to `process_refund_not_exchange`.
Block exchange-context refunds with a hook and let the error teach the agent.
Merge refunds and exchanges into one `resolve_return` tool.

questions.explanation: Tool descriptions should state boundaries — what the tool is for and what it is not for, naming the alternative. The agent chooses refunds because nothing signals exchanges are out of scope. B abuses naming to carry documentation. C teaches by failure at customer expense. D merges two flows with different semantics, creating a new selection problem inside one tool.

questions.prompt: After a quarter of feature growth, the resolution agent now has 17 tools spanning refunds, subscriptions, loyalty, shipping, and marketing consent. Selection errors have risen steadily with each addition. What is the architectural correction?

choices.text: Sort the tools array by usage frequency so common tools are found first.
Add a mandatory reasoning step before every tool call.
Scope tool access by role — split into specialized agents, each carrying only the tools its role needs.
Shorten all tool descriptions so the full list fits in less context.

questions.explanation: Selection reliability degrades as the tool count grows; the correction is scoped tool access — split by role so each agent carries only the handful of tools its job needs. A and D are cosmetic reorderings of an oversized surface. B adds latency to every call without reducing the decision complexity causing the errors.

choices.text: Continue — support tooling is too business-critical for community code.
Use an existing community MCP server; reserve custom effort for workflows unique to your team.
Skip MCP and call Zendesk's REST API from a hook.
Wrap Zendesk's API in your existing backend and expose one mega-tool.

questions.explanation: For standard integrations, prefer existing community MCP servers; custom development is reserved for team-specific workflows. Zendesk CRUD is as standard as it gets. A is not-invented-here. C bypasses the tool interface the agent needs. D creates an undifferentiated mega-tool — a selection and description problem waiting to happen.

questions.prompt: A platform wrapper catches all tool exceptions and returns `{}` with a success status "to keep conversations smooth." Yesterday the agent told a customer their refund was complete when `process_refund` had actually thrown. What is the design lesson?

choices.text: Wrappers should return `null` rather than `{}` so downstream code can detect the failures.
The agent should verify refunds with a follow-up lookup after every attempt.
The wrapper needs better logging so engineers catch these incidents sooner.
Failures must surface as structured errors, not be disguised as successes.

questions.explanation: Returning failures as successes is the silent-suppression anti-pattern: the agent cannot respond truthfully or recover from an error it never sees. The fix is structured errors that surface. A trades one sentinel for another — still not an error the agent can reason about. B adds a verification round-trip to compensate for lying infrastructure. C helps engineers, not the customer being told falsehoods.

questions.prompt: A customer writes: "This is the THIRD time I'm contacting you people about this broken blender!!" The issue is a standard damage replacement with photo evidence — fully within the agent's capability. Sentiment analysis scores the message as highly negative. What should the agent do?

choices.text: Acknowledge the frustration and repeated contact, then offer to resolve the replacement right now.
Escalate to a human immediately — high negative sentiment indicates a case the bot shouldn't touch.
Escalate if sentiment remains negative after the agent's first empathetic response.
Process the replacement silently without addressing the tone.

questions.explanation: Frustration over a resolvable issue calls for acknowledgment plus immediate resolution — escalate only if the customer asks for a human. Sentiment is an unreliable proxy for complexity (B), and gating on a second sentiment reading (C) still routes by mood rather than capability. D resolves the issue but ignores a customer who needs to be heard — hurting the interaction anyway.

Escalate — the policy is silent on this request, and policy gaps are escalation triggers.
Decline the request, since the policy does not authorize competitor matching.
Ask the customer for a screenshot and decide based on the price difference.

questions.explanation: Policy gaps are an escalation trigger: the published policy is silent on competitor matching, so the agent has no authority to improvise (A), refuse definitively (C), or invent criteria (D). Escalating routes the exception to someone empowered to set precedent.

choices.text: Pick the account matching the phone number the customer wrote in from.
Merge the three accounts, since they likely belong to one person.
Ask the customer for an additional identifier (order number, account email, billing zip) and match on that.
Proceed with the most recent account but flag the conversation for review.

questions.explanation: Multiple customer matches require clarification through additional identifiers, not heuristic selection. A is a heuristic (a phone number shared across the accounts makes it worse). B mutates customer data on a guess. D proceeds on the guess and merely documents it.

questions.prompt: In sessions where a customer raises several issues, the agent confuses details between them as the conversation grows — attributing order 8817's status to order 9902's refund. What is the recommended context structure?

choices.text: Limit customers to two issues per conversation.
Repeat all issue details in every agent response so they stay in recent context.
Handle issues strictly one at a time, closing each before discussing the next.
Persist each issue's structured data (order ID, amount, status, next action) in a separate context layer, keyed by issue.

questions.explanation: Multi-issue sessions need structured issue data — order ID, amount, status, next action per issue — persisted in a separate context layer rather than left to drift in conversational history. A and C constrain customers to fit the architecture. B bloats every response and still relies on the model keeping the issues straight.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: Reports on "the impact of an aging population" consistently cover only healthcare; labor markets, housing, and public pensions never appear. The coordinator's decomposition logs show subtasks like "hospital staffing shortages" and "elder-care costs." What is the fix?

choices.text: Improve the coordinator's decomposition: enumerate the topic's major domains first, then create subtasks against that list with coverage criteria.
Instruct the search agent to broaden every query it receives with additional sectors.
Add a fourth subagent dedicated to domains the others miss.
Have the synthesis agent note in the report which domains received less attention.

questions.explanation: The decomposition is the failure point: the coordinator collapsed a broad topic into one domain's subtasks. Fix decomposition — enumerate the topic's major domains first, then generate subtasks against that enumeration with coverage criteria. B patches queries downstream of bad assignments. C adds a guessing agent. D documents the gap instead of closing it.

questions.prompt: Each subagent currently posts its findings directly into a shared results channel, and the report agent assembles whatever it finds there. Findings arrive out of order, some overwrite others, and nobody detects missing pieces. Which component should own result collection, and why?

choices.text: The report agent, since it consumes the results anyway.
The shared channel, upgraded with ordering and dedup logic.
The coordinator — aggregation, completeness checks, and error handling belong at the hub.
Each subagent, verifying its own delivery with a read-back check.

questions.explanation: In hub-and-spoke architecture, aggregation belongs to the coordinator: one place for completeness checks, ordering, and error handling before synthesis. A gives the consumer an orchestration job. B rebuilds coordinator responsibilities inside a message bus. D verifies delivery without anyone owning the whole picture.

questions.prompt: After an expensive shared analysis of a 400-document corpus, you want to evaluate two competing report frameworks — thematic versus chronological — each developed independently from that same analysis. What mechanism does the Agent SDK provide?

choices.text: `--resume` the analysis session twice, once per framework.
`fork_session` — two independent branches from the shared analysis baseline, one framework in each.
Run the analysis twice in two fresh sessions, one per framework.
Develop both frameworks alternately within the single session.

questions.explanation: `fork_session` creates independent branches from a shared analysis baseline — each framework develops in isolation without re-paying for the 400-document analysis and without cross-contamination. A resumes one lineage twice into the same history. C re-buys the corpus analysis. D lets each framework bias the other.

questions.prompt: Your system produces (a) a weekly market digest with the same six sections every week, and (b) ad-hoc deep investigations of novel questions. How should the two pipelines be decomposed?

choices.text: Both dynamic — research is inherently unpredictable.
Both fixed — consistency simplifies operations.
The digest dynamic and the investigations fixed, since digests have more room for creativity.
The weekly digest as a fixed prompt chain; the ad-hoc investigations with dynamic decomposition.

questions.explanation: Match decomposition to predictability: the six-section weekly digest is a fixed prompt chain; novel ad-hoc investigations need dynamic decomposition that adapts to findings. A adds adaptive overhead to clockwork. B scripts the unscriptable. C assigns each pipeline the wrong pattern.

questions.prompt: Monday's run must gather updates from six independent news domains before synthesis. The coordinator currently delegates them one per turn. What single change most reduces wall-clock time?

choices.text: Have the coordinator emit all six Task tool calls in one response so they run in parallel.
Cache Friday's results and only fetch weekend changes.
Reduce each domain's search depth so sequential runs finish faster.
Move synthesis earlier so it overlaps with the last two searches.

questions.explanation: Independent gathering tasks parallelize by emitting all six Task calls in a single coordinator response. B changes what is fetched, not the serialization. C makes each sequential step cheaper but keeps six round-trips. D starts synthesis before its inputs exist.

questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: A reviewer flags this coordinator code: `if "DONE" in assistant_text: break` — paired with a system prompt instructing the model to "say DONE when research is complete." What is the professional assessment?

choices.text: Acceptable — explicit completion markers are a common convention in agent frameworks.
The marker should be structured (a JSON field) rather than a bare string in prose.
Termination should key off `stop_reason` (`"end_turn"`), not a natural-language marker.
The check is fine but should also require that no tool calls are pending in the response.

questions.explanation: Natural-language completion markers are the classic termination anti-pattern: they fire spuriously (the model discusses "DONE"), get paraphrased away, and duplicate what `stop_reason` already provides reliably. A normalizes the anti-pattern. B structures the wrong mechanism. D patches one failure mode of a signal that shouldn't be the signal.

questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. questions.prompt: Researching an extremely niche topic, the search subagent's query legitimately matches nothing. The tool returns an error, and the coordinator logs "search infrastructure degraded" and switches to a fallback provider — wasting a cycle. What is the correct contract?

choices.text: The tool should return the closest partial matches instead of nothing.
The coordinator should ping a health-check endpoint before interpreting errors.
Empty results and failures can share a response shape if the log message differs.
Zero matches is a successful query with an empty result set; errors are reserved for access failures.

questions.explanation: Zero matches from a valid query is a *successful* search; conflating it with failure caused a pointless failover. Tools must distinguish valid empty results from access failures. A substitutes wrong results for honest emptiness. B adds infrastructure to disambiguate what the response shape should state. C keeps the ambiguity and hides the distinction in logs the agent never sees.

questions.prompt: Your `search_corpus` tool truncates queries over 256 characters — silently. Agents regularly compose long, careful queries whose critical qualifiers get cut off, returning oddly irrelevant results no one can explain. Beyond fixing the truncation, what should the tool description have included?

choices.text: A version number so agents know the tool's behavior may change.
The input constraint and edge-case behavior: the maximum query length and what happens beyond it.
Usage statistics showing typical query lengths.
A warning that search quality varies by topic.

questions.explanation: Descriptions should document input formats, limits, and edge-case behavior — a 256-character truncation is exactly the constraint an agent needs to compose valid queries. A and C are metadata that don't prevent the failure. D is a disclaimer, not a contract.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. questions.prompt: The document analysis agent has access to a purpose-built `arxiv_search` MCP tool but keeps using the generic built-in WebSearch for academic queries, returning blog summaries instead of papers. `arxiv_search`'s description is "Searches arXiv." What is the recommended fix?

choices.text: Enhance the description: what it searches, what it returns, and when to prefer it over general web search.
Remove WebSearch from the agent so arxiv_search wins by default.
Add a system prompt rule to always use arxiv_search for anything containing the word "paper."
Lower WebSearch's priority via tool ordering.

questions.explanation: The agent prefers the tool it understands; "Searches arXiv" gives no case for selection. Enhance the description — what it searches, what it returns, when to prefer it over general web search. B removes a tool still needed for non-academic queries. C is keyword-matching brittleness. D — ordering isn't a documented selection mechanism; descriptions are.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: The document analysis agent abandons its entire assignment the first time a PDF-parsing call times out, reporting total failure to the coordinator even when 9 of 10 documents parsed fine. What error-handling design is missing?

choices.text: A longer parsing timeout so failures stop happening.
A coordinator-side retry of the whole document analysis task.
Local recovery: retry the failed parse, continue with the rest, and propagate only the unresolved failure with partial results.
Parallel parsing so one timeout doesn't serialize the rest.

questions.explanation: Subagents should recover locally from transient failures (retry the parse) and, failing that, continue the assignment — propagating only the unresolvable failure with partial results. Nine parsed documents is a report, not a total failure. A pretends timeouts can be configured away. B re-runs everything including the nine successes. D addresses throughput, not the give-up-entirely logic.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: While analyzing a corpus, the analysis agent finds two credible papers reporting incompatible efficacy figures. It currently discards the outlier and reports one clean number. What should it do instead?

choices.text: Report the average of the two figures with a note describing the variance.
Hold both papers back from synthesis until a human adjudicates.
Re-run the analysis with instructions to prefer the more recent paper.
Include both values, annotated with source and methodology, and let the coordinator decide reconciliation.

questions.explanation: Conflicting values from credible sources are completed analysis, not noise: include both, annotated with source and methodology, and let the coordinator decide reconciliation before synthesis. A invents a number no source reported, however carefully footnoted. B stalls the pipeline where annotation suffices. C encodes an arbitrary tiebreak (recency) as truth.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: The synthesis agent regularly misdates events and attributes findings to the wrong methodology. Upstream, the analysis agent's outputs are well-written prose summaries. What structural requirement fixes this?

choices.text: Give the synthesis agent web search access to verify dates itself.
Require the analysis agent to attach metadata — dates, source locations, methodology — to every structured finding.
Have the synthesis agent flag any date it is unsure about.
Use a stronger model for synthesis so it infers metadata more accurately.

questions.explanation: Synthesis can only be as accurate as its inputs; requiring structured outputs with metadata — dates, source locations, methodological context — on every finding removes the inference that produces the misdating. A sends synthesis hunting for facts upstream already had. C flags the symptom. D asks a better model to guess better.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: Your synthesis agent's context budget is small, and upstream agents currently send it full document excerpts plus their complete reasoning narratives. Synthesis truncates and quality collapses on large topics. What is the recommended change?

choices.text: Rotate synthesis across three agents, each taking a third of the material.
Raise the synthesis agent's budget and accept the cost.
Have synthesis summarize its input first, then synthesize the summary.
Have upstream agents return structured key facts, citations, and relevance scores sized for the consumer.

questions.explanation: When the downstream consumer's budget is limited, change what upstream produces: structured key facts, citations, and relevance scores instead of excerpts plus reasoning narratives. Refine and verify the prompt on a representative sample via the synchronous API first.

questions.explanation: With a fixed budget, first-pass success is everything: refine the prompt on a representative sample synchronously, verify, then submit the batch. A spends the budget discovering flaws at full scale. B tweaks a parameter instead of validating the prompt. C still burns half the budget on the unvalidated version.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Your extraction step ends with "double-check your extraction against the document" — and reports itself accurate. Auditors keep finding wrong values the self-check approved. What is the structural lesson?

choices.text: The self-check needs a rubric listing common error types.
The self-check should run twice, with disagreements escalated.
Verification should run as an independent instance, comparing output to source without the extractor's context.
Self-checks work if you also request a confidence score.

questions.explanation: A model verifying its own extraction retains the reasoning that produced the errors — self-checks approve their own mistakes. Verification must be an independent instance comparing output to source without the extractor's context. A gives the biased checker a rubric. B repeats the biased check. D scores it.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)

questions.prompt: Your dashboard proudly shows 96% extraction accuracy. An operations manager mentions that handwritten intake forms "seem to always be wrong." You segment the data: typed forms 99%, handwritten 61%. What is the lesson?

choices.text: Handwritten forms should be excluded from the accuracy metric.
Aggregate metrics mask segment failures — validate accuracy by document type and field before it justifies decisions.
The dashboard should show median accuracy instead of mean.
96% is accurate as an overall number, so no process change is needed.

questions.explanation: 96% aggregate coexisting with 61% on handwritten forms is exactly how aggregate metrics mask segment failures: validate by document type and field before the number justifies anything, and remediate the failing segment. A hides the problem from the metric. C changes the statistic, not the blindness. D accepts a segment that's wrong 4 times in 10.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. questions.prompt: After automating high-confidence extractions, you need an ongoing mechanism to catch error patterns the confidence model doesn't know about yet. What is it?

choices.text: Quarterly re-validation against the original benchmark set.
Alerting when confidence scores drift statistically.
Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions for continuous human review.
A user-facing "report an error" button on downstream systems.

questions.explanation: Novel error patterns in the automated stream are caught by stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions with ongoing human review — measuring true error rates where no one otherwise looks. A can't contain patterns that didn't exist at benchmark time. B watches the scores, not the truth. D makes customers the QA layer.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. questions.prompt: The model emits per-field confidence scores, and you plan to auto-accept above a threshold. A colleague proposes 0.9 "because it's high." What is the defensible way to choose?

choices.text: Calibrate against a labeled validation set: measure accuracy at each score level and set thresholds where it meets the requirement.
Adopt 0.9 but review the first month's auto-accepts.
Pick 0.95, splitting the difference between the proposal and maximum caution.
Average the last quarter's scores and use that as the threshold.

questions.explanation: Thresholds come from calibration: measure actual accuracy at each confidence level against labeled data, and set the cutoff (per field type if performance differs) where accuracy meets requirements. B and C are round numbers with different amounts of caution — neither is a measurement. D averages scores into a threshold with no connection to accuracy. --- *End of Practice Exam 10.*

In the repository's project-level `CLAUDE.md`.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)

A slash command developers invoke before changing controllers.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.

Add the issue permanently to user-level memory.
Provide the failing input, the current output, the exact expected output, and the relevant regression test.

questions.explanation: A concrete failing input, observed output, expected output, and regression test give Claude an exact correction target and preserve the fix. More effort without evidence and permanent memory do not clarify the transformation.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)

Put “use best practices” in `CLAUDE.md` and start direct execution.
Ask multiple agents to implement alternatives before clarifying acceptance criteria.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)

Add every issue to `CLAUDE.md` so later sessions can decide the order.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)

Copy only the last assistant response into a new conversation.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code (Questions 1–15)

Start fresh with a structured summary of durable conclusions, identify changed areas, and re-read the affected files.
Discard both the durable conclusions and all repository context.

questions.explanation: Major file changes make old tool results stale, so a fresh session seeded with durable conclusions and targeted re-reading is safer than resuming or forking stale evidence. Discarding durable architecture facts is unnecessary.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)

MCP resources, rather than tools, select which server becomes active.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)

Put the token in a project slash command.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.

questions.explanation: Existing maintained servers are preferred for standard integrations; custom work is warranted for team-specific contracts or behavior not otherwise available. Scope and authentication do not by themselves require a custom server.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.

Randomize between the tools and compare outputs later.
Force both tools on every item.

questions.explanation: Source-specific names and contracts move the distinction into the interface the model selects. Warnings, randomness, and always calling both do not remove overlapping semantics.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.

Keyword-sensitive prompt instructions that override or bias normal tool selection.
Whether the tools appear in different MCP servers.
Whether the response token limit is high enough.

questions.explanation: System-prompt wording can create keyword associations that overpower good descriptions. Property ordering, server placement, and response length do not explain the mandated archive preference.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.

`isError` plus a transient category, retryability, attempted operation, safe description, and suggested next action.
Only the provider's raw stack trace.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
