One large prompt for both to avoid coordination overhead.
A fixed chain for both so the step count is predictable and auditability takes priority over evidence discovered during the investigation.
A fixed chain for the repeatable control review and dynamic decomposition for the investigation.

questions.explanation: Known repeatable stages suit a fixed chain, while evidence-driven incident work needs adaptive decomposition. One decomposition style is not optimal for both predictable and open-ended work.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: The request is “add comprehensive tests to this unknown legacy service.” What should the coordinator do first?

choices.text: Generate one test file for every source file immediately.
Map the service, identify high-impact behavior and dependencies, then create subtasks that adapt to what the map reveals.
Apply the same fixed list of unit-test prompts used for every repository and rerun it unchanged whenever a test exposes a new dependency.
Delegate only to a test-writer and prohibit further exploration.

questions.explanation: An unknown legacy system must first be mapped so high-impact behavior and dependencies can drive the testing plan. Immediate file-by-file generation is a fixed guess and can miss integration risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A simple factual query needs one authoritative source, but the coordinator always invokes search, document analysis, statistics, synthesis, and report agents. What is the best change?

choices.text: Keep the pipeline but shorten every agent's response so latency and cost remain predictable for every query.
Cache every specialist's last answer.
Let the coordinator select only the specialists justified by the query and intermediate findings.
Replace all specialists with one unrestricted agent.

questions.explanation: The coordinator should scale delegation to query complexity and what is discovered. Making an unnecessary full pipeline cheaper or caching irrelevant work does not remove it.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A broad market study omits regional regulation because the coordinator decomposed it only by product feature. How should decomposition be improved?

choices.text: Partition the full scope across complementary dimensions or source types, then verify coverage before synthesis.
Ask the synthesis agent to invent a regulatory section from general knowledge and label it as an informed architectural estimate.
Make every existing subtask longer without changing scope.
Remove the coverage requirement to match the available research.

questions.explanation: Broad work needs complementary scope partitioning and a coverage check so no major dimension vanishes. Longer reports cannot recover an unassigned region, and synthesis must not fabricate it.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: An open-ended performance investigation has not yet established which component is slow. What is the strongest initial subtask?

choices.text: Rewrite the database layer because it is commonly slow, even if later measurements implicate a different component.
Ask every specialist to optimize its favorite component.
Measure and map the request path first, then generate prioritized subtasks from the observed bottlenecks.
Execute a fixed sequence of generic optimizations.

questions.explanation: Measurement and mapping identify actual bottlenecks, after which subtasks can adapt to evidence. Generic or preference-based optimization starts with unsupported assumptions.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: Forty files need the same predictable local checklist, followed by one cross-file compatibility review. Which decomposition best preserves depth?

choices.text: Run focused per-file passes and then a separate integration pass.
Use an open-ended dynamic investigation for every file even though the stages are known.
Put all files in one prompt and ask Claude to divide attention evenly.
Skip the integration pass because every local result passed.

questions.explanation: Predictable local checks benefit from focused per-file passes, and a separate integration pass catches cross-file behavior. One mega-prompt dilutes attention, while skipping integration leaves an explicit gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A dependency audit discovers midway that two services share a generated client, invalidating several planned subtasks. What should the coordinator do?

choices.text: Finish the original task list before acknowledging the dependency so the plan remains comparable with prior audit runs and reports.
Revise the plan and generate replacement subtasks that account for the shared client.
Restart the entire investigation without preserving valid findings.
Hide the discovery from specialists so assignments remain stable.

questions.explanation: Adaptive plans change when a newly discovered dependency invalidates prior assumptions, preserving still-valid findings while replacing affected work. Blind completion and wholesale restart are both wasteful.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: Which coordinator behavior most clearly distinguishes adaptive decomposition from a fixed workflow?

choices.text: It uses the same specialists in a different order each run while preserving the predefined task list and completion conditions.
It runs all predefined steps in parallel.
It asks for longer reports when evidence is thin.
It creates or revises subtasks in response to intermediate discoveries and remaining coverage gaps.

questions.explanation: Creating and revising subtasks from intermediate findings is the defining adaptive behavior. Reordering or parallelizing a fixed list does not change what work is generated.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: Initial synthesis is strong but lacks evidence for one geography. What should an iterative coordinator do?

choices.text: Identify the gap, delegate a targeted follow-up search, then resynthesize with the new evidence.
Add a generic disclaimer and stop despite the recoverable gap.
Restart every completed subtask from scratch.
Ask the synthesis agent to fill the section without sources and cite the originally assigned material despite its missing geographic coverage.

questions.explanation: Iterative orchestration evaluates synthesis, identifies a specific gap, commissions targeted evidence, and resynthesizes. Disclaiming or inventing content skips a recoverable refinement step.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A specialist repeatedly maps “active users” to total registered accounts. Which feedback is most useful?

choices.text: Tell it to think harder about metrics.
Raise the maximum output length.
Replace the agent without describing the observed failure and ask the replacement to infer the intended definition from previous reports.
Provide representative inputs, the incorrect mappings, the desired mappings, and a precise definition of “active.”

questions.explanation: Examples of the failure and desired mapping plus an exact definition teach the disputed boundary. Generic effort, length, or agent replacement supplies no corrective evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: Three findings arise from the same mistaken date-window assumption and will interact if fixed separately. How should the coordinator request refinement?

choices.text: Send each issue in isolation and withhold the shared assumption so every specialist can optimize its correction independently.
Batch the related issues in one detailed request that explains their common dependency.
Fix only the easiest finding and ignore the rest.
Add the errors to permanent user memory.

questions.explanation: Related failures caused by one assumption should be evaluated together so the fix is coherent. Isolating them hides the interaction; permanent memory is not an issue tracker.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: You resume a research session after editing three previously analyzed parsers. Most other context remains valid. What should you tell the agent?

choices.text: Nothing; resumption automatically detects every filesystem change.
Re-read the entire repository because targeted recovery is impossible.
Name the changed files and request targeted re-analysis while retaining unaffected findings.
Trust the old parser outputs because named resumption snapshots the current filesystem before the next answer.

questions.explanation: A resumed agent must be told what changed so it can refresh affected evidence without repeating valid exploration. Session history does not automatically know filesystem changes.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: You want two independent research strategies to begin from the same accepted source map without contaminating one another. What mechanism fits?

choices.text: Resume the same session in two terminals.
Copy only the user prompt into two blank sessions.
Run both strategies sequentially in one conversation.
Use `fork_session` to branch from the shared baseline.

questions.explanation: `fork_session` preserves the accepted baseline while isolating divergent reasoning. Concurrent resume shares the same branch, blank sessions lose context, and sequential work contaminates the comparison.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A research agent has `search_news` and `search_academic`, but the latter is almost never chosen even for peer-reviewed-evidence requests. What should its description add?

choices.text: A promise that it is always better than every other tool and an instruction to prefer it whenever the user requests credible evidence.
Its indexed sources, accepted query/date inputs, output metadata, example academic requests, and explicit contrast with news search.
Internal implementation details unrelated to selection.
A requirement that both tools run for every query.

questions.explanation: Selection improves when the academic tool says what it indexes, how to query it, what it returns, and when it wins over news search. Boasts, implementation trivia, and mandatory dual calls are not useful boundaries.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A search specialist sees a transient timeout that succeeds on a safe local retry. What error-handling structure best protects coordinator context?

choices.text: Let the specialist recover locally; propagate only unresolved failure context, attempts, and partial results.
Propagate every first failure immediately, let the coordinator retry it, and preserve a full transcript of every attempt in the main context.
Hide all failures, including permanent ones, from the coordinator.
Terminate every subagent when any tool reports an error.

questions.explanation: Specialists should recover locally from safe transient failures and spare coordinator context; unresolved errors should include attempts and usable partial results. Immediate propagation and total suppression are both brittle.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: Invoice extraction works on the layout used in the prompt but fails when totals appear in tables, footnotes, or sidebars. What is the strongest improvement?

choices.text: Make every field required so Claude searches harder.
Retry the same prompt until one run succeeds.
Add varied few-shot examples with correct outputs and explicit normalization guidance while retaining the structured schema.
Replace tool use with free-form prose and require downstream code to parse whichever layout-specific explanation the model returns.

questions.explanation: Diverse positive examples teach field-location patterns across layouts, while normalization guidance and schema enforcement preserve consistency. Repeated identical prompts and required fields do not teach layout variation.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: Dates appear as `03/04/26`, `4 March 2026`, and `2026-03-04`, while downstream systems require ISO 8601. What should accompany the schema?

choices.text: Explicit normalization instructions, including how to represent genuinely ambiguous dates rather than guessing.
Copy all date strings unchanged, then require downstream systems to infer locale from the customer account and vendor country.
A higher confidence threshold with no format rule.
A retry policy that omits the original date.

questions.explanation: The prompt must state the canonical format and define what to do when source notation is ambiguous. Confidence alone cannot decide day/month order, and silent guessing corrupts data.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: Some contracts legitimately contain no renewal date. The current required string field causes invented dates. What is the best correction?

choices.text: Keep the field required, add “do not hallucinate,” and reject any fabricated date through downstream validation in every run.
Make the field optional or nullable and instruct the model to use null when the source is silent.
Reject every contract without a renewal date.
Derive a date from the contract's signing date.

questions.explanation: Optional or nullable fields faithfully represent genuine absence and remove pressure to fabricate. Rejection or derivation invents a business rule the source does not support.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: Résumé extraction works for conventional corporate résumés but misses existing education and publication fields on academic CVs. Which change is most likely to generalize?

choices.text: Add a rule for the exact CV that failed and a growing exception for every new university template.
Force missing fields to empty strings.
Increase temperature so the model explores more sections.
Add representative examples showing the same target fields across corporate, academic, and international layouts.

questions.explanation: Representative layout diversity teaches transferable extraction behavior across document families. A one-off rule overfits, and temperature or forced empty strings do not locate existing information.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: A scanned form omitted the page containing the requested identifier. Validation fails on every retry. What should the system do?

choices.text: Recognize that the information is absent, stop model retries, and route to rescanning, null handling, or review.
Retry indefinitely with stronger wording.
Ask Claude to infer the identifier from neighboring records and label it model-generated so downstream teams know it was not scanned.
Mark the extraction successful with a fabricated placeholder.

questions.explanation: Retries cannot recover content missing from the source, so the system must stop and choose an operational path such as rescanning, null, or review. Guessing and indefinite retries manufacture confidence without evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: An extraction is schema-valid but fails a business check because line-item totals do not equal the stated subtotal. What should a corrective follow-up include?

choices.text: Only the phrase “try again.”
Provide only the failed subtotal and a generic instruction to change whichever value appears least plausible.
The original document, failed extraction, and specific validation discrepancy.
A random alternative subtotal that passes validation.

questions.explanation: Corrective retries need the evidence, failed candidate, and exact validation error so the model can repair the semantic defect. A vague retry or invented value cannot ground the correction.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: Tool use guarantees that output conforms to the JSON schema, but customer names are occasionally placed in the vendor field. What does this demonstrate?

choices.text: Strict schemas eliminate both syntax and semantic extraction errors.
Semantic validation and representative examples are still needed after structural compliance.
The schema should be removed because it caused the field swap.
A larger output token limit will correct field meaning.

questions.explanation: A schema guarantees shape, not that evidence was mapped to the correct field. Semantic validators and examples still define meaning and catch swaps.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: Payment methods are represented by a fixed enum, but valid new methods appear regularly. How should the schema avoid forced misclassification?

choices.text: Include an `other` value with a detail field, and an `unclear` representation when the source is ambiguous.
Map every unfamiliar method to the closest existing category and update a hard-coded category list every quarter.
Reject every document containing an unfamiliar value.
Replace the entire structured response with prose.

questions.explanation: `other` plus detail preserves novel valid values, while `unclear` represents ambiguity without guessing. Nearest-category mapping and rejection both lose source truth.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: A document has clear header fields but an illegible handwritten approval box. Routing is currently based on one document-level confidence average. What is better?

choices.text: Randomly review ten percent of documents regardless of field quality.
Review every document and require the reviewer to re-enter all header fields as well as interpret the approval box.
Accept every document whose average confidence exceeds 0.9.
Route based on field-level confidence, field risk, and the handwritten ambiguity while allowing clear fields to proceed.

questions.explanation: Field-level routing isolates the ambiguous, risky approval box while preserving clear header extraction. A document average can hide critical field uncertainty, and blanket or random review wastes effort.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: The team proposes auto-accepting fields above confidence 0.92 because the number “sounds safe.” How should the threshold be selected?

choices.text: Use 0.99 for every field without testing.
Average the confidence values produced last week.
Calibrate scores against labeled outcomes by field and document segment, then choose thresholds that meet the required accuracy.
Let each model response choose its own threshold without calibration and store that number for downstream systems to trust.

questions.explanation: Confidence scores become actionable only after calibration against labeled outcomes at the relevant field and segment. An intuitive number has no demonstrated relationship to accuracy.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: High-confidence extractions now bypass normal human review. How can the team detect new error patterns that the confidence model does not recognize?

choices.text: Review only low-confidence failures.
Continuously review a stratified random sample of auto-accepted outputs.
Trust the original benchmark indefinitely.
Retry a random sample without human labels and treat agreement between the two runs as proof that the original was correct.

questions.explanation: Stratified sampling of auto-accepted output detects blind spots and distribution drift that confidence alone misses. Reviewing only known failures cannot reveal unknown high-confidence errors.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: Which review policy best uses document characteristics and ambiguity?

choices.text: Route every hundredth document to a random reviewer.
Review every field in low-confidence documents with one generalist, even when only a single field is ambiguous.
Assign reviewers by arrival order to keep routing simple.
Route uncertain or high-risk fields to reviewers with relevant expertise, using confidence and source characteristics as signals.

questions.explanation: Effective routing combines ambiguity, field risk, source characteristics, and reviewer expertise. Random or aggregate-only routing ignores where uncertainty actually resides.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: The model confuses `extract_invoice` and `extract_purchase_order` when both documents contain totals and vendor names. What is the best tool-interface improvement?

choices.text: Give each tool explicit document cues, unique outputs, boundary examples, and guidance for distinguishing the two formats.
Force invoice extraction for every financial document.
Rename both tools to shorter generic names.
Ask downstream code to infer document type from whichever fields happen to be populated most often during every extraction.

questions.explanation: Similar document tools need explicit discriminators, examples, and distinct output contracts. Forced defaults, generic names, and downstream guessing leave the selection ambiguity intact.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: A refund extraction requests an amount prohibited by policy. Retrying cannot change the policy result. What should the tool surface?

choices.text: A transient retryable error with unlimited attempts so temporary and permanent policy outcomes share one recovery path.
A successful empty response.
A structured non-retryable business error with a customer-safe explanation and permitted next action.
Only an internal policy stack trace.

questions.explanation: A policy violation is a non-retryable business outcome and should include a safe explanation and allowed alternative. Treating it as transient wastes calls; empty success conceals the reason.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction service handles invoices, contracts, résumés, and scanned forms. A strict schema is already available, but accuracy varies across layouts and operational edge cases.
questions.prompt: An extraction tool cannot open a restricted document collection. Which response gives the agent the clearest recovery path?

choices.text: A generic “operation failed” message.
A structured permission error marked non-retryable without changed access, with a suggestion to request access or escalate.
A valid empty extraction object.
A transient category that retries until the same restricted collection has failed a fixed number of times before escalation.

questions.explanation: A typed permission error tells the agent that retries will not help until access changes and provides a concrete escalation path. Generic, empty, or transient responses drive the wrong behavior. *End of Practice Exam 13.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: A customer says, “My replacement never arrived, and now the original card was charged again.” Identity is already verified, and the shipment and charge investigations are independent until the final response. What should the coordinator do?

choices.text: Run a fixed shipping-only workflow because the first concern determines the case type, then open billing only after shipping closes.
Create separate shipment and billing subtasks, run them concurrently, then synthesize one case resolution.
Escalate immediately because any multi-concern request exceeds autonomous scope.
Let two agents respond directly to the customer without coordinator synthesis.

questions.explanation: Independent concerns can be investigated in parallel after their shared prerequisite, while coordinator synthesis preserves one coherent customer resolution. Serializing or escalating by default wastes capability; direct specialist replies fragment the case.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: Address changes always require verify identity → validate new address → update account. Account-takeover reports branch according to device, login, and payment evidence discovered during investigation. Which decomposition is best?

choices.text: Use dynamic decomposition for both because customer state can always change and newly discovered evidence can always expand scope.
Run both workflows as one unrestricted prompt.
Use one fixed pipeline for both so auditing is simpler.
Use a fixed chain for address changes and adaptive decomposition for takeover investigations.

questions.explanation: Predictable address changes suit a fixed prerequisite chain, whereas takeover investigations must branch as evidence changes. Using one decomposition style for both ignores the difference between known stages and open-ended discovery.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: A fraud investigation discovers that the disputed transaction belongs to a second customer profile sharing the same email domain. What should happen to the existing investigation plan?

choices.text: Add a targeted identity-linkage subtask and revise dependent work while preserving unaffected findings.
Complete every original subtask before considering the new profile.
Restart the case from an empty context and discard verified evidence.
Ignore the second profile because it was not in the initial plan and preserve the original timeline for audit consistency.

questions.explanation: Adaptive orchestration incorporates the new identity evidence by adding focused work and updating only dependent tasks. Blindly completing the original plan or discarding verified evidence is not responsive decomposition.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: The agent must investigate “why refund completion times rose this month,” but the cause could be policy, provider latency, regional routing, or case mix. What is the strongest first step?

choices.text: Ask the payment specialist to optimize retries immediately.
Run the same fixed refund checklist used for individual customers.
Map the process and relevant metrics, then generate prioritized subtasks from the observed contributors.
Assign one specialist to write a final explanation before gathering evidence, then ask the other specialists to support that conclusion.

questions.explanation: An unknown systemic cause requires mapping and measurement before subtasks can target observed contributors. Immediate optimization and individual-case checklists assume the answer before gathering evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: `lookup_order` receives an identifier with an invalid checksum. Retrying unchanged cannot succeed, but the customer can correct the value. What error should the tool return?

choices.text: A transient error with exponential backoff that keeps resending the identical invalid identifier until a retry succeeds.
A successful empty result.
A permission error requiring supervisor access.
A structured validation error marked non-retryable until input changes, including the required format.

questions.explanation: The identifier is invalid input, so the tool should state a validation category, explain the accepted format, and avoid retry until the input changes. Empty success and unrelated error categories lead to incorrect recovery.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: The shipping provider times out once, and the lookup is safe to repeat. Where should the first recovery attempt occur?

choices.text: In a human escalation queue before any retry.
Locally in the specialist, with only unresolved failure context propagated to the coordinator.
In the final response by asking the customer to try again later without exposing internal provider details.
In every other specialist so one of them may reach the provider.

questions.explanation: A safe transient retry belongs near the failure in the specialist, protecting coordinator context from routine recovery. Escalation and cross-specialist retries add cost without improving the first recovery path.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: A refund specialist successfully verifies identity and policy eligibility but cannot reach the payment provider after safe retries. What should it return to the coordinator?

choices.text: Only “refund failed.”
A false success so the case can continue.
The verified partial results, attempted actions, typed transient failure, retry status, and available next steps.
The entire raw provider log, including headers and internal identifiers, with no summary of what remains recoverable.

questions.explanation: Structured partial results and failure metadata let the coordinator preserve completed checks and decide between retry, escalation, or an alternative. Generic text, false success, and raw logs remove operational meaning.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: The agent swaps `get_customer_profile` and `get_customer_authorizations` because both descriptions say “gets customer information.” What should be changed first?

choices.text: Give each description distinct use cases, identifiers, output fields, examples, and explicit guidance about when to use the other tool.
Force both calls for every customer request.
Add more customer tools so Claude has additional choices.
Route by a growing hard-coded list of words such as “customer,” “profile,” and “authorization,” then revise it after each misroute.

questions.explanation: Distinct purposes, identifiers, outputs, examples, and boundaries give the model the selection evidence it lacks. Forced dual calls, extra tools, and keyword routing do not clarify the interface.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: A generic `modify_account(action, value)` tool can change contact details, disable MFA, or close the account. The wrong mode has caused destructive calls. What redesign most directly improves reliability?

choices.text: Keep the generic tool but make the action enum longer.
Split sensitive operations into purpose-specific tools with separate contracts and permissions.
Add “be careful” to the coordinator prompt.
Require the generic tool to run twice and compare its own arguments.

questions.explanation: Purpose-specific tools make destructive intent explicit and allow separate permissions and contracts. More modes retain the ambiguous high-risk interface, while prompt warnings remain probabilistic.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: Most fields on a refund claim are clear, but the claimed amount is handwritten, low-confidence, and financially consequential. What review routing is best?

choices.text: Accept the whole claim because its average confidence is high and treat that average as proof no individual field needs attention.
Send a random unrelated field for review to preserve sampling.
Route the amount field to a qualified reviewer while allowing unambiguous low-risk fields to continue.
Reject the whole claim automatically because handwriting appears anywhere.

questions.explanation: Review should follow field-level uncertainty and consequence, so the ambiguous amount receives human attention without discarding clear data. Averages and random sampling are not sufficient for a known high-risk ambiguity.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: Warranty photos require visual-damage expertise, while ambiguous policy exceptions require a policy specialist. How should reviewer assignment work?

choices.text: Route by the uncertain field's characteristics and required expertise, not by reviewer availability alone.
Send both types to the same randomly selected reviewer.
Route only according to whole-document confidence.
Let the model choose a reviewer from an unvalidated self-confidence score and accept whichever specialty it predicts.

questions.explanation: Document and field characteristics determine the expertise needed for efficient, accurate review. Random or aggregate-only routing ignores the type of judgment required.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: The model emits confidence 0.94 for extracted order numbers. Before using that value to skip human review, what is required?

choices.text: A prompt saying 0.94 means “very certain.”
A higher threshold chosen by intuition.
Agreement between two copies of the same response in one context.
Calibration against labeled outcomes for that field and relevant document types.

questions.explanation: A confidence value has no operational meaning until labeled outcomes establish its calibration for the relevant field and sources. Wording, intuition, and same-context agreement do not measure accuracy.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: The support MCP server is required for every teammate, but its OAuth client secret differs by environment. Which setup is correct?

choices.text: Put the server in one operator's `~/.claude.json`, share screenshots, and make each teammate reproduce it on every workstation.
Commit the client secret alongside the server command.
Commit the server definition in project `.mcp.json` and expand the secret from an environment variable.
Describe the server in `CLAUDE.md` without configuring it.

questions.explanation: Shared tooling belongs in project `.mcp.json`, while environment expansion keeps environment-specific secrets out of version control. User scope and documentation alone do not distribute a usable server.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: You resume a week-old customer case. The agreed refund amount and customer authorization remain valid, but order status and payment-provider state may have changed. How should state be restored?

choices.text: Trust every prior tool result because the session was named.
Preserve durable case facts, refresh volatile backend state, and tell the resumed agent what changed.
Discard the authorization and make the customer repeat identity verification without cause.
Fork the session and assume branching refreshes provider state while preserving every prior operational result.

questions.explanation: Durable agreements can remain in the resumed context, but volatile order and provider state must be refreshed, with changes made explicit. Naming or forking a session does not update external systems.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent (Questions 1–15)
questions.scenario_context: Your support agent handles billing, fulfillment, account access, and policy questions through MCP tools. It must adapt to ambiguous cases while keeping deterministic controls and clear human-review paths.
questions.prompt: A prior session mapped the support architecture, but the tool contracts and routing rules were substantially redesigned before work resumed. What is safest?

choices.text: Resume and prohibit all tool calls so stale schemas cannot fail.
Fork the old session, compare two branches that share the same stale contracts, and merge whichever branch fails less often.
Reuse old tool outputs because architectural intent is unchanged.
Start a fresh session with a structured summary of durable goals and re-analyze the changed contracts and routes.

questions.explanation: Redesigned contracts make old operational context unsafe; a fresh session seeded with durable goals and targeted re-analysis avoids stale tool assumptions. Resuming or forking preserves the stale interface evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Claude Code for CI/CD (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Your organization runs Claude Code in pull-request workflows and maintains shared conventions for a large monorepo. The configuration must load at the right time, and refinement must converge on observable criteria.
questions.prompt: All YAML workflow files scattered across the repository must follow a release-security convention, but ordinary code should not load it. What should you create?

choices.text: A `.claude/rules/` file with a `paths: ["**/.github/workflows/*.yml", "**/.github/workflows/*.yaml"]` scope.
A user-level `CLAUDE.md` on the CI maintainer's workstation, manually replicated in every workflow repository.
A manually invoked skill that developers may forget.
A root instruction that loads the convention for every file.

questions.explanation: Glob-scoped rules apply automatically to workflow files wherever they live without taxing ordinary code sessions. User memory is not shared, skills are opt-in, and root guidance loads too broadly.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Claude Code for CI/CD (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Your organization runs Claude Code in pull-request workflows and maintains shared conventions for a large monorepo. The configuration must load at the right time, and refinement must converge on observable criteria.
questions.prompt: Each package needs centrally maintained testing guidance plus its own language-specific conventions. Copying the shared text has caused drift. Which mechanism composes the relevant files without duplication?

choices.text: Put every standard in every package's `CLAUDE.md`.
Turn standards into MCP tools.
Use `@import` from package `CLAUDE.md` files to include the appropriate shared guidance.
Store the shared standards only in personal memory and ask every CI runner to copy the maintainer's setup.

questions.explanation: `@import` composes maintained standards into the packages that need them without copying. MCP tools and user memory do not replace repository instruction composition.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Claude Code for CI/CD (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Your organization runs Claude Code in pull-request workflows and maintains shared conventions for a large monorepo. The configuration must load at the right time, and refinement must converge on observable criteria.
questions.prompt: A `/release-audit` workflow is shared by the team, runs only on demand, produces verbose exploration, and must not write files. How should it be configured?

choices.text: As always-loaded root memory with a prose warning not to edit.
As a personal command with unrestricted tools.
As a path rule for every source file.
As a project skill using `context: fork` and read-only `allowed-tools`.

questions.explanation: A team-shared, on-demand workflow is a project skill; `context: fork` isolates verbose output, and `allowed-tools` structurally enforces read-only access. Always-loaded or personal mechanisms miss one or more requirements.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Claude Code for CI/CD (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Your organization runs Claude Code in pull-request workflows and maintains shared conventions for a large monorepo. The configuration must load at the right time, and refinement must converge on observable criteria.
questions.prompt: CI must never read `.env.production`, whether through Read, Grep, or Bash. The forbidden paths are stable and do not require business-state evaluation. What is the strongest primary control?

choices.text: A sentence in `CLAUDE.md` asking Claude not to inspect secrets.
Settings permission-deny rules covering the relevant tools and paths.
A PostToolUse hook that reports the leak after access.
An inline reminder in each pull request.

questions.explanation: Stable access prohibitions belong in settings permissions that cover every relevant tool and path. A PostToolUse hook reacts too late, and prompt reminders are not deterministic controls.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Claude Code for CI/CD (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Your organization runs Claude Code in pull-request workflows and maintains shared conventions for a large monorepo. The configuration must load at the right time, and refinement must converge on observable criteria.
questions.prompt: A release command is allowed only when the version matches the signed manifest currently produced by the build. Which mechanism should make the decision at execution time?

choices.text: A path-scoped formatting rule.
A project slash command with no validation.
A `PreToolUse` hook that compares the command arguments with the signed manifest and blocks mismatches.
A permanent reference to last week's manifest in `CLAUDE.md` that the release team updates manually for every build.

questions.explanation: This decision depends on current tool arguments and a live signed artifact, making `PreToolUse` the correct dynamic enforcement point. Static guidance or last week's state cannot prove the current version.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Claude Code for CI/CD (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Your organization runs Claude Code in pull-request workflows and maintains shared conventions for a large monorepo. The configuration must load at the right time, and refinement must converge on observable criteria.
questions.prompt: Review standards, fixture conventions, and required test commands apply to every CI invocation of Claude Code. Where should that recurring context live?

choices.text: In committed project `CLAUDE.md` guidance available to the CI session.
In a one-time inline prompt maintained separately in each workflow run.
In a developer's user-level command directory.
In the generated review JSON output.

questions.explanation: Recurring shared CI context belongs in committed project memory available to every invocation. Inline duplication drifts, user commands are personal, and output cannot configure the request that produced it.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Claude Code for CI/CD (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Your organization runs Claude Code in pull-request workflows and maintains shared conventions for a large monorepo. The configuration must load at the right time, and refinement must converge on observable criteria.
questions.prompt: A generated migration maps blank strings incorrectly. Which prompt addition communicates the desired transformation most effectively?

choices.text: “Handle blanks correctly in all circumstances.”
Two or three concrete input/output examples covering blank, null, and nonblank values.
A higher output token limit.
A request to use a more sophisticated design pattern and infer blank-value semantics from the surrounding code style.

questions.explanation: Concrete examples show exactly how blank, null, and ordinary inputs must transform. Vague wording and more tokens do not define the disputed boundary.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Claude Code for CI/CD (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Your organization runs Claude Code in pull-request workflows and maintains shared conventions for a large monorepo. The configuration must load at the right time, and refinement must converge on observable criteria.
questions.prompt: A parser fix repeatedly repairs one fixture while breaking another. What workflow best drives convergence?

choices.text: Ask Claude to remember previous behavior without tests and treat recent conversation history as the permanent regression archive.
Fix the newest failure and delete older fixtures.
Increase temperature between attempts.
Establish a regression suite first, then feed specific failing tests back during iteration.

questions.explanation: A regression suite preserves working cases, while specific failures drive each correction toward convergence. Deleting fixtures or varying temperature hides regressions rather than resolving them.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Claude Code for CI/CD (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Your organization runs Claude Code in pull-request workflows and maintains shared conventions for a large monorepo. The configuration must load at the right time, and refinement must converge on observable criteria.
questions.prompt: A new deployment queue requires decisions about retries, idempotency, ordering, and partial failure, but stakeholders have not specified them. What should happen before implementation?

choices.text: Use the interview pattern to surface and resolve those design choices.
Start coding the default behavior and document it afterward.
Ask Claude to infer every policy, including retries and idempotency, from analogous code elsewhere in the repository.
Run the formatter to reveal the missing requirements.

questions.explanation: The interview pattern surfaces unresolved product and reliability decisions before implementation. Code and formatting cannot decide stakeholder policy implicitly.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Claude Code for CI/CD (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Your organization runs Claude Code in pull-request workflows and maintains shared conventions for a large monorepo. The configuration must load at the right time, and refinement must converge on observable criteria.
questions.prompt: Four review findings all stem from the same incorrect assumption about generated files; two unrelated typos are also present. How should feedback be sequenced?

choices.text: Put all six in separate sessions so no context is shared, then resolve conflicting patches manually after every session completes.
Put all six in one message because issue relationships never matter.
Ignore the typos until the next release.
Batch the four interacting findings with their shared context, and handle the independent typos separately.

questions.explanation: Interacting findings should be evaluated together with their common assumption, while independent typos can be handled separately. Universal batching or universal isolation ignores dependency structure.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Claude Code for CI/CD (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Your organization runs Claude Code in pull-request workflows and maintains shared conventions for a large monorepo. The configuration must load at the right time, and refinement must converge on observable criteria.
questions.prompt: A CI investigation first needs every file matching `**/*contract-test*.ts`, regardless of content. What tool should locate the candidates?

choices.text: Grep.
Glob.
Read.
Edit.

questions.explanation: Glob finds candidate paths from filename patterns. Grep searches content, while Read and Edit are later operations.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Claude Code for CI/CD (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Your organization runs Claude Code in pull-request workflows and maintains shared conventions for a large monorepo. The configuration must load at the right time, and refinement must converge on observable criteria.
questions.prompt: After locating the contract tests, you need to find which ones call `seedRemoteAccount` and understand the surrounding setup. What is the efficient next move?

choices.text: Read every located test in full before searching.
Glob repeatedly using the function name as a filename until path patterns appear to cover every helper call.
Grep the candidates for the symbol, then Read only the matching files and relevant helpers.
Replace the helper and see which tests fail.

questions.explanation: Grep narrows the candidates by symbol usage, and targeted Read supplies only the relevant setup and helpers. Exhaustive reading consumes context before the discriminating search.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Claude Code for CI/CD (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Your organization runs Claude Code in pull-request workflows and maintains shared conventions for a large monorepo. The configuration must load at the right time, and refinement must converge on observable criteria.
questions.prompt: A review bot flags harmless log statements because its only example shows a real credential leak. How should few-shot prompting reduce these false positives?

choices.text: Remove examples and ask for high confidence.
Add many copies of the same credential-leak example, varying their wording and order so the set appears diverse.
Require every log statement to be reported.
Add varied positive and negative boundary examples showing sensitive values versus safe identifiers.

questions.explanation: Positive and near-miss negative examples teach the review boundary between real secret exposure and harmless identifiers. Repetition of one positive case cannot reduce the observed false-positive class.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Claude Code for CI/CD (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Your organization runs Claude Code in pull-request workflows and maintains shared conventions for a large monorepo. The configuration must load at the right time, and refinement must converge on observable criteria.
questions.prompt: Pull-request descriptions use dates, severity labels, and file paths in inconsistent formats, but the review schema expects normalized values. What should be added?

choices.text: Explicit normalization rules and examples for the accepted canonical forms.
More required fields without formatting guidance.
A random retry whenever formatting differs.
A prose-only output that downstream code normalizes by guessing and repairs after review comments have already been posted.

questions.explanation: Schemas define shape, while normalization rules and examples define canonical values across inconsistent source formats. More required fields and unguided retries do not establish formatting semantics.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Claude Code for CI/CD (Questions 16–30)
questions.scenario_context: Your organization runs Claude Code in pull-request workflows and maintains shared conventions for a large monorepo. The configuration must load at the right time, and refinement must converge on observable criteria.
questions.prompt: The review tool always emits schema-valid objects, but it sometimes labels test-only failures as production blockers. What additional control is needed?

choices.text: Remove the schema so the model can explain itself.
Force the same tool a second time.
Semantic criteria and validation that distinguish severity using observable impact.
A larger context window with no new examples or criteria.

questions.explanation: Structural validity does not decide severity; observable semantic criteria and validation must map impact to the correct label. Repeating the same tool or expanding context without criteria preserves the error.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your coordinator produces technical due-diligence reports using web, document, data, and synthesis specialists connected to several MCP servers.
questions.prompt: A routine request asks for one documented API limit, while a strategic report needs market, security, cost, and implementation analysis. How should orchestration differ?

choices.text: Both should invoke every specialist so reports are consistent.
Both should use a fixed one-agent workflow.
The coordinator should choose the minimum suitable path for the factual query and dynamically assemble broader specialists for the strategic report.
Escalate the factual query and reserve multi-agent work for requests that contain several explicit user questions before tool selection begins.

questions.explanation: Delegation should scale with task complexity and evidence needs: a direct authoritative lookup does not need a full research organization, while strategy work does. Always invoking all agents wastes cost and context.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your coordinator produces technical due-diligence reports using web, document, data, and synthesis specialists connected to several MCP servers.
questions.prompt: A global infrastructure study has repeatedly omitted smaller regions. What decomposition best protects coverage?

choices.text: Partition by complementary regions and evidence types, assign explicit coverage goals, and check the combined result for gaps.
Ask every agent to research the entire world independently.
Decompose only by the largest vendors because they have the most sources and assume their coverage represents smaller regions.
Make the final report longer without changing assignments.

questions.explanation: Complementary partitioning plus explicit coverage checks prevents small regions from disappearing. Duplicated whole-world assignments increase overlap, and longer synthesis cannot recover unassigned scope.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your coordinator produces technical due-diligence reports using web, document, data, and synthesis specialists connected to several MCP servers.
questions.prompt: A review of 80 modules requires the same security and performance checks on each, plus one architecture-wide dependency pass. Which pattern is most appropriate?

choices.text: One open-ended agent that reads all modules simultaneously while relying on a larger context window to preserve equal attention.
Fixed focused module passes followed by a separate cross-module integration review.
Dynamic task generation with no stable checklist.
Independent local passes with no final synthesis.

questions.explanation: Known repeated checks suit focused fixed passes, with a separate architecture review for interactions. One huge prompt dilutes attention, while local-only review misses cross-module behavior.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your coordinator produces technical due-diligence reports using web, document, data, and synthesis specialists connected to several MCP servers.
questions.prompt: Synthesis reveals that all cost estimates assume one deployment model, but a newly discovered regulatory rule requires a second model in two regions. What should the coordinator do?

choices.text: Preserve the original tasks unchanged for reproducibility.
Delete all completed research and restart globally.
Ask synthesis to estimate the second model without source work and mark the resulting regional costs as provisional.
Generate targeted regional and cost subtasks, then update affected synthesis while retaining unaffected findings.

questions.explanation: The new rule changes only part of the research, so targeted adaptive subtasks should refresh affected regions and estimates while preserving valid work. Blind completion, invention, and global restart are weaker.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your coordinator produces technical due-diligence reports using web, document, data, and synthesis specialists connected to several MCP servers.
questions.prompt: The whole team needs a stable internal-document MCP server after cloning the repository. Where should it be defined?

choices.text: In each person's `~/.claude.json` with manually copied settings.
In committed project `.mcp.json`.
In the coordinator's natural-language prompt.
In a user-level slash command.

questions.explanation: A required team server belongs in committed project `.mcp.json`. User configuration is personal, and prompts or commands do not establish MCP connections.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your coordinator produces technical due-diligence reports using web, document, data, and synthesis specialists connected to several MCP servers.
questions.prompt: The shared server requires a different token for each environment. How should authentication be represented in the committed definition?

choices.text: As an encrypted-looking literal token in `.mcp.json`.
As a token pasted into `CLAUDE.md` at session start.
As a value returned by an unrestricted MCP tool.
As environment-variable expansion resolved outside version control.

questions.explanation: Environment expansion lets one committed definition resolve credentials securely per environment. Literals, memory, and unrestricted credential-returning tools expose secrets.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your coordinator produces technical due-diligence reports using web, document, data, and synthesis specialists connected to several MCP servers.
questions.prompt: The research application connects to document, statistics, and news MCP servers. What happens during connection?

choices.text: Tools from all configured servers can be discovered and exposed together to the agent.
Only tools from the alphabetically first server are available.
Project scope disables every user-scoped server.
The coordinator must reconnect each time it changes specialists and cache that connection only for the current specialist turn.

questions.explanation: MCP clients discover configured servers' tools at connection time and can expose them simultaneously. No alphabetical, scope-exclusive, or per-specialist reconnection rule applies.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your coordinator produces technical due-diligence reports using web, document, data, and synthesis specialists connected to several MCP servers.
questions.prompt: Agents waste calls asking which datasets, reports, and schemas exist. What should the servers expose?

choices.text: A generic tool that guesses a dataset name.
Larger error messages listing every asset after a failed call.
MCP resources that catalog the available content and structures.
A PostToolUse hook that repeats every search.

questions.explanation: Resources provide stable catalogs and schemas without exploratory action calls. Guessing tools and failure messages make discovery indirect and wasteful.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your coordinator produces technical due-diligence reports using web, document, data, and synthesis specialists connected to several MCP servers.
questions.prompt: `query_metrics` and `search_reports` both accept text, and the model uses them interchangeably. Which description change matters most?

choices.text: Describe their implementation languages and deployment regions.
Shorten both descriptions so the model reads them faster and rely on names and server placement to imply the difference.
Give both the same examples to emphasize consistency.
State the distinct data sources, query formats, output shapes, boundaries, and example questions for each.

questions.explanation: The model needs source, query, output, and boundary distinctions plus examples to select reliably. Implementation trivia, shorter ambiguity, and identical examples do not differentiate the tools.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your coordinator produces technical due-diligence reports using web, document, data, and synthesis specialists connected to several MCP servers.
questions.prompt: A source-selection prompt says, “Whenever the user says current, always use web search,” causing live database metrics to be ignored. What is the best diagnosis?

choices.text: The system prompt creates an overly broad keyword association that should be revised alongside the tool contracts.
The database tool needs longer JSON property names and aliases ordered by data recency so the model notices it first.
MCP discovery cannot expose database and web tools together.
The model requires a random selection policy.

questions.explanation: The prompt's unconditional “current” keyword rule is overriding a valid tool distinction and should be narrowed. Server discovery and property naming do not explain the systematic bias.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your coordinator produces technical due-diligence reports using web, document, data, and synthesis specialists connected to several MCP servers.
questions.prompt: A generic `process_source(mode=search|extract|verify)` tool frequently receives the wrong mode. What interface change gives the model clearer decisions?

choices.text: Add more modes to cover edge cases.
Hide the mode field, ask downstream code to infer it from the original prompt, and preserve one generic permission boundary.
Split it into purpose-specific tools with separate schemas and permissions.
Force the generic tool on every turn.

questions.explanation: Purpose-specific names and schemas remove mode ambiguity and permit least-privilege permissions. Adding or hiding modes keeps the core selection risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your coordinator produces technical due-diligence reports using web, document, data, and synthesis specialists connected to several MCP servers.
questions.prompt: A statistics provider returns HTTP 503. What metadata most directly tells the agent whether another attempt is sensible?

choices.text: The provider's full HTML error page, requiring the agent to parse retry instructions from untrusted markup.
A transient error category, `isRetryable: true`, attempted operation, and suggested backoff.
A successful empty dataset.
A non-retryable business-rule category.

questions.explanation: A 503 is normally transient; explicit category, retryability, operation, and backoff tell the agent how to recover. Empty success and business-error labeling misrepresent the failure.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your coordinator produces technical due-diligence reports using web, document, data, and synthesis specialists connected to several MCP servers.
questions.prompt: A well-formed query legitimately finds no studies in the requested date range. How should that differ from access denial?

choices.text: Return a successful empty result for no matches; return a typed permission error for denied access.
Return the same generic error for both and ask the coordinator to distinguish it from ordinary conversational text.
Mark both as retryable because neither returned data.
Represent both as successful prose messages.

questions.explanation: Successful absence is valid data, while access denial is an operational permission error with a different recovery path. Treating them identically causes false conclusions or wasted retries.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your coordinator produces technical due-diligence reports using web, document, data, and synthesis specialists connected to several MCP servers.
questions.prompt: A named session has an accurate source taxonomy, and only two ingestion adapters changed. You want to continue the investigation. What should you do?

choices.text: Start blank, discard the source taxonomy, and rebuild it from public documentation before inspecting the changed adapters.
Resume without mentioning the adapters.
Fork solely to refresh filesystem state.
Resume the named session, identify the changed adapters, and request targeted re-analysis.

questions.explanation: Most context remains valid, so named resumption plus explicit changed-adapter re-analysis preserves work without trusting stale files. Forking is not a refresh mechanism.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System (Questions 31–45)
questions.scenario_context: Your coordinator produces technical due-diligence reports using web, document, data, and synthesis specialists connected to several MCP servers.
questions.prompt: Two teams want to compare incompatible synthesis architectures from the same accepted evidence map. Which session mechanism preserves the shared baseline and isolates later reasoning?

choices.text: Run both architectures sequentially in the same conversation.
Fork the session into independent branches.
Resume the same named session twice and allow concurrent edits.
Start two blank sessions with no evidence map.

questions.explanation: Forking creates independent branches from one accepted baseline, exactly matching the comparison need. Sequential work cross-contaminates reasoning, and blank sessions lose evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction platform handles procurement documents from many regions and vendors. It already uses tool schemas, but accuracy and reviewer efficiency vary across formats.
questions.prompt: Purchase-order numbers appear in page headers, table captions, and barcode-adjacent labels. The extractor handles only headers. What should you add first?

choices.text: Few-shot examples demonstrating the same field correctly extracted from each representative placement.
A requirement that every order number appear in the header, rejecting valid orders that use another source layout.
A retry that repeats the unchanged prompt.
A free-form answer instead of the existing schema.

questions.explanation: Representative examples teach the same field across multiple visual locations and generalize beyond one header layout. Requiring a nonexistent convention or repeating the same prompt does not add evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction platform handles procurement documents from many regions and vendors. It already uses tool schemas, but accuracy and reviewer efficiency vary across formats.
questions.prompt: Some source documents genuinely omit shipping terms. The current required string causes plausible invented terms. Which schema behavior is appropriate?

choices.text: Substitute the most common term for that vendor.
Reject every document with no term.
Keep the field required, ask the model to be honest, and make runtime validation responsible for detecting invention.
Allow null or omission and state that missing source information must not be invented.

questions.explanation: Nullable or optional representation accurately preserves genuine absence and removes pressure to fabricate. Defaults, rejection, and prose warnings retain or worsen the required-field problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction platform handles procurement documents from many regions and vendors. It already uses tool schemas, but accuracy and reviewer efficiency vary across formats.
questions.prompt: A contract-type enum does not include a newly encountered but valid category, and some scans are too degraded to classify at all. How should both cases be represented?

choices.text: Map both to the nearest known enum value even when the source distinguishes a novel category from unreadable evidence.
Remove the enum and accept arbitrary prose.
Use `other` plus a detail for the valid novel category, and `unclear` for genuinely ambiguous evidence.
Reject both documents.

questions.explanation: `other` with detail preserves a valid unforeseen category, while `unclear` preserves ambiguity. Conflating either with the nearest known class fabricates certainty.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction platform handles procurement documents from many regions and vendors. It already uses tool schemas, but accuracy and reviewer efficiency vary across formats.
questions.prompt: Validation says `subtotal + tax != total`. What should the self-correction request contain?

choices.text: Only the desired total value.
The source, failed extraction, and exact arithmetic validation error.
A new schema with all fields optional.
A demand to return different numbers without evidence and accept any values that happen to satisfy the schema.

questions.explanation: Semantic correction requires the source, failed candidate, and exact arithmetic discrepancy. Supplying an answer without evidence encourages a schema-valid but unsupported value.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction platform handles procurement documents from many regions and vendors. It already uses tool schemas, but accuracy and reviewer efficiency vary across formats.
questions.prompt: A requested signature is absent because the scan ends before the signature page. Which response is correct?

choices.text: Keep retrying with varied temperature and wording until the model supplies a signature-like value.
Infer the signer from the contract owner.
Stop extraction retries and route to rescanning, review, or a documented missing value.
Use a fabricated “signature present” default.

questions.explanation: Missing source content cannot be recovered by model retry; the pipeline must choose rescanning, review, or an explicit missing value. Inference and defaults fabricate evidence.
