questions.scenario_context: Your extraction platform handles procurement documents from many regions and vendors. It already uses tool schemas, but accuracy and reviewer efficiency vary across formats.
questions.prompt: Monetary values arrive as `$1,200.50`, `1.200,50 €`, and `1200.5 USD`. What should accompany the structured schema?

choices.text: Explicit currency and numeric normalization rules with examples and ambiguity handling.
A rule to discard currency information.
Higher temperature to encourage format creativity.
A random retry after every non-US format, treating the first US-style parse as the canonical baseline.

questions.explanation: Canonical numeric and currency rules plus examples define how each source form maps downstream and what to do when ambiguous. Temperature and retries do not define locale semantics.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction platform handles procurement documents from many regions and vendors. It already uses tool schemas, but accuracy and reviewer efficiency vary across formats.
questions.prompt: Documents arrive with unknown type, and one of several extraction tools must be called so downstream processing never receives conversational prose. Which configuration is most reliable?

choices.text: `tool_choice: "auto"` and a request to prefer tools.
Prefill an opening JSON brace in a text response, then parse and repair whichever document-specific fields follow in downstream code.
Force the invoice tool regardless of document type.
Use structured extraction tools and `tool_choice: "any"` so a tool call is guaranteed while Claude selects the matching schema.

questions.explanation: Tool schemas enforce structure, and `tool_choice: "any"` guarantees some extraction tool while leaving schema selection to Claude. Auto permits prose, while forcing one document type can select the wrong schema.

questions.prompt: The model flags every handwritten annotation as a fraud indicator, though most are harmless initials. Which few-shot set best sharpens the decision boundary?

choices.text: Ten examples of confirmed fraud annotations only.
Representative positive examples plus near-miss negative examples such as harmless initials and reviewer notes.
Use no examples, request conservative scoring, and discard every prediction that falls below a high intuitive confidence threshold.
One example with no explanation of the label.

questions.explanation: Positive and close negative examples sharpen the classification boundary that the extractor currently lacks. Positive-only repetition explains fraud but not why harmless initials are different.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction platform handles procurement documents from many regions and vendors. It already uses tool schemas, but accuracy and reviewer efficiency vary across formats.
questions.prompt: Bank-account fields are high risk, while optional marketing codes are low risk. Both have confidence 0.82. What should routing do?

choices.text: Apply field-specific risk and ambiguity thresholds, sending the bank field to review while allowing policy-defined handling for the low-risk code.
Treat equal confidence as equal operational risk, apply the same review threshold, and ignore field consequence, source ambiguity, or reviewer expertise during downstream decisions.
Average both fields into one document confidence.
Randomly choose one field for review.

questions.explanation: Equal model confidence does not imply equal operational risk; field-specific consequence and ambiguity should determine routing. Whole-document averages and random choice hide the dangerous field.

questions.prompt: Confidence thresholds were calibrated before adding new languages and a substantially revised prompt. What should happen before continued auto-acceptance?

choices.text: Keep the thresholds because the output schema did not change and assume field-level accuracy remains stable across languages.
Lower every threshold by the same amount.
Recalibrate on labeled data representing the new languages, prompt, fields, and document segments.
Ask the model whether its confidence remains accurate.

questions.explanation: Prompt and language changes alter the score-to-accuracy relationship, so thresholds require new labeled calibration across the changed distribution. Schema stability does not preserve calibration.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction platform handles procurement documents from many regions and vendors. It already uses tool schemas, but accuracy and reviewer efficiency vary across formats.
questions.prompt: What monitoring practice can reveal a new high-confidence error pattern after automation?

choices.text: Review only cases already rejected by validation.
Human-review a stratified sample of auto-accepted extractions and track error types over time.
Compare confidence scores without examining ground truth.
Rerun successful documents with the identical prompt, assume agreement means correctness, and use repeated agreement as the monitoring metric.

questions.explanation: Stratified human sampling of auto-accepted data supplies ground truth for unknown high-confidence failures and drift. Confidence agreement without labels cannot prove correctness.

questions.prompt: A single extraction change causes amount parsing, tax calculation, and currency labeling failures because all three share one normalization rule. How should refinement feedback be presented?

choices.text: Correct each symptom in isolated sessions without mentioning the shared rule, then reconcile inconsistent patches after all changes merge.
Fix only the first failing field and hope the others follow.
Add every failure permanently to `CLAUDE.md`.
Batch the interacting failures with the shared normalization context so one coherent fix can be evaluated.

questions.explanation: One shared normalization defect requires one consolidated evaluation of its interacting symptoms. Isolated fixes can conflict or repeatedly patch the same cause.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction platform handles procurement documents from many regions and vendors. It already uses tool schemas, but accuracy and reviewer efficiency vary across formats.
questions.prompt: The extractor mishandles a nested table only when a row contains both a null quantity and a discount. What feedback most directly guides correction?

choices.text: “Improve table support.”
A longer system prompt describing common table shapes generally while omitting the actual failing input and expected output.
The exact source fragment, failed output, expected output, and a regression case for that edge condition.
A higher maximum token count.

questions.explanation: The exact failing evidence, observed output, expected output, and regression case give a testable correction target. General wording and more tokens do not identify the compound edge condition.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction platform handles procurement documents from many regions and vendors. It already uses tool schemas, but accuracy and reviewer efficiency vary across formats.
questions.prompt: A personal prototype extraction server and a shared production server are both needed on one developer's machine. What setup preserves the intended scopes?

choices.text: Keep production in project `.mcp.json` with environment-based credentials and the prototype in user `~/.claude.json`; both can be discovered together.
Put both in project `.mcp.json`, ask teammates to ignore the prototype, and require each person to edit the file locally before use.
Put both in user scope so no configuration is committed.
Describe one server in `CLAUDE.md` instead of configuring it.

questions.explanation: Production remains shared through project scope and environment credentials, while the prototype remains personal; MCP discovery can expose both on that developer's machine. Putting either in the wrong scope violates the intended audience.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction (Questions 46–60)
questions.scenario_context: Your extraction platform handles procurement documents from many regions and vendors. It already uses tool schemas, but accuracy and reviewer efficiency vary across formats.
questions.prompt: You need to determine which parsers handle `.xlsx` files and then understand only their normalization paths. What is the best context-conscious exploration sequence?

choices.text: Read every parser and dependency before searching.
Glob for likely parser files, Grep for `.xlsx` handlers, then Read the matching code and relevant imports.
Grep generated output only and use recurring examples as a proxy for the current source implementation and normalization path.
Edit the first parser whose filename contains `excel`.

questions.explanation: Path matching narrows likely parsers, content search identifies actual `.xlsx` handling, and targeted Read follows only relevant normalization code. Exhaustive reading and filename guessing waste context or risk premature edits. *End of Practice Exam 14.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: An engineer implements the agentic loop so that it exits whenever the assistant's text contains phrases like "your issue is resolved" or "is there anything else." In production, the loop sometimes exits while the agent still intends to call `process_refund`, and other times keeps looping after the conversation is clearly finished. What is the correct loop termination design?

choices.text: Expand the phrase list to cover more terminal expressions and add fuzzy matching to catch paraphrases.
Continue the loop while `stop_reason` is `"tool_use"`, executing requested tools and returning results; terminate when `stop_reason` is `"end_turn"`.
Set a maximum of 10 iterations and terminate when the cap is reached, since most support cases complete in fewer turns.
Terminate whenever the response contains no text content, since a tool-only response indicates the agent is still working.

questions.explanation: The agentic loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it is `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Parsing natural-language signals (A) is exactly the anti-pattern producing the observed failures — text can look terminal while a tool call is pending. Iteration caps (C) are a safety backstop, not a primary stopping mechanism, and truncate legitimate long cases. D inverts the semantics: absence of text says nothing definitive about completion.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: Your agent calls `process_refund` and your code executes the refund successfully. What must happen next so the agent can correctly continue the conversation?

choices.text: Append the tool result to the conversation history as a `tool_result` block (referencing the `tool_use` ID) in a user-role message, then send the updated conversation back to Claude.
Store the refund confirmation in your application database and include a summary of all tool activity in the final response to the customer.
Inject the refund confirmation into the system prompt so it persists across all subsequent turns of the conversation.
Start a new conversation seeded with a summary of the prior turns plus the refund result, to keep context small.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended to the conversation history as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the whole conversation is sent back so the model can incorporate the result into its next reasoning step. B keeps the result away from the model entirely — it can't confirm the refund. C misuses the system prompt for turn-level data. D destroys conversational state mid-task and is unnecessary here.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: Your MCP tools come from different backend teams: `get_customer` returns ISO 8601 dates, `lookup_order` returns Unix timestamps, and order statuses are numeric codes in one tool but strings in another. The agent occasionally miscompares dates and misreads statuses when reasoning across tools. What is the most reliable fix?

choices.text: Add a system prompt section documenting each tool's formats and instructing the agent to convert values before comparing them.
Ask each backend team to migrate their APIs to a common format standard before the agent ships.
Add a validation step at the end of each conversation that checks the agent's final answer for date and status errors.
Implement a `PostToolUse` hook that normalizes timestamps, dates, and status codes into consistent formats before the model processes the tool results.

questions.explanation: A `PostToolUse` hook deterministically normalizes heterogeneous formats before the model ever sees them, removing the error class entirely. Prompt instructions (A) rely on probabilistic per-turn conversions and will still fail occasionally. B is organizationally impractical and out of your control. C detects errors after they've influenced the conversation instead of preventing them.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: Company policy requires human approval for any refund over $500. Your system prompt states this rule prominently, but production logs show that about 2% of refunds above $500 are still processed autonomously. What should you do?

choices.text: Move the rule to the very top of the system prompt and repeat it before the tool definitions to increase its salience.
Add few-shot examples showing the agent escalating refunds of $501, $750, and $1,200 to reinforce the boundary.
Implement a hook that intercepts `process_refund` calls, blocks any call with an amount above $500, and redirects the agent to the human escalation workflow.
Reduce the model temperature so the agent follows the system prompt instructions more deterministically.

questions.explanation: A business rule with financial consequences needs deterministic enforcement: intercept the tool call, block amounts over $500, and redirect to escalation. Prompt salience (A), few-shot examples (B), and temperature (D) all still rely on probabilistic compliance — the observed 2% failure rate is precisely why prompt-only enforcement is insufficient here.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: A customer writes one message reporting a damaged item, a duplicate charge on their card, and an address change for an upcoming shipment. The agent resolves the damaged item and ends the conversation without addressing the other two concerns. What is the best design change?

choices.text: Detect multi-issue messages with a classifier and ask the customer to submit each issue as a separate ticket.

Instruct the agent to decompose multi-concern messages into distinct items, investigate each (in parallel where possible) using the shared conversation context, and synthesize a unified resolution covering all items.
Route any message containing more than one concern directly to `escalate_to_human`, since multi-issue cases exceed single-agent capability.
Handle the concerns sequentially in separate sessions, one new session per concern, so each gets a clean context window.

questions.explanation: The recommended pattern is decomposing multi-concern requests into distinct items, investigating each in parallel with shared context, then synthesizing one unified resolution. A pushes work onto the customer. C escalates cases the agent could resolve, hurting first-contact resolution. D discards the shared context (customer identity, verification) that the concerns have in common.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: When the agent escalates a billing dispute to a human agent, the human team works in a separate system with no access to the AI conversation transcript. Human agents report spending 10+ minutes reconstructing each case. What should the escalation include?

choices.text: The complete raw conversation transcript exported as text, so the human can read everything the agent saw.
The customer ID and a link to open the customer's profile, keeping the handoff lightweight.
A sentiment analysis of the conversation so the human knows how frustrated the customer is.
A structured handoff summary containing the customer ID, root cause analysis, the disputed/refund amount, and a recommended action.

questions.explanation: Humans without transcript access need a structured handoff: customer ID, root cause analysis, amount, recommended action — everything needed to act immediately. A raw transcript (A) forces the human to reconstruct the case anyway, just from more text. B omits the case analysis entirely. C conveys mood, not the facts needed to resolve the dispute.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: You are deciding which agent behaviors need programmatic enforcement (hooks) versus system-prompt guidance. Which requirement is the strongest candidate for a hook rather than prompt instructions?

choices.text: The agent should maintain an empathetic, professional tone with frustrated customers.
Refunds must only ever be issued to the verified original payment method on the order.
The agent should keep responses concise and avoid unnecessary technical jargon.
The agent should offer troubleshooting alternatives before proposing a refund.

questions.explanation: "Refunds only to the verified original payment method" is a hard compliance rule where any violation has financial/fraud consequences — the case for programmatic enforcement (a hook gating `process_refund`). Tone (A), conciseness (C), and offering alternatives first (D) are behavioral guidance where occasional imperfection is acceptable, so prompt instructions are appropriate.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: A product manager proposes replacing the agent's reasoning with a fixed sequence — always call `get_customer`, then `lookup_order`, then either resolve or refund — arguing it will make behavior predictable. Why is model-driven tool selection the better fit for this workload?

choices.text: Support requests are high-ambiguity, so the appropriate tools and their order vary per case; a fixed sequence wastes calls on some cases and cannot adapt when intermediate results change what is needed.
Fixed sequences are not supported by the Claude Agent SDK, which requires the model to choose every tool call.
Model-driven selection is always cheaper because the model skips the reasoning tokens needed to follow a script.
Decision trees cannot invoke MCP tools, so the fixed sequence would only work with built-in tools.

questions.explanation: This workload is explicitly high-ambiguity: the right tools and their order genuinely vary per case, and intermediate results (e.g., what `lookup_order` reveals) change what should happen next — the core argument for model-driven decision-making. B is false; you can hardcode sequences around the SDK. C is false in general (and irrelevant). D is false — decision trees can call any tool; that's not the issue.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: Every failure from `process_refund` currently returns the same response: `"Operation failed"`. Logs show the agent retrying policy-violation failures repeatedly (which will never succeed) and giving up immediately on transient gateway timeouts (which would succeed on retry). What is the best fix?

choices.text: Wrap all tool calls in an automatic retry-3-times policy at the application layer so the agent never has to reason about retries.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to judge from conversation context whether a failure is likely to be retryable.
Return structured error responses that include an `errorCategory` (transient/validation/permission/business), an `isRetryable` boolean, and a human-readable description.
Increase the payment gateway timeout so transient failures become rare enough to ignore.

questions.explanation: Structured error metadata (`errorCategory`, `isRetryable`, description) gives the agent what it needs to retry transient failures and stop retrying non-retryable ones. Blanket retry (A) wastes calls on business errors and hides retry decisions from the agent. B asks the model to guess what the tool already knows. D reduces one error type's frequency without fixing the decision-making problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: A customer requests a refund for an order purchased 47 days ago; policy allows refunds within 30 days. What should `process_refund` return so the agent handles this well?

choices.text: An error with the MCP `isError` pattern containing a business-rule category, `retriable: false`, a customer-friendly explanation ("outside the 30-day return window — purchase was 47 days ago"), and a suggested alternative such as store credit.
A standard HTTP 400 status code with no body, letting the agent infer the cause from the request it sent.
A success response with an empty body, so the agent doesn't alarm the customer with error language.
An error containing the full server-side stack trace so the agent has maximum information to reason with.

questions.explanation: Business-rule violations should come back as structured errors with `retriable: false` and a customer-friendly explanation so the agent can communicate accurately and pivot to alternatives (store credit). B gives the agent nothing to reason with. C silently misrepresents a failure as success — the agent may tell the customer the refund happened. D leaks internals and buries the relevant fact (policy window) in noise.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). questions.prompt: When a customer has no orders on file, `lookup_order` currently returns an error, and the agent responds by apologizing for "technical difficulties" and retrying the lookup. What should change?

choices.text: Add a system prompt note explaining that this particular error usually means the customer has no orders.
Suppress the error in a hook and replace it with a message telling the agent to end the conversation.
Have the agent call `get_customer` again first, since the error may indicate a bad customer ID.
Return a successful response with an empty result set (and a note like "no orders found for this customer"), reserving errors for actual access failures.

questions.explanation: "No orders" is a valid empty result of a successful query, not a failure; conflating the two causes exactly the observed misbehavior (apologizing, retrying). Errors should be reserved for access failures. A patches the symptom with prompt text while the contract stays broken. B hides real signal behind a hook. C invents a spurious recovery path for a non-error.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. questions.prompt: Your tool descriptions are detailed and well-differentiated, yet the agent calls `lookup_order` even for general return-policy questions where no order is involved. You find this line in the system prompt: "Use lookup_order to help with any customer question about their purchases." What is the most likely fix?

choices.text: Rewrite the `lookup_order` description to explicitly say it should not be used for policy questions.
Add few-shot examples of policy questions being answered without tool calls.
Reword or remove the keyword-sensitive system prompt instruction, which is creating an unintended tool association that overrides the well-written descriptions.
Rename `lookup_order` to `lookup_order_by_id` so the model understands an ID is required.

questions.explanation: Keyword-sensitive system prompt instructions can create unintended tool associations that override even good tool descriptions — "any customer question about their purchases" is sweeping policy questions into `lookup_order`. A and D modify the tool when the tool isn't the problem. B adds token overhead to counteract an instruction you can simply fix at the source.

questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. questions.prompt: The support team wants to expand the agent from its current 4 tools to 18 by adding loyalty-program, marketing-preferences, subscription, and gift-card tools — all attached to the single resolution agent. What is the primary risk?

choices.text: The MCP protocol limits each server to 10 tools, so the configuration will fail at connection time.

Tool selection reliability degrades as the number of available tools grows, increasing decision complexity and misrouting; tools should be scoped to the agent's role or split across specialized agents.
The additional tool schemas will exceed the model's context window before any conversation begins.
The agent will slow down because it must call every available tool at least once per conversation.

questions.explanation: Growing from 4 to 18 tools on one agent increases decision complexity and degrades tool selection reliability. The fix is scoped tool access per role (or splitting into specialized agents). A and C describe nonexistent limits. D misdescribes how tool use works — agents don't call every available tool.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: Compliance requires that every conversation begin with a call to a `classify_request` tool before any other tool runs, with no exceptions. What is the most reliable implementation?

choices.text: State in the system prompt that `classify_request` is mandatory and must always come first.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the first request so the model is guaranteed to call a tool before responding.
Add few-shot examples showing `classify_request` being called first in several conversation types.
Set `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "classify_request"}` on the first API request, then use normal tool choice on subsequent turns.

questions.explanation: Forced tool selection (`tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "classify_request"}`) on the first request is the only option that *guarantees* that specific tool runs first; later turns then proceed normally. A and C are probabilistic. B (`"any"`) guarantees *some* tool call, but not which one — the agent could call `get_customer` first.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. questions.prompt: In long billing-dispute conversations, your context management summarizes older turns. After summarization, the agent starts misstating specifics — quoting "around $80" for a refund the customer was promised at exactly $83.47. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Extract transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers, statuses) into a persistent "case facts" block that is included in every prompt outside the summarized history.
Increase the summary length limit so the summarizer preserves more detail from older turns.
Re-run `lookup_order` and `get_customer` on every turn so fresh data is always in context.
Ask the customer to re-confirm key amounts whenever the conversation exceeds 20 turns.

questions.explanation: Extracting transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers, statuses) into a persistent case-facts block that rides outside the summarized history is the recommended defense against progressive summarization degrading precise values into vague ones ("around $80"). B only delays the loss. C works but adds cost and latency on every turn for data that isn't changing. D pushes the system's memory problem onto the customer.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.
questions.prompt: You maintain your team's coding standards in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on your machine. A new teammate clones the repository, but Claude Code ignores all of those standards for them. Why?

choices.text: The new teammate needs to run `/memory` once to activate memory files after cloning.
CLAUDE.md files require an explicit `@import` from the project root before they take effect.

`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is user-level configuration that applies only to your account and is not shared through version control; team standards belong in a project-level CLAUDE.md committed to the repository.
The standards file exceeds the size limit for automatic loading and is being silently truncated.

questions.explanation: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is user-level configuration: it applies to your account only and never travels through version control. Team-wide standards belong in a project-level CLAUDE.md committed to the repo. A misstates what `/memory` does (it inspects loaded memory; it doesn't "activate" anything). B — project CLAUDE.md loads without imports. D invents a failure mode.

The root CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines and every session loads all of it regardless of which package is being edited. Package maintainers know their own conventions best. What is the most maintainable structure?

Duplicate the full 900-line standards document into each package directory so every package is self-contained.
Keep the single root CLAUDE.md but add a table of contents so the model can navigate to the relevant section.
Move all standards into a wiki and add a CLAUDE.md instruction telling Claude to ask developers for conventions when unsure.

Run `/memory` to verify which memory files are actually loaded in the affected sessions.
Run `/compact` to clear stale context that may be overriding the conventions.
Delete and recreate the project CLAUDE.md to rule out file corruption.

questions.explanation: Inconsistent behavior across sessions is the classic symptom of different memory files being loaded in different sessions; `/memory` shows exactly which files are in effect, so diagnose before rewriting anything. Add `allowed-tools` frontmatter so the skill can only read files, reducing the volume of output it produces.
Add `context: fork` to the skill's frontmatter so it runs in an isolated sub-agent context and returns only a summary, keeping the verbose output out of the main conversation.

Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations, so Bash is unavailable during skill execution.
Convert the skill into a slash command, since commands cannot run tools.

Put both in CLAUDE.md so nothing depends on developers remembering to invoke a skill.
Put both in skills so the context cost is only paid when each is needed.
Put the conventions in a skill and the release-notes workflow in CLAUDE.md, since workflows need to be always available.

Spawn an Explore subagent to investigate the surrounding module first.
Use `fork_session` to try two candidate fixes in parallel branches.
Use direct execution — the change is simple, well-scoped, and the location is already known, so planning overhead adds no value.

Use the Explore subagent for the discovery phase so the verbose exploration happens in an isolated context and only a summary returns to the main conversation.
Ask Claude to skip exploration and infer the auth architecture from the directory names.
Split the work across two terminal windows, one for reading and one for writing.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent is designed for exactly this: verbose discovery runs in an isolated context and returns a summary, preserving the main conversation's context for the implementation phase. questions.prompt: You've described a data transformation to Claude in prose three separate times, and each implementation handles the edge cases differently. What is the most effective way to communicate the expected behavior?

choices.text: Write a longer, more precise prose specification covering every edge case you can think of.
Ask Claude to restate the requirements before implementing, and correct any misunderstandings.
Provide 2–3 concrete input/output examples demonstrating the transformation, including the edge cases.
Lower the temperature so the implementations are at least consistent with each other.

A produces more prose subject to the same interpretation problem. B surfaces misunderstandings but doesn't pin down edge-case behavior the way examples do. D makes outputs consistent, not correct.

questions.prompt: Two hours into a legacy-codebase exploration session, Claude starts describing "typical repository patterns" instead of the actual classes it read earlier, and gives inconsistent answers about code it correctly explained an hour ago. Ask Claude to "focus on the actual code, not typical patterns" whenever it drifts.
Paste the important files into the conversation again each time the drift appears.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so drift takes longer to appear.

questions.explanation: Context degradation in extended sessions (drifting to "typical patterns" instead of discovered specifics) is counteracted by persisting key findings to a scratchpad file and referencing it for subsequent questions — the findings survive outside degrading conversational context. B asks the model to fix a context problem with willpower. C repeatedly re-spends context and accelerates the problem. D delays symptoms without adding persistence.

Increase `max_tokens` so responses can be longer.
Read only the first 50 lines of each file to reduce volume.
Spawn subagents to investigate specific questions ("find all test files," "trace the refund flow dependencies") while the main agent preserves its context for high-level coordination.

questions.explanation: Delegating specific investigation questions to subagents isolates the verbose file-dump output in their contexts, while the main agent keeps its context for high-level coordination. Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.
Delete the project CLAUDE.md temporarily to free up context space.
Keep working — Claude automatically ignores old context when it becomes irrelevant.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to reduce context usage while preserving key information — the right mid-session relief valve when you need to keep working. questions.prompt: You finished a week-long analysis phase for a large migration and are about to spawn implementation subagents for each module. How should the analysis inform the subagents?

choices.text: Rely on the subagents inheriting the coordinator session's memory of the analysis automatically.
Have each subagent redo its own analysis of the relevant module from scratch to guarantee freshness.
Summarize the key findings from the exploration phase and inject the relevant summary into each subagent's initial context.
Pass the full multi-day session transcript to every subagent so nothing is lost.

questions.explanation: The reliable pattern is summarizing key findings from the completed phase and injecting the relevant summary into each subagent's initial context. A fails because subagents do not inherit parent context automatically. B re-spends a week of analysis. D floods each subagent's context with mostly-irrelevant transcript, inviting lost-in-the-middle problems.

questions.prompt: Your overnight multi-agent refactoring job occasionally crashes around hour three, and today's restart lost all progress. What design provides crash recovery?

choices.text: Have each agent export structured state (completed work, key findings) to a known location, and have the coordinator load a manifest of these exports on resume and inject them into agent prompts.
Increase the job timeout so the crash-prone window is less likely to be hit.
Run the full job twice in parallel so one copy is likely to survive.
Shrink the job scope so it finishes before the crash typically occurs.

questions.explanation: Structured state persistence is the crash-recovery pattern: each agent exports completed work and key findings to a known location; on resume the coordinator loads the manifest and injects state into agent prompts, resuming rather than restarting. B and D reduce crash odds but don't recover from one. C doubles cost for a coin-flip.

questions.prompt: You concatenated per-module analyses of 30 modules into a single prompt and asked for architecture recommendations. The recommendations consistently cite modules from the beginning and end of the input but ignore the middle third. What is the best mitigation?

Add an instruction: "Pay equal attention to every module, especially those in the middle."
Switch to a model with a larger context window so all 30 modules fit more comfortably.
Place a key-findings summary at the beginning of the input and organize the detailed module results under explicit section headers to mitigate position effects.

questions.explanation: This is the lost-in-the-middle effect: models reliably process the beginning and end of long inputs but may omit middle sections. The mitigation is a key-findings summary up front plus explicit section headers organizing the detail. A changes ordering without addressing position effects. B — instructions don't fix attention position biases. C — the effect persists in larger windows.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: Cost analysis shows that every query — including simple factual ones like "What is the current federal funds rate?" — runs the full search → analysis → synthesis → report pipeline, taking 4+ minutes. What should change?

choices.text: Cache pipeline outputs so repeated queries return instantly.
Design the coordinator to analyze each query's requirements and dynamically invoke only the subagents the query actually needs, rather than always routing through the full pipeline.
Reduce each subagent's token budget so the full pipeline completes faster.
Add a fifth "quick answer" subagent and route all queries through it first.

questions.explanation: The coordinator should analyze query requirements and dynamically select which subagents to invoke; simple factual queries shouldn't traverse the full pipeline. A only helps repeated queries. C makes every stage worse instead of skipping unneeded stages. D adds a fifth stage to a pipeline whose problem is mandatory stages.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: The synthesis subagent produces generic, thin output that ignores specific data the search agent found. Logs show the synthesis agent's prompt contains only: "Synthesize the findings on renewable energy storage." What is the root cause?

choices.text: The synthesis agent's system prompt lacks instructions about depth and specificity.
The synthesis agent needs a larger context window to see the coordinator's conversation.
Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history — the search results and analysis outputs must be included directly in the synthesis agent's prompt.
The search agent is returning results in a format the synthesis agent cannot parse.

questions.explanation: Subagents operate with isolated context: they do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history. The synthesis prompt must include the actual search results and analysis outputs. A would deepen prose style but can't conjure data the agent never received. B misunderstands isolation — window size is irrelevant if the content is never passed. D is contradicted by the logs: nothing was passed at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. questions.prompt: A research task involves four independent subtopics. The coordinator currently delegates them one at a time, waiting for each subagent to finish before starting the next, quadrupling latency. How should the coordinator spawn the subagents to run them in parallel?

choices.text: Emit multiple Task tool calls in a single coordinator response, one per subtopic.
Wrap the Agent SDK in an external async job queue that launches four coordinator processes.
Combine all four subtopics into one prompt for a single subagent to handle together.
Enable streaming on the coordinator so subagent calls overlap automatically.

questions.explanation: Parallel subagents are spawned by emitting multiple Task tool calls in a single coordinator response, rather than one per turn. B bolts external infrastructure onto a problem the SDK pattern already solves. C serializes the work inside one context and loses parallelism. D — streaming affects token delivery, not tool-call concurrency.

questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. questions.prompt: Your coordinator is configured with `allowedTools: ["WebSearch", "Read"]`. Instead of delegating, it attempts all research itself and never invokes any subagent. What is wrong?

choices.text: The subagent definitions are missing `description` fields, so the coordinator cannot see them.
The coordinator's model tier is too low to support delegation.
Subagents must be registered in `.mcp.json` before they can be spawned.
The coordinator's `allowedTools` must include `"Task"` — the Task tool is the mechanism for spawning subagents.

questions.explanation: The Task tool is the mechanism for spawning subagents; if `"Task"` isn't in the coordinator's `allowedTools`, it cannot delegate and will attempt the work itself. A affects selection quality among subagents, not the total inability to spawn. B and C describe requirements that don't exist.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. questions.prompt: An engineer proposes letting the search agent pass results directly to the analysis agent, bypassing the coordinator to "cut a hop." What is the main argument against this?

choices.text: Direct subagent-to-subagent communication doubles token usage because results are serialized twice.
Routing all communication through the coordinator preserves observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow — direct channels sacrifice all three.
The Agent SDK blocks direct communication between subagents at the protocol level, so the proposal cannot be built.
The analysis agent would need the search agent's tool permissions, violating scoping rules.

questions.explanation: Hub-and-spoke routing through the coordinator is what provides observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow; a direct side channel sacrifices all three. A invents a token penalty. C is false — you could build it, it's just a bad idea. D is a side detail, not the main architectural argument.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: Completed reports are coherent but often have coverage gaps — for instance, missing major recent developments the search agent never looked for. The pipeline currently makes a single pass. What is the most effective architectural improvement?

choices.text: Add an iterative refinement loop: the coordinator evaluates the synthesis output for gaps, re-delegates targeted queries to the search and analysis subagents, and re-invokes synthesis until coverage is sufficient.
Double the number of search results each query returns so more material is available in the first pass.
Add an instruction to the synthesis agent to write longer, more comprehensive reports.
Switch the search agent to a more capable model so its first pass finds everything.

questions.explanation: Coverage gaps are addressed with an iterative refinement loop: the coordinator evaluates synthesis output for gaps, re-delegates targeted queries, and re-invokes synthesis until coverage is sufficient. B adds volume, not targeted coverage. C asks for length — the missing material was never gathered. D still makes a single pass with no gap-checking.

questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. questions.prompt: You run two search subagents in parallel for broad topics, but their result sets overlap by roughly 60%, wasting tokens and analysis time. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Merge the two search agents into one so overlap is impossible.
Add a deduplication step in the coordinator that discards repeated sources after both agents finish.
Partition the research scope when delegating — assign each search agent distinct subtopics or source types so their coverage is complementary.
Have the second agent wait for the first agent's results and manually avoid its sources.

questions.explanation: Partitioning research scope — assigning each agent distinct subtopics or source types — prevents duplication at the source. B deduplicates after the tokens and analysis time are already spent. A gives up the parallelism that motivated two agents. D serializes the agents, also defeating parallelism.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: Your coordinator prompt gives each subagent a rigid 12-step procedure to follow. Subagents perform well on topics that fit the procedure but fail badly on topics that don't. How should the coordinator's delegation prompts change?

choices.text: Expand the procedure to 20 steps covering more topic types.
Add branching logic to the procedure: "if the topic is technical, do steps 4a–4c instead."
Remove all instructions and let each subagent improvise from its system prompt alone.
Specify the research goals and quality criteria for each delegation, rather than step-by-step procedural instructions, so subagents can adapt their approach to the topic.

questions.explanation: Coordinator prompts should specify research goals and quality criteria rather than step-by-step procedures, enabling subagents to adapt their approach to each topic. A and B double down on rigid proceduralism — there will always be topics outside the script. C removes direction entirely; goals and quality bars are still needed.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: Your system has two tools: `analyze_content` ("Analyzes content and returns insights") and `analyze_document` ("Analyzes documents and returns findings"). Agents misroute between them about 30% of the time. What is the most effective first fix?

choices.text: Rename the tools to reflect their actual distinct purposes (e.g., `extract_web_results` for the web one) and rewrite each description to state its purpose, expected inputs, outputs, and when to use it versus the other.
Add a system prompt rule: "When in doubt, prefer analyze_document."
Remove one of the tools and route all analysis through the remaining one.
Have the coordinator intercept and correct misrouted calls with a `PostToolUse` hook.

questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism for tool selection; near-identical names and descriptions cause misrouting. Renaming to purpose-specific names and rewriting descriptions (purpose, inputs, outputs, when-to-use-vs-the-other) fixes the root cause. B papers over ambiguity with a default. C may discard needed functionality. D corrects symptoms downstream and needs its own routing logic — the very thing that's broken.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: `analyze_document` accepts a `mode` parameter that switches between extraction, summarization, and claim verification. Agents frequently pass the wrong mode and get output they didn't expect. What is the best redesign?

choices.text: Make `mode` an enum with better documentation for each value.
Split the tool into three purpose-specific tools — `extract_data_points`, `summarize_content`, and `verify_claim_against_source` — each with a defined input/output contract.
Default `mode` to summarization, the most common case, so wrong modes matter less.
Have the tool infer the intended mode from the shape of the input.

questions.explanation: A generic tool with mode switches invites wrong-mode calls; splitting into purpose-specific tools (`extract_data_points`, `summarize_content`, `verify_claim_against_source`) with clear contracts makes selection explicit. A keeps the confusing single entry point. C substitutes a silent wrong behavior for an error. D makes behavior unpredictable and undebuggable.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. questions.prompt: The synthesis agent's toolset was copy-pasted from the search agent's config and includes `web_search`. You discover it performing new searches mid-synthesis and weaving unvetted, uncited claims into reports. What is the right fix?

choices.text: Add a system prompt rule telling the synthesis agent to only search when strictly necessary.

Add a post-hoc citation checker that flags uncited claims in the final report.
Restrict each subagent's toolset to its role — remove search tools from the synthesis agent so it works only from the findings it is given.

questions.explanation: Agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them; the synthesis agent's job is to work from provided findings, so search tools should be removed from its set (scoped tool access). questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. questions.prompt: The document analysis agent begins every task with 8–10 exploratory `list_documents` and `search_library` calls just to learn what's in the research library. How can you eliminate this overhead?

Paste the full library listing into the agent's system prompt and update the prompt whenever documents change.
Expose the document catalog as an MCP resource so the agent has visibility into available documents without exploratory tool calls.
Increase the agent's tool-call budget so the exploration completes faster.

questions.explanation: MCP resources exist to expose content catalogs — giving agents visibility into available data without exploratory tool calls. A makes the waste cheaper, not gone. B is a manual, drift-prone copy of what resources provide natively. D speeds up the overhead instead of eliminating it.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: The document analysis agent has a generic `fetch_url` tool and occasionally pulls arbitrary blog pages instead of documents from your vetted research library. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Replace `fetch_url` with a constrained `load_document` tool that validates requested URLs against the vetted document library.
Add a system prompt instruction listing which domains are acceptable to fetch.
Log all fetched URLs and review them weekly for policy violations.
Reduce the agent's temperature so it makes more conservative fetching choices.

questions.explanation: Replacing the generic `fetch_url` with a constrained `load_document` that validates URLs against the vetted library makes the boundary structural rather than behavioral. B relies on prompt compliance. C detects violations after they've contaminated research. D doesn't address capability at all.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: Final reports contain claims with no traceable source. Investigation shows the analysis agent summarizes findings into prose, and by the time synthesis runs, the source associations are gone. What is the fix?

choices.text: Have the report agent add citations at the end by searching for a plausible source for each claim.

Require subagents to output structured claim-source mappings (claim, source URL or document name, relevant excerpt), and require the synthesis agent to preserve and merge these mappings rather than compressing findings into prose.
Append a bibliography of all consulted sources to the end of each report.
Instruct the synthesis agent to only include claims it can remember the source for.

questions.explanation: Attribution survives only if subagents emit structured claim-source mappings (claim, source, excerpt) and the synthesis agent is required to preserve and merge them; prose summarization is where provenance dies. A fabricates citations after the fact — worse than none. C lists sources without linking claims to them. D relies on memory of information that was already compressed away.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: Two credible sources report the market size for the same year as $4.2B and $6.8B. The synthesis agent currently picks one value, seemingly at random. What should it do instead?

choices.text: Average the two values and report $5.5B with a footnote.
Always prefer the more recently published source and discard the other value.
Present both values, explicitly annotated as a conflict, with source attribution and any methodological context explaining the difference.
Omit the statistic entirely, since conflicting data cannot be trusted.

questions.explanation: Conflicting statistics from credible sources should be presented with explicit conflict annotation, source attribution, and methodological context — not resolved arbitrarily. A invents a number no source reported. B assumes recency explains the difference (it may be methodology or scope). D throws away material information the reader needs.
