questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Your CI bot has three response tools: `comment_inline`, `open_issue`, and `request_changes`. For clear-cut cases it chooses well, but for ambiguous ones (a real bug that's out of the PR's scope; a severe issue in unchanged code) it picks inconsistently. What most improves these decisions?

choices.text: A decision matrix in prose mapping issue attributes to tools.
Removing `open_issue` so there are fewer choices.
A few targeted few-shot examples of exactly these ambiguous cases, each showing the chosen tool *and the reasoning* why it beat the plausible alternatives.
Making `request_changes` the default for any uncertainty.

questions.explanation: Ambiguous cases are the targeted-few-shot case: examples of exactly these situations, showing the chosen tool *and the reasoning* over plausible alternatives, teach judgment the model generalizes. A describes the mapping in prose — already too coarse for edge cases. B removes a legitimate output. D hardcodes one answer to varied situations.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: You want every PR summary the bot posts to follow the same five-column markdown table. Instructions describing the table produce close-but-drifting variants (merged columns, extra sections). What reliably locks the format?

choices.text: A markdown linter that rejects malformed summaries and triggers regeneration.
Lowering temperature to reduce formatting creativity.
A stricter prose description of the table with column widths specified.
Few-shot examples showing complete, exact sample summaries in the required table format — demonstration beats description for format consistency.

questions.explanation: Format consistency comes from demonstration: complete sample summaries in the exact required table. Description (C), even stricter, keeps producing drift; that's the observed failure. A regenerates until lucky. B reduces variance around a format the model hasn't internalized.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Which statement about `tool_choice` is correct?

choices.text: `"auto"` guarantees at least one tool call per response.
With `"auto"` the model may respond with text and no tool call; `"any"` forces some tool call but leaves the choice of tool to the model; `{"type": "tool", "name": ...}` forces one specific tool.
`"any"` lets the model call any number of tools, while `"auto"` limits it to one.
Forced tool selection applies to every subsequent turn until reset.

questions.explanation: The correct trio: `"auto"` permits text-only responses; `"any"` mandates some tool call, model's choice; forced selection mandates one named tool. A describes "any." C invents count semantics. D — forcing applies per-request, not until reset.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Developers dismiss many of the bot's test-generation suggestions, and you want to learn systematically which kinds of code constructs produce the unwanted suggestions. What enables that analysis?

choices.text: A `detected_pattern` field in each suggestion's structured output identifying the construct that triggered it — dismissals can then be aggregated by pattern.
Exit interviews with developers who dismiss the most suggestions.
A dashboard of dismissal counts by repository.
Free-form "reason for dismissal" text boxes, reviewed monthly.

questions.explanation: A structured `detected_pattern` field ties every suggestion to the construct that triggered it, so dismissals aggregate into pattern-level insight — the systematic feedback loop. B and D produce anecdote at low volume. C counts dismissals without capturing what caused them.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: The review bot's finding — "this implementation may not match the approved design" — fails validation because it cites a design document the bot was never given. Will retry-with-error-feedback resolve it?

choices.text: Yes — the validation error will make the bot reason more carefully about the design.
Yes, if the retry also raises `max_tokens` for deeper analysis.
No — the design document is absent from the input; retries can't recover information that was never provided. Supply the document in context, or scope the review to what's available.
No — findings referencing external documents should be auto-deleted.

questions.explanation: The design document was never in the input; no retry recovers information that isn't there. Provide the document, or scope the review to available material. A and B retry harder at reading an absent file. D deletes a category wholesale when the fix is supplying context.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Two jobs are proposed for the Message Batches API: (1) a nightly "explain every lint suppression in the repo" report read weekly; (2) the PR-blocking security gate developers wait on before merging. Evaluate.

choices.text: Both fit — the 50% savings applies to both equally.
Neither fits — CI workloads need real-time APIs across the board.
Job 2 fits better, since security scans are heavier and benefit more from discounts.
Job 1 fits (latency-tolerant, non-blocking); job 2 does not — a blocking gate cannot depend on a service with an up-to-24-hour window and no latency SLA.

questions.explanation: Batch fits latency-tolerant, non-blocking work: the nightly report is ideal; a merge-blocking gate cannot ride a no-SLA, up-to-24-hour service. A ignores the blocking constraint. B overcorrects — the report genuinely fits. C prices workloads instead of matching latency requirements.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Your overnight batch analyzes 300 open PRs. When results return, the poster must attach each analysis to the right PR. How is the mapping maintained?

choices.text: Results return in submission order, so index alignment suffices.
Set each request's `custom_id` to its PR number at submission, and use the `custom_id` on each result to route it — the Batch API's correlation mechanism.
Ask the model to embed the PR number in its own output text.
Submit 300 separate single-request batches so each result is unambiguous.

questions.explanation: `custom_id` is the Batch API's request/response correlation mechanism: set it to the PR number at submission, read it on each result. A relies on ordering the API doesn't promise. C trusts model output for plumbing. D abandons batching's economics to avoid using the feature built for this.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: One pipeline job generates a bug fix and then, in the same session, reviews that fix before auto-merging. Post-incident analysis shows the reviews approve nearly everything, including a fix that broke production. What is the structural correction?

choices.text: Split generation and review into separate jobs, with the review running as an independent instance that receives the diff but none of the generator's session context.
Add "assume the fix is wrong until proven otherwise" to the review prompt.
Require two self-review passes before the auto-merge.
Auto-merge only fixes under 20 lines, reviewing larger ones manually.

questions.explanation: Generation and review must be separated: an independent review instance receives the diff without the generator's session context, avoiding the self-approval bias that shipped the bad fix. B and C prompt or repeat a structurally biased review. D limits exposure without fixing the reviewer.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: An 18-file PR gets inconsistent review depth — thorough on early files, thin on later ones — and the bot approved a cross-file API change in one file while flagging its mirror image in another. How should the review be restructured?

choices.text: Reverse file order on a second pass and merge both passes' findings.
Cap PRs at 6 files via repository policy.
Split the review into per-file passes for local issues plus a dedicated cross-file integration pass for API consistency and data flow — eliminating the attention dilution causing both symptoms.
Increase the review job's `max_tokens` so later files get more budget.

questions.explanation: Declining depth across files plus contradictory verdicts on mirrored code are attention dilution; the restructure is per-file passes for local issues and a separate integration pass for cross-file consistency. A averages two diluted passes. B constrains developers to fit the tool. D — token budget doesn't reallocate attention across a long input.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: You want findings the bot is demonstrably reliable about to post automatically, while shakier ones queue for human moderation. The bot emits a per-finding confidence score. What makes this routing sound?

choices.text: Trust findings at confidence ≥ 9/10; models rarely overstate certainty at the top of the scale.
Route by category instead — security findings to humans, everything else auto-posts.
Auto-post everything but add a "low confidence" label where the score is low.

Validate the scores first: measure accuracy against a labeled set of past findings at each confidence level, and set the auto-post threshold where measured precision meets your bar — self-reported confidence is only usable once calibrated.

questions.explanation: Confidence becomes routable only after calibration: measure accuracy at each score level against labeled outcomes and place the threshold where precision meets the bar. A trusts raw self-report at the extreme — where miscalibration concentrates. B discards per-finding signal for category stereotype. C posts everything anyway, labeling the risk instead of routing it. --- *End of Practice Exam 4.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: Claude follows your API conventions perfectly on your laptop but ignores them on your desktop, in the same repository. What is the right first diagnostic?

choices.text: Compare Claude Code versions on the two machines and upgrade the older one.

Run `/memory` on both machines to see which memory files each session actually loaded — the difference is almost certainly a configuration-loading difference (e.g., user-level files present on one machine only).
Re-clone the repository on the desktop.
Run `/compact` on the desktop session to clear interfering context.

questions.explanation: Same repo, different behavior across machines points at configuration loading, and `/memory` shows exactly which memory files each session loaded — diagnose before changing anything. The likely culprit is user-level configuration present on one machine only. A, C, and D change things before establishing what differs.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: Your monorepo's `frontend/` packages need the React standards file and the accessibility standards file; `backend/` packages need the API standards and database standards files. All four files live in `standards/`. How do you wire this up without duplication?

choices.text: Concatenate all four files into the root CLAUDE.md.
Copy the relevant files into each package directory.
Reference all four from every package CLAUDE.md, letting Claude judge relevance.
In each package's CLAUDE.md, use `@import` to pull in only the standards files relevant to that package.

questions.explanation: `@import` lets each package's CLAUDE.md include only the standards files relevant to it — one copy of each standard, selectively composed. A loads everything everywhere. B duplicates and drifts. C loads all four and hopes the model scopes them correctly.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: Your CLAUDE.md mixes testing standards, Git workflow, security rules, code style, and deployment steps in one 1,000-line file that three teams edit and constantly conflict over. What is the recommended reorganization?

choices.text: Split it into focused topic files under `.claude/rules/` (`testing.md`, `git-workflow.md`, `security.md`, …), each owned by the appropriate team.
Freeze the file and require RFC approval for changes.
Move it to a wiki and link from CLAUDE.md.
Auto-generate it nightly from team documentation.

questions.explanation: The recommended structure for a contested monolith: topic-specific files under `.claude/rules/`, each owned by the team that owns the topic — smaller diffs, fewer conflicts, clearer ownership. B freezes the pain in place. C removes the content from Claude's view. D generates a monolith instead of splitting it.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: Your database-seeding workflow — 300 lines of steps, fixtures, and cleanup logic — is used about once a week. Universal code conventions are used in every session. Where does each belong?

choices.text: Both in CLAUDE.md, since both matter.
Both in skills, to minimize context cost.
Conventions in CLAUDE.md (always loaded); the seeding workflow as a skill in `.claude/skills/` (loaded on demand when invoked).
Conventions in a skill; the seeding workflow in CLAUDE.md.

questions.explanation: The dividing line: universal always-applicable content in CLAUDE.md; occasional task-specific workflows as skills loaded on invocation. A pays 300 lines of seeding logic in every session. B makes universal conventions opt-in. D is backwards on both.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: Your `/explore-alternatives` skill generates several competing design sketches. After it runs, the main session's context carries all the rejected sketches, and Claude later resurrects abandoned ideas as if they were current. What frontmatter fixes this?

choices.text: `argument-hint`, so the skill is scoped to one design question.
`allowed-tools`, so the skill can't write the sketches to files.
`paths`, restricting the skill to design documents.
`context: fork` — the exploration runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only the selected direction returns to the main conversation.

questions.explanation: Exploratory content that shouldn't persist is what `context: fork` isolates: the sketches live in the fork, and only the chosen direction returns. A narrows scope without isolating the residue. B affects file writes, not conversation context. C isn't the mechanism for this.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: Your `/update-changelog` skill needs only to read the git log and edit `CHANGELOG.md`. An incident review found a run where it also executed `git tag` and pushed the tag. What is the structural fix?

choices.text: Add "never create or push tags" to the skill's SKILL.md.
Set `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to the minimal set (read operations and file editing) so shell commands aren't available during the skill.
Have developers review each skill run's transcript.
Protect tags server-side so pushes fail.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` restricted to reads plus file editing means the skill physically cannot run `git tag` or push — structural, not advisory. A is the advisory approach that already failed. C reviews after the fact. D catches only the push, not the local mutation, and depends on server config.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: Your `/fix-issue` skill needs a ticket number to look up the issue before fixing it. Developers regularly invoke it bare and it fabricates an interpretation of "the issue." Which frontmatter option addresses the invocation problem?

choices.text: `argument-hint`, so invoking the skill without arguments prompts the developer for the required ticket number.
`context: fork`, so the fabricated interpretations stay isolated.
A SKILL.md instruction to refuse when no ticket is given.
`allowed-tools` restricted to read-only until a ticket is provided.

questions.explanation: `argument-hint` prompts for the required parameter when the skill is invoked bare — fixing the invocation gap that causes the fabrication. B isolates the bad output instead of preventing it. C handles the failure politely rather than collecting the input. D misuses tool permissions as input validation.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: End-to-end test specs (`*.e2e.ts`) live next to the features they test, in dozens of directories. They must all follow your Playwright conventions. Which mechanism applies the conventions to exactly those files?

choices.text: A CLAUDE.md in the `tests/` directory, where some of the specs live.
The root CLAUDE.md with a section headed "For e2e files only."
A `.claude/rules/` file with frontmatter `paths: ["**/*.e2e.ts"]` — glob-scoped rules load whenever a matching file is edited, regardless of directory.
A skill that developers run before writing e2e tests.

questions.explanation: Files identified by naming convention and spread across directories are the glob-rule case: `paths: ["**/*.e2e.ts"]` loads the conventions exactly when those files are edited. A covers only one location of many. B loads always and scopes never. D depends on someone remembering.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: You're adding a caching layer. Three integration approaches are viable — sidecar, library, or gateway-level — each with different infrastructure requirements, and the choice constrains several services. How do you start?

choices.text: Enter plan mode: explore the affected services, weigh the three approaches, and commit to a design before writing code.
Direct execution starting with the simplest approach, switching if it fails.
Implement all three behind a feature flag and benchmark.
Ask Claude to vote for one approach and implement it immediately.

questions.explanation: Multiple viable architectures with cross-service constraints is plan mode's core criterion: explore, compare, and commit to a design before code. B ships the first idea and discovers constraints by failure. C triples the work to avoid a decision. D takes the recommendation without the exploration that justifies it.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: A user reports that phone numbers with spaces fail validation. The regex lives in one function; the failing input and expected behavior are both known. How do you proceed?

choices.text: Plan mode, to consider validation architecture holistically.
An Explore subagent to find all validation patterns first.
A `fork_session` to compare two candidate regexes.
Direct execution — a single-function fix with a clear reproduction needs no planning phase.

questions.explanation: Single function, known reproduction, clear expected behavior: direct execution. Planning (A), repo-wide exploration (B), and session forking (C) add process where there is no design uncertainty.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: Claude's fixes to your date-parsing utility keep regressing other formats: each fix breaks a previously working case. What iteration structure stops the whack-a-mole?

choices.text: Ask Claude to enumerate all formats before each fix.
Freeze the utility and write a new one alongside it.
Write a test suite first covering all supported formats and edge cases, then iterate by sharing failing tests — the suite pins previously working behavior while failures focus each round.
Fix formats in order of usage frequency.

questions.explanation: Regressions on previously working cases mean nothing is pinning existing behavior: write the test suite first (all formats, edge cases), then iterate on failing tests. The suite converts whack-a-mole into convergence. A relies on enumeration without enforcement. B abandons instead of stabilizing. D orders the moles without stopping the whacking.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: You're deep in a productive session; context is nearly full of file dumps from earlier exploration, and you have an hour of implementation left. You want to preserve key decisions but reclaim space. What do you do?

Run `/compact` — it summarizes the conversation, reducing context usage while preserving key information, letting the session continue.
Ask Claude to respond more tersely for the remainder.
Export the transcript and continue in a text editor.

questions.explanation: `/compact` is the mid-session relief valve: summarize the conversation, reduce usage, preserve key information, keep working. A discards the decisions unless you can reconstruct them perfectly. C conserves output, not context. D takes the work out of the tool entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: Your main session must design a refactor, but first you need answers to three verbose research questions (where is X implemented, who calls Y, how is Z configured). How do you keep the main session's context clean?

Answer the three questions first, then `/compact` before designing.
Design first from assumptions, verifying afterwards.
Use three terminal tabs and copy conclusions between them.

questions.explanation: Delegate the verbose questions to subagents and let summaries return — exploration happens in their contexts while the main session keeps its budget for design. B spends the main context first and compresses after. C designs on assumptions. D is manual subagents with copy-paste as the protocol.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.

Trim the tool's output to the violations list before it enters context — verbose fields that are never used should not accumulate.

A second Claude instance auditing in parallel for cross-checking.
An audit scratchpad file where findings are recorded as they're confirmed, consulted when answering later questions — persistent findings that don't degrade with the context.
Re-reading every module before each new question.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: Analytics show that 30% of user queries are simple definitions or single facts, yet every query traverses search → analysis → synthesis → report. What should the coordinator do differently?

choices.text: Assess each query's complexity first and invoke only what it needs — answering simple factual queries with a single search (or directly), reserving the full pipeline for genuinely complex research.
Add a cache in front of the pipeline for repeated questions.
Shorten each stage's prompt so the pipeline is cheaper per query.
Reject simple queries with a message directing users to a search engine.

questions.explanation: Coordinators should match invocation to query complexity: simple factual queries get a single search or a direct answer; the full pipeline is for real research. B helps only repeats. C makes every unnecessary stage cheaper instead of skipping it. D turns an efficiency fix into a product regression.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: Reviewing the coordinator wrapper, you find: `for turn in range(8): response = send(...)` with no other exit condition, and users report reports that stop mid-topic. What is the correct redesign?

choices.text: Raise the range to 20 — telemetry shows 95% of tasks finish by then.
Add a check that breaks early when the response "looks complete."
Loop on `stop_reason` — continue while `"tool_use"`, exit on `"end_turn"` — keeping any iteration bound strictly as an emergency backstop.
Let users configure the turn budget per query.

questions.explanation: A bare `range(8)` makes an arbitrary cap the only termination — hence mid-topic truncation. Loop on `stop_reason`, with any bound kept strictly as an emergency backstop. A tunes the wrong mechanism. B adds a "looks complete" heuristic — a second anti-pattern. D makes users configure a bug.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: The report agent produces beautiful reports with invented citations. Investigating, you find its prompt contains the synthesis text but not the claim-source mappings the synthesis agent produced. What is the fix?

choices.text: Instruct the report agent to only cite when certain.

Pass the claim-source mappings explicitly in the report agent's prompt alongside the synthesis — subagents receive only what is put in their prompts, and citation data that never arrives cannot be used.
Give the report agent a search tool to find real citations.
Have a post-processor verify and correct the citations.

questions.explanation: Subagents use only what their prompts contain: the mappings existed upstream but never reached the report agent, so it improvised. Pass the claim-source mappings explicitly with the synthesis. A asks for restraint while withholding the data. C invites fresh, unvetted sourcing. D corrects fabrications after generation instead of preventing them.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: Five regional market analyses are needed before a global rollup; each is independent. The coordinator currently runs them one per turn, and latency is five times the single-region time. What fixes the latency?

choices.text: Merge the five analyses into one subagent prompt.
Precompute regions on a nightly schedule so requests hit a cache.
Shorten each regional analysis to a summary.
Emit five Task tool calls in a single coordinator response — parallel subagent execution for independent work.

questions.explanation: Independent analyses parallelize via multiple Task calls in one coordinator response — five subagents at once, latency near single-region time. A serializes inside one context. B changes freshness semantics to dodge an orchestration fix. C trades quality for speed unnecessarily.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: An engineer wired the search agent to hand results directly to the analysis agent and the analysis agent directly to synthesis, bypassing the coordinator "for speed." Direct handoffs are fine, but each agent needs retry logic.

Hub-and-spoke exists for a reason: routing inter-agent communication through the coordinator provides observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow — the properties that vanished.
The speed gain proves the coordinator was unnecessary overhead.

questions.explanation: The lost properties — failure localization, non-vanishing partial results — are exactly what hub-and-spoke routing through the coordinator provides: observability, consistent error handling, controlled information flow. A synthesis prompt instruction to "always include pricing."
A required `pricing` section in the report template, left blank when data is missing.

A search-string-generation subagent feeding the search agent.

questions.prompt: Your agent calls Grep, your harness executes it and appends the `tool_result` — and then nothing happens; the agent never produces its answer. The harness logs show no further API call was made. What is missing?

choices.text: A `tool_choice` setting on the follow-up request.
The Grep result was too large and must be truncated.
A `continue: true` flag on the tool result block.
The continuation request — after appending tool results, the harness must send the updated conversation back to the model; the loop is send → execute → append → send again.

questions.explanation: The loop is send → execute → append → **send again**: after appending tool results, the updated conversation must go back to the model. Nothing happens because the continuation request was never made. A, B, and C decorate a request that isn't being sent.

Start fresh — sessions should not span multiple days.
`fork_session` so Friday's session stays pristine.
Start fresh but paste in Friday's final message.

questions.explanation: Unchanged code and valid prior context is exactly what `--resume` with a named session is for: continuing a named investigation across work sessions. B discards a day of context on principle. C forks with no divergence to explore. D recovers one message out of a day's understanding.

`--resume` the analysis session twice concurrently.

Parallelize everything first, since parallelism usually dominates.
Ask the team which step feels slowest and optimize that.

questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. questions.prompt: Your invoice extractor prompts for "a JSON response" and parses the text. Failures cluster around markdown fences and apologetic preambles ("Here is the extracted data:"). What eliminates the failure class?

A prompt rule: "no prose, no fences, JSON only."
Tool use — define an extraction tool whose input schema is the invoice structure and read the guaranteed-shape data from the `tool_use` block.
A tolerant parser that strips fences and leading prose.

questions.explanation: Tool use eliminates the failure class: the extraction tool's input schema guarantees structure — no fences, no preambles, no prose. A (prefill) narrows the failure without a guarantee — drift can still appear mid-output and nothing enforces the schema. B is an instruction, already being violated. D is an arms race with formatting variety.

questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. questions.prompt: Receipts often genuinely lack a due date, but `due_date` is required in your schema — and audits found the model quietly inserting a date 30 days after the purchase date. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Make `due_date` optional/nullable and instruct the model to return null when the document has none — a required field the source can't satisfy invites fabrication.
Keep it required but add "never invent dates" to the prompt.
Post-validate that due dates appear verbatim in the source text.
Default the field server-side to 30 days, making the model's behavior official.

questions.explanation: A required field the source may not contain pressures the model to fabricate; make `due_date` nullable and instruct null when absent. B keeps the pressure and adds a plea. C catches some fabrications after the fact (and fails on reformatted dates). D institutionalizes the fabrication.

Make the field free text and classify downstream.
Reject documents with unrecognized payment methods.
Add `"other"` to the enum with a companion detail field capturing the actual method — the extensible-category pattern.

questions.explanation: The extensible-category pattern: `"other"` plus a detail field capturing the actual method — novel categories are represented faithfully, and the enum stays machine-readable. A chases reality quarterly and always trails it. B pushes classification downstream, unsolved. C rejects valid business documents.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. questions.prompt: A shared intake pipeline receives invoices, contracts, and HR forms mixed together, each with its own extraction tool defined. You need guaranteed structured output on every document without pre-classifying. Which setting?

choices.text: `tool_choice` forced to the invoice tool, the most common type.
`tool_choice: "any"` — the model must call one of the tools and picks the schema matching the document.
`tool_choice: "auto"` plus a prompt instruction to always extract.
Three pipeline lanes with a rules-based classifier in front.

questions.explanation: Multiple extraction schemas, unknown document type, structured output required: `tool_choice: "any"` — a tool call is guaranteed, and the model selects the schema fitting the document. A forces the wrong schema onto two of three types. C permits prose. D builds a router to replicate what "any" does.

questions.prompt: Contracts occasionally arrive with a stated term whose end date precedes its start date (drafting or OCR errors). Downstream date math silently produces negative durations. What extraction design surfaces the problem?

choices.text: Swap the dates when end precedes start, since that's obviously the intent.
Reject any contract whose dates are out of order.
Extract both dates as stated and set a `conflict_detected` boolean when the ordering is impossible — inconsistent source data gets flagged for review, neither silently passed nor silently "fixed."
Extract only the start date, deriving the end from the stated term length.

questions.explanation: Impossible source data is neither passed through silently nor silently corrected: extract as stated and flag with `conflict_detected` for review. A "fixes" data it cannot verify — the drafting error might be in either field. B stalls legitimate documents over a flag-able condition. D derives from data already suspect.

questions.prompt: `signatory_date` keeps failing extraction on a batch of scanned agreements. Sampling shows the signature page simply wasn't scanned — the date isn't in the input. The retry system has been resubmitting these documents for days. What is the correct assessment?

choices.text: Increase retries with prompt variations until the model finds the dates.
The retries would work with a larger context window.
The field should be removed from the schema.
These retries can never succeed — the information is absent from the input. Detect this case, stop retrying, and route to the rescanning workflow (or accept null with a documented reason).

questions.explanation: The date isn't in the input, so no retry can extract it — days of resubmission bought nothing. Detect information-absent failures, stop retrying, and route to rescanning or accept a documented null. A and B retry harder at reading an unscanned page. questions.prompt: You added few-shot examples covering three vendors' invoice layouts. Extraction then also improved markedly on a fourth vendor whose layout none of the examples showed. What explains this?

choices.text: Few-shot examples teach the underlying judgment — how to locate and map fields across layout variation — which the model generalizes to novel structures, rather than memorizing the specific layouts shown.
The fourth vendor's layout must coincidentally match one of the three.
The examples increased the prompt length, which always improves accuracy.
A model update shipped at the same time; the examples were irrelevant.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples teach transferable judgment — how to locate and map fields across layout variation — which generalizes to unseen structures; that's why they beat exhaustive per-layout rules. B is possible but explains nothing generalizable and contradicts "markedly improved." C — prompt length isn't a quality mechanism. D is an unfalsifiable dodge.

Run three extractors, one per presentation style, and merge.
Restrict extraction to the tables and flag the rest for humans.

questions.prompt: Two workloads: (1) re-extracting your ten-year document archive with an improved schema, results needed "sometime this quarter"; (2) extracting data from documents customers upload during a live onboarding flow. Assign the APIs.

choices.text: Synchronous for both — simpler to operate.
Batch for both — the discount is too large to pass up.
Batch for the onboarding flow since volume is high; synchronous for the archive.
Batch API for the archive (massive, latency-tolerant, 50% cheaper); synchronous API for onboarding (a customer is waiting on the result).

questions.prompt: Your contract guarantees extraction results within 36 hours of document receipt. Batch processing takes up to 24 hours. Documents arrive continuously. Which accumulation window keeps the guarantee?

choices.text: 24 hours — one daily batch is operationally cleanest.
16 hours, since batches usually complete in far less than 24.
8 hours — worst case 8 + 24 = 32 hours, within the guarantee with margin.
48 hours with an expedite lane for old documents.

questions.explanation: The guarantee must hold in the worst case: 8-hour accumulation + 24-hour processing = 32 ≤ 36 with margin. A gives 48 worst case. B's 16 + 24 = 40 breaches the SLA, and "usually faster" isn't a guarantee. D starts beyond the SLA and patches with an expedite lane.

choices.text: Refine and verify the prompt on a representative sample via the synchronous API first — maximizing first-pass success so the fixed budget isn't spent on a flawed full run.
Submit the full batch immediately; failures can be resubmitted within budget.
Submit the batch at half temperature to be safe.
Split into two 5,000-form batches and correct between them.

questions.explanation: With a fixed budget, first-pass success is everything: refine the prompt on a representative sample synchronously, verify, then submit the batch. questions.prompt: Your extraction step ends with "double-check your extraction against the document" — and reports itself accurate. Auditors keep finding wrong values the self-check approved. What does the guide say about this design?

choices.text: The self-check needs a rubric listing common error types.
A model checking its own extraction retains the reasoning that produced the errors; verification should run as an independent instance comparing output to source without the extractor's context.
The self-check should run twice, with disagreements escalated.
Self-checks work if you also request a confidence score.

questions.explanation: A model verifying its own extraction retains the reasoning that produced the errors — self-checks approve their own mistakes. The dashboard should show median accuracy instead of mean.
96% was still accurate as an overall number, so no process change is needed.

Aggregate metrics mask segment failures — accuracy must be validated by document type (and field) before it can justify decisions like reducing review, and segments like handwritten forms need their own remediation.

questions.explanation: 96% aggregate coexisting with 61% on handwritten forms is exactly how aggregate metrics mask segment failures: validate by document type and field before the number justifies anything, and remediate the failing segment. A hides the problem from the metric. B changes the statistic, not the blindness. C accepts a segment that's wrong 4 times in 10.

Alerting when confidence scores drift statistically.
Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions for continuous human review — measuring the true error rate and surfacing novel error patterns in the automated stream.

questions.prompt: The model emits per-field confidence scores, and you plan to auto-accept above a threshold. A colleague proposes 0.9 "because it's high." What is the defensible way to choose?

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: An engineer implements the agentic loop so that it exits whenever the assistant's text contains phrases like "your issue is resolved" or "is there anything else." In production, the loop sometimes exits while the agent still intends to call `process_refund`, and other times keeps looping after the conversation is clearly finished. What is the correct loop termination design?

choices.text: Expand the phrase list and add fuzzy matching to catch paraphrased terminal expressions.
Cap the loop at 10 iterations, since most support cases resolve in fewer turns.
Continue the loop while `stop_reason` is `"tool_use"`, executing tools; terminate on `"end_turn"`.
Terminate whenever a response arrives with no text content, treating tool-only turns as complete.

questions.explanation: The agentic loop must key off `stop_reason`: continue while it is `"tool_use"` (execute tools, return results), stop at `"end_turn"`. Parsing natural-language signals (A) is exactly the anti-pattern producing the observed failures — text can look terminal while a tool call is pending. Iteration caps (B) are a safety backstop, not a primary stopping mechanism, and truncate legitimate long cases. D inverts the semantics: absence of text says nothing definitive about completion.

Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: Your agent calls `process_refund` and your code executes the refund successfully. What must happen next so the agent can correctly continue the conversation?

choices.text: Store the confirmation in your database and summarize all tool activity in the final customer response.
Inject the refund confirmation into the system prompt so it persists across later turns.
Start a new conversation seeded with a summary of prior turns plus the refund result.
Append a `tool_result` block (with the `tool_use` ID) in a user message and resend the conversation.

questions.explanation: Tool results must be appended to the conversation history as a `tool_result` block referencing the `tool_use` ID, then the whole conversation is sent back so the model can incorporate the result into its next reasoning step. A keeps the result away from the model entirely — it can't confirm the refund. B misuses the system prompt for turn-level data. C destroys conversational state mid-task and is unnecessary here.

questions.prompt: Your MCP tools come from different backend teams: `get_customer` returns ISO 8601 dates, `lookup_order` returns Unix timestamps, and order statuses are numeric codes in one tool but strings in another. The agent occasionally miscompares dates and misreads statuses when reasoning across tools. What is the most reliable fix?

choices.text: Document each tool's formats in the system prompt with conversion instructions.
Normalize dates, timestamps, and status codes in a `PostToolUse` hook before the model sees them.
Ask the backend teams to migrate their APIs to one shared format standard.
Validate the agent's final answer for date and status errors at conversation end.

questions.explanation: A `PostToolUse` hook deterministically normalizes heterogeneous formats before the model ever sees them, removing the error class entirely. Prompt instructions (A) rely on probabilistic per-turn conversions and will still fail occasionally. C is organizationally impractical and out of your control. D detects errors after they've influenced the conversation instead of preventing them.

questions.prompt: Company policy requires human approval for any refund over $500. Your system prompt states this rule prominently, but production logs show that about 2% of refunds above $500 are still processed autonomously. What should you do?

choices.text: Intercept `process_refund` calls with a hook that blocks amounts over $500 and redirects to escalation.
Move the rule to the top of the system prompt and repeat it before the tool definitions.
Add few-shot examples of the agent escalating refunds of $501, $750, and $1,200.
Lower the temperature so the agent follows system prompt instructions more consistently.

questions.explanation: A business rule with financial consequences needs deterministic enforcement: intercept the tool call, block amounts over $500, and redirect to escalation. Prompt salience (B), few-shot examples (C), and temperature (D) all still rely on probabilistic compliance — the observed 2% failure rate is precisely why prompt-only enforcement is insufficient here.

Route messages containing more than one concern to `escalate_to_human` for manual handling.
Handle each concern in its own fresh session so every issue gets a clean context window.
Decompose the message into distinct items, investigate each with shared context, and synthesize one resolution.

questions.explanation: The recommended pattern is decomposing multi-concern requests into distinct items, investigating each in parallel with shared context, then synthesizing one unified resolution. A pushes work onto the customer. B escalates cases the agent could resolve, hurting first-contact resolution. A structured summary: customer ID, root cause, disputed amount, and recommended action.
The customer ID plus a profile link, keeping the handoff lightweight for the queue.
A sentiment analysis of the conversation showing the customer's frustration level.

questions.prompt: A product manager proposes replacing the agent's reasoning with a fixed sequence — always call `get_customer`, then `lookup_order`, then either resolve or refund — arguing it will make behavior predictable. Why is model-driven tool selection the better fit for this workload?

choices.text: Model-driven selection is always cheaper, since the model skips the reasoning tokens needed to follow a script.
Support requests vary too much for one sequence: the tools needed differ per case, and intermediate results change what should happen next.
A fixed sequence would break session resumption, which requires model-chosen tool ordering.

questions.explanation: This workload is explicitly high-ambiguity: the right tools and their order genuinely vary per case, and intermediate results (e.g., what `lookup_order` reveals) change what should happen next — the core argument for model-driven decision-making, and a fixed script also wastes calls on cases that don't need them. D is false — a scripted sequence can be given any context you choose.

Increase the payment gateway timeout so transient failures become rare.

Suppress the error in a hook and instruct the agent to end the conversation gracefully.
Have the agent call `get_customer` again first, in case the customer ID was wrong.

Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: Compliance requires that every conversation begin with a call to a `classify_request` tool before any other tool runs, with no exceptions. What is the most reliable implementation?

choices.text: Set `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "classify_request"}` on the first request, then normal tool choice afterward.
State in the system prompt that `classify_request` is mandatory and must always come first.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the first request so a tool call is guaranteed before any response.
Add few-shot examples showing `classify_request` being called first in several conversation types.

questions.explanation: Forced tool selection (`tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "classify_request"}`) on the first request is the only option that *guarantees* that specific tool runs first; later turns then proceed normally. B and D are probabilistic. C (`"any"`) guarantees *some* tool call, but not which one — the agent could call `get_customer` first.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. questions.prompt: In long billing-dispute conversations, your context management summarizes older turns. After summarization, the agent starts misstating specifics — quoting "around $80" for a refund the customer was promised at exactly $83.47. What is the best fix?

choices.text: Increase the summary length limit so more detail from older turns survives.
Re-run `lookup_order` and `get_customer` on every turn so fresh data is always in context.
Extract transactional facts into a persistent "case facts" block included in every prompt.
Ask the customer to re-confirm key amounts whenever the conversation exceeds 20 turns.

questions.explanation: Extracting transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers, statuses) into a persistent case-facts block that rides outside the summarized history is the recommended defense against progressive summarization degrading precise values into vague ones ("around $80"). A only delays the loss. B works but adds cost and latency on every turn for data that isn't changing. D pushes the system's memory problem onto the customer.

questions.prompt: You maintain your team's coding standards in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on your machine. A new teammate clones the repository, but Claude Code ignores all of those standards for them. Why?

choices.text: The new teammate needs to run `/memory` once to activate memory files after cloning.
User-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` applies only to your account; team standards belong in a project-level CLAUDE.md.
CLAUDE.md files require an explicit `@import` from the project root before they take effect.
The standards file exceeds the size limit for automatic loading and is being silently truncated.

questions.explanation: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is user-level configuration: it applies to your account only and never travels through version control. Team-wide standards belong in a project-level CLAUDE.md committed to the repo. A misstates what `/memory` does (it inspects loaded memory; it doesn't "activate" anything). C — project CLAUDE.md loads without imports. D invents a failure mode.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.
questions.prompt: Your monorepo has six packages with mostly shared standards but some package-specific conventions. The root CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines and every session loads all of it regardless of which package is being edited. Package maintainers know their own conventions best. What is the most maintainable structure?

choices.text: Duplicate the full standards document into each package directory so every package is self-contained.
Keep the single root CLAUDE.md but add a table of contents so the model can navigate to sections.
Move all standards into a wiki and instruct Claude to ask developers for conventions when unsure.
Keep shared standards in focused files; each package's CLAUDE.md uses `@import` to pull in only what applies.

questions.explanation: `@import` keeps CLAUDE.md modular: each package's CLAUDE.md pulls in only the relevant shared standards files, and package maintainers with domain knowledge own the selection. A creates six diverging copies. B still loads all 900 lines every session — a table of contents doesn't reduce context. C makes standards invisible to Claude by default.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.
questions.prompt: Claude Code follows your API error-handling conventions in some sessions but not others, with no obvious pattern. What is the best first diagnostic step?

choices.text: Run `/memory` to verify which memory files are actually loaded in the affected sessions.
Rewrite the conventions section of CLAUDE.md with stronger, more imperative language.
Run `/compact` to clear stale context that may be overriding the conventions.
Delete and recreate the project CLAUDE.md to rule out file corruption.

questions.explanation: Inconsistent behavior across sessions is the classic symptom of different memory files being loaded in different sessions; `/memory` shows exactly which files are in effect, so diagnose before rewriting anything. B and D change content before you know whether content is the problem. C addresses context pressure, not configuration loading.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.
questions.prompt: Your team's `/analyze-deps` skill walks the dependency graph and prints thousands of lines of package data. Developers complain that after running it, Claude's answers about their actual coding task get noticeably worse. What change fixes this?

choices.text: Add `argument-hint` frontmatter so developers scope the analysis to one package at a time.
Move the dependency analysis instructions into CLAUDE.md so no skill invocation is needed.
Add `context: fork` so the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent context and returns a summary.
Add `allowed-tools` frontmatter so the skill can only read files, reducing its output volume.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context so its verbose output never enters (pollutes) the main conversation — only the useful summary returns. A reduces volume but the output still lands in the main context. B makes it worse: always-loaded verbosity. D restricts capability, not output destination.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Code Generation with Claude Code

questions.prompt: Your `/scaffold-component` skill should only ever create new files from templates. During an audit you find a session where it also ran shell commands, including a `git checkout` that discarded a developer's uncommitted changes. What is the right guardrail?

choices.text: Add a warning to the skill's SKILL.md instructions telling Claude never to run shell commands.
Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only file-creation operations.
Require developers to commit their work before running any skill.
Convert the skill into a slash command, since commands cannot run tools.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` in the skill frontmatter is the enforcement mechanism: restrict the skill to file-creation operations and Bash simply isn't available during execution. A is prompt-based and probabilistic — the failure already happened despite the skill's instructions. C mitigates damage rather than preventing it. D is false — slash commands don't disable tools.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. questions.prompt: Your team has two assets: (1) universal naming and error-handling conventions that apply to all code Claude writes, and (2) a release-notes generation workflow used once per sprint. How should each be configured?

choices.text: Put both in CLAUDE.md so nothing depends on developers remembering to invoke a skill.
Put both in skills so the context cost is only paid when each is needed.
Conventions in the project CLAUDE.md; the release-notes workflow in a skill under `.claude/skills/`.
Conventions in a skill; the release-notes workflow in CLAUDE.md so it is always available.

questions.explanation: Universal, always-applicable standards belong in CLAUDE.md (loaded every session); task-specific workflows used occasionally belong in skills (loaded on demand). A pays the release-notes workflow's context cost in every session. B means conventions only apply when someone remembers to invoke them. D is backwards on both counts.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Code Generation with Claude Code

questions.prompt: A production bug report includes a stack trace pointing to a single function with an obvious off-by-one error. The fix is one line in one file. How should you proceed in Claude Code?

choices.text: Use direct execution — the change is simple, well-scoped, and already located.
Enter plan mode to explore the codebase before committing to an approach.
Spawn an Explore subagent to investigate the surrounding module first.
Use `fork_session` to try two candidate fixes in parallel branches.

questions.explanation: A single-file, single-line fix with a stack trace pointing at the location is the textbook case for direct execution; plan mode (B), exploration subagents (C), and session forking (D) all add overhead with no decision-making or architectural payoff for a change this well-scoped.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.
questions.prompt: You are starting a multi-phase task: first understand how authentication works across a large unfamiliar codebase, then implement a change. The discovery phase will involve reading dozens of files, and you're worried the exploration output will exhaust context before implementation begins. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Read files in alphabetical order and run `/compact` after every ten files.
Do the discovery in one session, then `--resume` it in a fresh terminal for the implementation phase.
Front-load all the file reads into the first turn so summarization compresses them together.
Use the Explore subagent for discovery so only a summary returns to the main conversation.

questions.explanation: The Explore subagent is designed for exactly this: verbose discovery runs in an isolated context and returns a summary, preserving the main conversation's context for the implementation phase. A still floods the main context between compactions. B — resuming carries the full exploration context into the implementation phase; nothing is isolated. C changes when the flooding happens, not whether it happens.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. questions.prompt: You've described a data transformation to Claude in prose three separate times, and each implementation handles the edge cases differently. What is the most effective way to communicate the expected behavior?

choices.text: Write a longer, more precise prose specification covering every edge case you can think of.
Provide 2–3 concrete input/output examples demonstrating the transformation and its edge cases.
Ask Claude to restate the requirements before implementing, and correct any misunderstandings.
Lower the temperature so the implementations are at least consistent with each other.

questions.explanation: Concrete input/output examples are the most effective way to communicate expected transformations when prose is being interpreted inconsistently — they pin down the edge cases directly. A produces more prose subject to the same interpretation problem. C surfaces misunderstandings but doesn't pin down edge-case behavior the way examples do. D makes outputs consistent, not correct.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Code Generation with Claude Code

questions.prompt: Two hours into a legacy-codebase exploration session, Claude starts describing "typical repository patterns" instead of the actual classes it read earlier, and gives inconsistent answers about code it correctly explained an hour ago. Which practice best counteracts this for ongoing long sessions?

choices.text: Ask Claude to "focus on the actual code, not typical patterns" whenever it drifts.
Paste the important files into the conversation again each time the drift appears.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so drift takes longer to appear.
Have Claude keep a scratchpad file of key findings and reference it for later questions.

questions.explanation: Context degradation in extended sessions (drifting to "typical patterns" instead of discovered specifics) is counteracted by persisting key findings to a scratchpad file and referencing it for subsequent questions — the findings survive outside degrading conversational context. A asks the model to fix a context problem with willpower. B repeatedly re-spends context and accelerates the problem. C delays symptoms without adding persistence.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Code Generation with Claude Code

questions.prompt: You're mapping a large legacy system. The main session's context is filling with raw file contents from exploration, leaving little room for the architectural reasoning you actually need. What is the best structural fix?

choices.text: Spawn subagents to investigate specific questions while the main agent coordinates high-level understanding.
Summarize each file immediately after reading it and remove the original contents from the conversation.
Read only public interfaces and type signatures, skipping the implementation bodies entirely.
Increase `max_tokens` so responses can be longer during the mapping phase.

questions.explanation: Delegating specific investigation questions to subagents isolates the verbose file-dump output in their contexts, while the main agent keeps its context for high-level coordination. B — the raw contents have already consumed context by the time they're summarized, and prior turns can't be selectively removed mid-session. C sacrifices the implementation-level understanding a legacy mapping needs. D is unrelated — `max_tokens` governs response length, not context accumulation.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.
questions.prompt: Mid-session, your context is nearly full of verbose discovery output, but you still need to implement the change in this session and want to keep the essential findings. What should you do?

choices.text: Start a brand-new session and rely on memory of what you learned.
Move the essential findings into the system prompt and clear the rest of the conversation.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation and reduce context usage while preserving key information.
Run `/clear` to reset context, keeping CLAUDE.md as the only persistent state.

questions.explanation: `/compact` summarizes the conversation to reduce context usage while preserving key information — the right mid-session relief valve when you need to keep working. A discards the findings (Claude has no cross-session memory of them). B isn't an available mid-session operation — the system prompt isn't an editable store for conversation findings. questions.prompt: You finished a week-long analysis phase for a large migration and are about to spawn implementation subagents for each module. How should the analysis inform the subagents?

choices.text: Rely on the subagents inheriting the coordinator session's memory of the analysis automatically.
Summarize the key findings and inject the relevant summary into each subagent's initial context.
Have each subagent redo its own analysis of the relevant module from scratch to guarantee freshness.
Pass the full multi-day session transcript to every subagent so nothing is lost.

questions.explanation: The reliable pattern is summarizing key findings from the completed phase and injecting the relevant summary into each subagent's initial context. A fails because subagents do not inherit parent context automatically. C re-spends a week of analysis. D floods each subagent's context with mostly-irrelevant transcript, inviting lost-in-the-middle problems.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. questions.prompt: Your overnight multi-agent refactoring job occasionally crashes around hour three, and today's restart lost all progress. What design provides crash recovery?

choices.text: Increase the job timeout so the crash-prone window is less likely to be hit.
Commit code changes to git after each module so completed work survives a crash.
Shrink the job scope so it finishes before the crash typically occurs.
Have agents export structured state to a known location; the coordinator loads this manifest on resume.

questions.explanation: Structured state persistence is the crash-recovery pattern: each agent exports completed work and key findings to a known location; on resume the coordinator loads the manifest and injects state into agent prompts, resuming rather than restarting. A and C reduce crash odds but don't recover from one. B preserves code edits but loses the agents' analysis state, task assignments, and findings — the coordinator still can't resume intelligently.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.
questions.prompt: You concatenated per-module analyses of 30 modules into a single prompt and asked for architecture recommendations. The recommendations consistently cite modules from the beginning and end of the input but ignore the middle third. What is the best mitigation?

choices.text: Place a key-findings summary first and organize the detail under explicit section headers.
Alphabetize the module sections so the ordering is neutral.
Add an instruction: "Pay equal attention to every module, especially those in the middle."
Switch to a model with a larger context window so all 30 modules fit more comfortably.

questions.explanation: This is the lost-in-the-middle effect: models reliably process the beginning and end of long inputs but may omit middle sections. The mitigation is a key-findings summary up front plus explicit section headers organizing the detail. B changes ordering without addressing position effects. C — instructions don't fix attention position biases. D — the effect persists in larger windows.
