questions.scenario: Scenario C: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: You're writing the GitHub Actions step that runs the automated review. It must run without any interactive input and emit output your comment-posting script can parse. Which invocation is correct?

choices.text: `claude "Review this PR" --interactive=false --format=structured`
`CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true claude "Review this PR" --parse`
`claude --batch "Review this PR" > findings.json`
`claude -p "Review this PR" --output-format json --json-schema review-schema.json`

questions.explanation: `-p` runs Claude Code non-interactively (print result and exit), and `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` yields machine-parseable, schema-conforming output. A, B, and C are built from flags and environment variables that don't exist (`--interactive`, `CLAUDE_HEADLESS`, `--batch`).

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Your pipeline generates code with Claude Code, then resumes the same session for the review step "so the reviewer understands why the code was written." The reviews almost never find issues, but human reviewers do. What should change?

choices.text: Run the review as an independent instance without the generation session's context.
Add "be maximally critical of the changes" to the review step's prompt.
Enable extended thinking for the review step so it reasons more deeply.
Keep the shared session but review each file twice.

questions.explanation: A session that generated the code retains the reasoning that produced it and is unlikely to question its own decisions; independent review instances catch what self-review misses. The "understands why" intuition is precisely the bias. B and C intensify a structurally biased review. D repeats it.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: The nightly test-generation job keeps proposing test scenarios that already exist in your spec files. What is the most direct fix?

choices.text: Run a deduplication pass comparing generated test names against existing test names.
Have Claude generate twice as many tests so at least some are novel.
Provide the existing test files in context and instruct Claude to propose only uncovered scenarios.
Limit generation to newly created source files, which cannot have tests yet.

questions.explanation: Provide the existing test files in context and instruct generation to avoid scenarios already covered — the model can't avoid duplicating tests it has never seen. A catches only name collisions, not semantic duplicates. B generates more duplicates alongside the novelty. D abandons coverage improvement for existing code, which was the point.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Your senior engineers each keep excellent review criteria in their personal `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` files. The CI runner's automated reviews follow none of these criteria. Why, and what is the fix?

choices.text: The CI runner needs the `--memory` flag to load user-level CLAUDE.md files.
User-level CLAUDE.md never reaches the CI environment — move the criteria into the project-level CLAUDE.md.
The criteria files are too large for non-interactive mode; they need to be under 10KB.
CI-invoked Claude Code cannot read CLAUDE.md at all; criteria must be passed as prompt flags.

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md lives in each engineer's home directory; the CI runner has no such files. Project-level CLAUDE.md is in the repository, so the CI checkout carries it. The fix is moving the criteria there (which also shares them with the whole team). A, C, and D describe flags and limits that don't exist.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Your CI review skill only needs to read code and report findings. A pipeline audit found one run where it executed `npm install` and modified `package-lock.json` in the workspace. What is the correct constraint?

choices.text: Run the CI job in a container where writes fail at the filesystem level.
Add "never install packages or modify files" to the skill's instructions.
Have the pipeline revert any workspace changes after the review step.
Configure `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to permit only read and reporting operations.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` in the skill frontmatter removes execution tools from availability during the skill — a structural guarantee that read-and-report is all it can do. A contains damage at the infrastructure layer but lets the harness misbehave inside it. B is instruction-based and already failed once. C cleans up afterward instead of preventing.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Your 400-line review checklist currently lives in the root CLAUDE.md. Every interactive session pays its token cost, though it's only needed when reviews run. The checklist must stay identical for interactive `/review` use and CI. Where should it live?

choices.text: In a review skill under `.claude/skills/`, loaded on demand when invoked by developers or CI.
Split across ten smaller CLAUDE.md sections so no single block is large.
In CLAUDE.md still, with an instruction telling Claude to ignore it outside reviews.
In user-level CLAUDE.md so only reviewers pay the cost.

questions.explanation: On-demand, task-specific content belongs in a skill: invoked identically by developers and CI, absent from unrelated sessions. That's the skills-vs-CLAUDE.md dividing line (always-loaded universal standards vs. on-demand workflows). B still loads everything, just in pieces. C pays full cost and adds an ignore instruction. D hides team-shared material in personal config.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Your changelog-generation step turns merged-PR titles into release notes. The prose spec ("group by type, past tense, link each PR") is interpreted differently across runs — grouping and tense drift. What is the most effective fix?

choices.text: Rewrite the spec with stricter language and bolded MUST requirements.
Add 2–3 concrete examples to the prompt: sample input commit lists with the exact changelog output expected.
Convert the spec into a numbered checklist the model must follow step by step.
Generate three drafts per run and have a second model choose the most compliant.

questions.explanation: When prose specs are interpreted inconsistently, concrete input/output examples are the most effective correction — they show the exact grouping, tense, and linking expected. A is stronger prose with the same ambiguity. C is still prose instructions, restructured — the interpretation variance remains. D spends three generations plus a judgment call to avoid writing two examples.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: You're using Claude to fix a data-transform module that intermittently fails in CI. You want an iteration loop that converges instead of whack-a-mole fixes. What is the best structure?

choices.text: Describe all known symptoms and ask for one comprehensive fix.
Ask Claude to review the module line by line and fix everything suspicious.
Rewrite the module from scratch, since accumulated fixes indicate unfixable design.
Write a test suite first covering behavior, edge cases, and performance; iterate by sharing failing output.

questions.explanation: Test-driven iteration: write the suite covering expected behavior, edge cases, and performance first, then iterate by sharing failures. The tests define "done" and each round has an objective target. A and B are single-shot or unfocused passes with no convergence criterion. C throws away working behavior on a hunch.

questions.prompt: You're about to build Claude Code into your deployment-approval flow — a domain with rollback semantics, partial-failure modes, and compliance constraints you haven't fully articulated. Which technique best surfaces the hidden requirements before implementation?

choices.text: Implement a minimal version first and let production incidents reveal the missing requirements.
Write the complete specification yourself before involving Claude at all.
Use the interview pattern — have Claude question you about failure modes and edge cases before implementing.
Copy the integration design from a published blog post by a team with a similar stack.

questions.explanation: The interview pattern is designed for unfamiliar domains with unarticulated constraints: Claude asks the questions that surface failure modes and edge cases you didn't think to specify. A discovers requirements via incidents. B assumes you can enumerate considerations you haven't anticipated — the exact gap. D imports another team's constraints, not yours.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Your review prompt has three problems that interact: the severity definitions conflict with the category definitions, which in turn contradict the output examples. Fixing them one at a time has caused regressions — each fix breaks under the next. How should you deliver the corrections?

choices.text: Address all three in a single detailed message explaining each problem and how they interact.
Fix them in three sequential messages, verifying each fix before the next.
Rebuild the prompt from an empty file, reintroducing requirements one by one.
Open three parallel sessions, fixing one problem in each, then merge the best parts.

questions.explanation: Interacting problems must be fixed together: one detailed message addressing all three and how they interrelate. Sequential fixes (B) are what's already regressing — each fix optimizes against soon-to-change context. C discards the working parts along with the broken ones. D produces three prompts that each still contain two of the conflicts.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Before your CI can validate it, you must migrate the repo's test framework — 45+ files, several valid migration strategies, and infrastructure implications for the CI runners themselves. How should you begin in Claude Code?

choices.text: Use direct execution file by file, since each individual file change is small.
Ask Claude to generate a shell script that performs the whole migration mechanically.
Enter plan mode to explore the codebase and compare migration strategies before changing anything.
Fork 45 parallel sessions, one per file, to complete the migration fastest.

questions.explanation: Multi-file scope (45+), multiple valid strategies, and infrastructure implications are the plan-mode trifecta: explore, compare approaches, and commit to a design before changing anything. A starts changing files before the strategy exists. B mechanizes a decision that hasn't been made. D parallelizes without an agreed approach — 45 sessions, several strategies.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Generated tests cover happy paths well but consistently miss branch-level gaps — error paths, boundary conditions, early returns. Detailed instructions ("cover all branches, including error handling") haven't changed the behavior. What is the most effective next step?

choices.text: Raise the coverage threshold in CI so incomplete test PRs fail automatically.
Add few-shot examples that demonstrate finding a function's branch-level gaps and writing the closing tests.
Switch the generation prompt to ask for twice as many tests per function.
Run mutation testing and feed surviving mutants back for another pass.

questions.explanation: When instructions fail to change behavior, few-shot examples demonstrating the analysis — here, spotting branch-level gaps and writing the closing tests — teach the judgment so the model generalizes it. A fails PRs without improving them. C multiplies happy-path tests. D is real but heavyweight infrastructure to reach for before trying examples.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: You're preparing your first Batch API run: overnight tech-debt analysis across 900 repositories with a prompt that has never been tested at scale. What should you do first?

choices.text: Submit all 900 and treat the first run as the test — batch costs are already discounted 50%.
Split the batch into two 450-repo halves so a bad prompt only wastes half the spend.
Add a retry wrapper that automatically resubmits any repo whose analysis looks wrong.
Refine the prompt on a small representative sample with the synchronous API, then submit the full batch.

questions.explanation: Refine the prompt on a representative sample before batch-processing large volumes: first-pass success is what controls cost when a batch is 900 items and results arrive up to 24 hours later. A risks 900 bad analyses and a full resubmission cycle. B halves the waste instead of preventing it. C automates resubmission of a prompt that was never validated.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Your overnight batch of 500 analysis requests completes with 38 failures, all caused by oversized diffs exceeding context limits. What is the correct recovery?

choices.text: Identify the failures by `custom_id`, chunk their oversized diffs, and resubmit only those 38.
Resubmit the full 500-request batch with a larger context configuration.
Rerun the 38 through the synchronous API unchanged, since it handles large inputs better.
Drop the 38 — a 92% completion rate is within tolerance for a nightly job.

questions.explanation: Batch failure handling: identify failed requests by `custom_id`, fix the cause (chunk the oversized diffs), and resubmit only those. B re-pays for 462 successful analyses (and "larger context configuration" isn't a batch setting). C re-sends the same oversized inputs to the same context limits. D silently drops the repos most likely to harbor debt — the biggest diffs.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: You want the pipeline to auto-approve PRs the review bot deems clean, but only where that trust is justified. The bot can emit a confidence score per finding. What makes the confidence usable for routing?

choices.text: Trust scores above 8/10, since models are generally reliable at the extremes.
Ask the model to justify each confidence score, and trust the ones with good justifications.
Calibrate it against a labeled validation set of past reviews and set routing thresholds from that data.
Use PR size instead — small PRs are safe to auto-approve regardless of bot confidence.

questions.explanation: Self-reported confidence is only usable after calibration: measure it against a labeled validation set with known outcomes and derive thresholds from measured accuracy. A trusts raw self-report — known to be poorly calibrated. B swaps numeric self-report for verbal self-report. D substitutes a proxy (size) for the measurement you need.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Your extraction prompt asks Claude to "respond with a JSON object" in its text reply. About 7% of responses fail parsing — trailing commas, markdown code fences, explanatory text before the JSON. What is the most reliable fix?

choices.text: Add "Respond with ONLY raw JSON, no markdown, no commentary" to the prompt.
Strip code fences and trailing commas with a preprocessing regex before parsing.
Switch the output format to XML, which tolerates minor malformation better.
Define an extraction tool whose input schema is your structure and read the data from the `tool_use` block.

questions.explanation: Tool use with a JSON schema is the reliable mechanism for structured output: the extraction "tool" input conforms to your schema, eliminating trailing commas, fences, and preambles as a failure class. A reduces frequency but keeps the class. B is an arms race with formatting drift. C changes the syntax without adding any guarantee.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Some invoices legitimately lack a PO number, but your schema marks `po_number` as required. Sampling reveals the model sometimes invents plausible-looking PO numbers for those invoices. What is the correct schema fix?

choices.text: Add a validation rule that rejects PO numbers not matching your company's format.
Make `po_number` optional/nullable and instruct the model to return null when the document has none.
Prompt the model to leave required fields as empty strings when data is missing.
Cross-check every extracted PO number against the purchasing database and drop mismatches.

questions.explanation: Required fields pressure the model to fabricate; fields that may legitimately be absent should be optional/nullable with instructions to return null. That removes the incentive to invent. A rejects fabrications after inviting them. C misuses empty strings as a null substitute while keeping the pressure. D is a downstream audit for an upstream schema problem.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Your `document_type` enum is `["invoice", "receipt", "purchase_order"]`. New document types keep arriving (credit memos, delivery notes), and the model shoehorns them into the closest existing value. How should the schema evolve?

choices.text: Remove the enum and make `document_type` free text so anything can be represented.
Add every document type your industry uses to the enum preemptively.
Add an `"other"` enum value paired with a free-text detail field describing the actual type.
Reject any document that doesn't match the three known types and queue it for humans.

questions.explanation: The extensible-category pattern: an `"other"` enum value plus a detail string. Novel types are captured faithfully instead of forced into the nearest wrong bucket. A loses the machine-readable categories downstream systems rely on. B guesses the future and still misses something. D turns every novel type into manual work.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: You defined three extraction tools — `extract_invoice`, `extract_contract`, `extract_resume` — and documents arrive with unknown type. Sometimes the model responds with prose about the document instead of extracting. Which configuration guarantees structured output while letting the model pick the right schema?

choices.text: `tool_choice: "any"` — the model must call some tool and selects the appropriate extraction schema.
`tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}` — force the most common type.
`tool_choice: "auto"` with a prompt instruction to always use a tool.
A separate classification model that routes each document to a forced single-tool call.

questions.explanation: `tool_choice: "any"` guarantees a tool call while leaving the choice of tool to the model — exactly right when multiple extraction schemas exist and the document type is unknown. B forces the invoice schema onto contracts and résumés. C ("auto") is what permits the prose responses today. D adds a model and a routing layer to replicate what "any" already does.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Contract extractions repeatedly fail validation with `governing_law: null`. Sampling shows the governing-law clause typically lives in a master agreement referenced by, but not included with, the contracts you send. Will retry-with-error-feedback fix this?

choices.text: Yes — include the validation error and the model will look harder at the contract text.
No — retries can't recover information absent from the input; supply the master agreement or accept the null.
Yes, but only with 3+ retries and escalating temperature to explore more readings.
No — the field should be dropped from the schema since it cannot be extracted.

questions.explanation: Retries correct format and structural errors; they cannot recover information that is absent from the provided input. The governing law lives in a document the model never sees. Fix the input pipeline or handle the null explicitly. A and C retry harder at reading text that isn't there. D deletes a business-required field because the pipeline starves it.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Invoice line items sometimes don't sum to the stated total — occasionally an OCR artifact, occasionally a genuine source-document error. Downstream systems must not silently receive bad totals. What extraction design handles this?

choices.text: Have the model recompute the total from line items and output the corrected value in place of the stated one.
Reject any invoice where the arithmetic fails and return it to the sender.
Trust `stated_total` always — the document is the source of truth.
Extract `calculated_total` alongside `stated_total`, with a `conflict_detected` flag when they disagree.

questions.explanation: Extracting `calculated_total` alongside `stated_total` with a `conflict_detected` flag is the self-correction/validation design: discrepancies are surfaced, not silently passed through (C) or silently overwritten (A — which hides genuine source-document errors that may matter legally). B treats every OCR artifact as a sender problem and stalls the pipeline.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Résumé extraction works well on standard corporate résumés but returns null for required-in-source fields on academic CVs and international formats, where the information exists but appears in unfamiliar sections. What is the most effective fix?

choices.text: Lengthen the field descriptions in the schema so the model knows the fields matter.
Run two extraction passes and merge the non-null values from each.
Add few-shot examples showing correct extraction from an academic CV and an international format.
Preprocess all documents into a standardized layout before extraction.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples demonstrating extraction from varied document structures are the established fix for structure-driven misses — they show where the information lives in each format, and the model generalizes to further variants. A re-describes fields the model already understands. B reruns the same blindness twice. D presumes a reliable universal normalizer, which is the original problem restated.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Source documents write dates as "3/4/25", "March 4th, 2025", and "04-03-2025" (ambiguous day/month order), while your schema requires ISO 8601. What should accompany the strict output schema?

choices.text: Format normalization rules in the prompt: how to map each source format to ISO 8601, how to resolve ambiguous orderings, and when to mark a date unresolvable.
A post-processing date parser that converts whatever the model outputs.
A looser schema accepting dates as free text, normalized downstream.
Rejection of documents whose dates aren't already ISO 8601.

questions.explanation: Strict output schemas should be paired with format normalization rules in the prompt: how to map each source format to ISO 8601, how to disambiguate day/month order (e.g., from document context), and when to mark a value unresolvable. B pushes ambiguity downstream to a parser with even less context than the model had. C just relocates the problem. D rejects most real-world documents.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Your extraction system reports 97% overall accuracy, and leadership wants to cut human review by 80%. What must you verify before agreeing?

choices.text: That the 97% was measured within the last quarter.
That accuracy holds up when segmented by document type and by field.
That accuracy exceeds 97% on the most recent week of documents specifically.
That reviewer headcount can be reabsorbed elsewhere if the cut proceeds.

questions.explanation: Aggregate accuracy can mask severe failures on specific segments; before reducing review, verify accuracy by document type and field. A flat 97% is consistent with near-total failure on one vendor's layout. A and C re-slice by time, not by segment. D is a staffing question, not a validation of the automation's safety.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: You automated the pipeline for high-confidence extractions. Six months from now, how will you know whether new error patterns have crept into the extractions no human looks at?

choices.text: Human review already covers the low-confidence extractions; errors would appear there first.
Track the distribution of confidence scores over time and investigate when the average drifts.
Re-run the original validation benchmark quarterly against the same benchmark documents.
Keep stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions under ongoing human review.

questions.explanation: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions provides ongoing error-rate measurement and catches novel error patterns in exactly the population no one otherwise inspects. A assumes new errors will conveniently arrive with low confidence — miscalibration means they won't. B monitors the model's opinion of itself, not actual accuracy; confidently-wrong errors never move the average. C can't detect novel patterns absent from the original benchmark.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: You calibrated the field-level confidence thresholds that decide which extractions skip human review against a labeled validation set six months ago. This week you substantially revised the extraction prompt to support several new document types. What should happen to the thresholds?

choices.text: Keep them — thresholds attach to the output schema, which did not change.
Recalibrate against labeled data before trusting them; the confidence-accuracy mapping may have shifted.
Raise them by a fixed 10% margin until a quarter of new production data accumulates.
Lower them temporarily, since the revised prompt should be more accurate than the old one.

questions.explanation: Calibration maps confidence to measured accuracy *for a specific system*; substantially changing the prompt changes that mapping, so thresholds must be re-validated against labeled data before extractions skip review on their strength. A ties calibration to the wrong artifact — the schema didn't drive the mapping, the model+prompt did. C and D adjust blindly in opposite directions; neither is a measurement.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Your reviewers can inspect 500 documents daily out of 10,000 processed, and your goal is to catch as many extraction errors as possible with that fixed capacity. Which routing strategy best serves the goal?

choices.text: Review the 500 highest-dollar-value documents, since errors there cost the most.
Review a uniform random 5% so every document type has equal audit probability.
Route low-confidence extractions and those from ambiguous or contradictory sources to review.
Review the newest documents first, since recent formats are least familiar to the model.

questions.explanation: To catch the most errors with fixed capacity, route review to where errors are most likely: low model confidence and ambiguous or contradictory source documents. A targets cost-of-error, not likelihood-of-error — high-value documents are mostly extracted correctly. B spreads capacity evenly over mostly-fine documents. D uses recency as a weak proxy for difficulty.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Your extraction service supports a multi-turn correction chat: users point out extraction mistakes and the model revises. Users report the model "forgets" corrections from two turns earlier. The service sends each API request with only the latest user message. What is the fix?

choices.text: Send the complete conversation history in every API request.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the model to remember all prior corrections.
Cache the model's last response client-side and re-send it with each new message.
Store corrections in a database and have the model query them through a tool.

questions.explanation: The API is stateless: conversational coherence requires passing the complete conversation history in every request. Sending only the latest message *is* the bug. B instructs the model to remember context it was never sent. C restores one turn of history — corrections from two turns back stay lost. D rebuilds conversation memory as external infrastructure.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Each extraction is enriched via a vendor-lookup MCP tool that returns 40+ fields per call, of which your workflow uses 5. Long enrichment sessions degrade noticeably and sometimes overflow context. What is the right fix?

choices.text: Call the vendor-lookup tool less often by batching several vendors per call.
Move to a model with a larger context window to absorb the verbose results.
Summarize the conversation with /compact after every ten enrichments.
Trim the tool output to the relevant fields before it accumulates in context.

questions.explanation: Verbose tool outputs consume context disproportionately to their relevance; trimming to the relevant fields before results accumulate (tool-side or via a PostToolUse transformation) fixes the accumulation at the source. A changes call frequency, not per-call bloat. B delays the overflow and doesn't address degradation. C summarizes after the tokens are already spent, repeatedly.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: A nightly job must cross-reference 20 related documents in a single request (they reference each other, so they can't be processed separately). Fields sourced from documents in the middle of the concatenated input show markedly higher miss rates than those near the start and end. What is the best mitigation?

choices.text: Randomize document order nightly so no document is always in the middle.
Duplicate the middle documents at the end of the input so they appear twice.
Add a key-facts summary at the beginning and organize the documents under labeled section headers.
Instruct the model: "Documents in the middle are equally important; do not skip them."

questions.explanation: This is the lost-in-the-middle effect. Since splitting the request isn't possible, apply the position mitigations: a key-facts summary at the beginning and explicit, labeled section headers organizing the detail. A rotates which fields get missed. B doubles input size and still buries other documents. D — position effects are not fixed by exhortation. --- *End of Practice Exam 7.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: A teammate's loop implementation treats any response containing text content as the end of the conversation. In testing, the loop terminates on responses like "Let me look up that order for you" that also contain a pending `tool_use` block. What is the flaw?

choices.text: The text check should be inverted: responses with no text content indicate completion.
The model should be prompted to never emit text and tool calls together, making the check safe.
The loop should wait for two consecutive text-bearing responses before terminating.
Text is not a completion signal — the loop must inspect `stop_reason` and continue on `"tool_use"`.

questions.explanation: Text content is not a completion signal: responses routinely carry narration alongside `tool_use` blocks. The loop must inspect `stop_reason` and continue on `"tool_use"`. A inverts a check that shouldn't exist. B prompts around a control-flow bug. C doubles down on the wrong signal.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.scenario_context: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.prompt: Your agent updated a shipping address after matching only the customer's stated name, and the package went to the wrong person's account. The system prompt already says identity must be verified first. How do you make verification a hard guarantee?

choices.text: Add the verification rule to both the system prompt and the `update_address` tool description.
Block `update_address` and other account mutations until `get_customer` has returned a verified ID.

Require the customer to type a confirmation phrase before the agent proceeds.

The intent matcher should be a small classifier model instead of regex.

Keyword pre-routing overrides the model's contextual judgment — remove it and let Claude reason about intent.

questions.prompt: Your pipeline requires `extract_metadata` to run on every document before any enrichment tool may be called. The model usually complies with the prompt instruction but occasionally jumps straight to enrichment. What guarantees the ordering?

choices.text: Force it: `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}` on the first request, then normal tool choice.
Set `tool_choice: "any"` so a tool is always called first.
List `extract_metadata` first in the tools array, since order implies priority.
Add few-shot examples demonstrating metadata-first ordering.

questions.explanation: Guaranteeing that a specific tool runs first requires forced tool selection: `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}` on the first request, with enrichment handled in follow-up turns. B guarantees *a* tool, not *that* tool. C — array order carries no such semantics. D remains probabilistic.

questions.prompt: You're designing the invoice schema and must decide which fields are `required`. Which principle is correct?

choices.text: Mark all business-critical fields required so the model knows they matter.
Mark everything optional to maximize extraction flexibility.
Require only fields genuinely present in every document; make possibly-absent fields optional/nullable.
Mark required whatever downstream systems need, regardless of the documents.

questions.explanation: Required should mean "genuinely always present." Fields that may legitimately be absent must be optional/nullable, or the model is pressured to fabricate values to satisfy the schema. A confuses importance with presence. B loses real invariants. D encodes downstream wishes the documents can't honor.

Instruct the model to "never guess" in the system prompt.
Route all logs containing the word "about" to human review.
Add few-shot examples mapping informal measurements to estimates (with a flag) or to null.

The original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation errors together.

questions.prompt: Documents arrive continuously and your contract guarantees results within 30 hours. Batch processing can take up to 24 hours. Which submission schedule guarantees the SLA while minimizing submission overhead?

Every 12 hours with a priority flag on older documents.
Every 8 hours — the tighter cadence usually leaves several hours of margin in practice.
Submit a batch every 4 hours.

questions.prompt: An extracted vendor name matches three different vendor records in your master file. The pipeline currently auto-selects the most recently active vendor. What should it do instead?

choices.text: Treat the multiple match as ambiguity: disambiguate with identifiers from the document, else route to review.
Auto-select the vendor with the closest string match instead of recent activity.
Create a new vendor record to avoid guessing among the three.
Auto-select the highest-transaction-volume vendor, the statistically likeliest match.

questions.explanation: Multiple matches are an ambiguity to resolve with additional identifiers (address, tax ID from the document), not a heuristic pick; when identifiers don't resolve it, route to human review. B and D swap one heuristic for another — statistically likely is still a guess with someone's money. C corrupts the master file.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Your extraction summary report converts everything to prose paragraphs — including line-item tables and numeric comparisons — and reviewers say checking figures is painful. What is the recommended presentation?

choices.text: Convert everything to tables instead, since reviewers prefer them.
Provide raw JSON to reviewers, who can format it as needed.
Render each content type appropriately — tables for financial data, prose for narrative, lists for findings.
Add a "figures appendix" repeating all numbers at the end of the prose.

questions.explanation: Content types should render in the form that fits them: financial data as tables, narrative as prose, findings as structured lists — uniform formatting is the anti-pattern in both directions. questions.prompt: Your loop executes the agent's tool calls but the next API request fails with a 400 error complaining about `tool_use` blocks that have no corresponding `tool_result` blocks. What did the implementation skip?

Appending each tool's result as a `tool_result` block (matched to its `tool_use` ID) before the next request.
Clearing the previous assistant message before sending the new request.
Re-registering the tool definitions on every request.

questions.explanation: Every executed `tool_use` must be answered with a matching `tool_result` block appended to the conversation before the next request; the 400 error is the API telling you the loop skipped that step. A, C, and D are unrelated request mechanics — none satisfies the missing-result contract.

Add a second model that reviews each refund decision before execution.
Move the gift-card rule into the `process_refund` tool description.
Intercept `process_refund` with a hook that blocks gift-card refunds and redirects to goodwill credit.

questions.explanation: A monthly-violated financial policy needs interception: a hook that blocks gift-card refunds at the tool-call level and redirects to the goodwill workflow. C relocates prompt text; descriptions guide selection, they don't enforce.

Few-shot examples of the agent politely refusing unverified email changes.
A prerequisite gate: `update_email` stays blocked until verification has actually completed in the current session.
A daily audit report of email changes for the fraud team.

Use an adaptive investigation plan: form a hypothesis, run a lookup, and let each finding set the next step.
Escalate immediately, since no runbook exists for this symptom pattern.
Run every available lookup tool once, then decide from the combined results.

questions.explanation: No-runbook, unknown-cause investigations call for adaptive plans: hypothesize, look up, let findings drive the next step. Resume yesterday's session unchanged — continuity matters most.
Resume yesterday's session and instruct the agent to distrust any tool results.
Start fresh with no context and let the customer re-explain the situation.

Identity must be verified before account mutations.
Responses should acknowledge the customer's frustration before presenting solutions.
Refunds must go only to the original payment method.

questions.prompt: The agent calls `lookup_order` with the date "next Tuesday" in a field expecting `YYYY-MM-DD`. How should the tool respond so the agent can recover in one step?

choices.text: `isError` with a generic "invalid request" so the agent tries something else.
Silently interpret "next Tuesday" server-side using the current date.
A transient-category error so the agent retries the same call.
A validation error naming the field, stating the expected format (`YYYY-MM-DD`), and marked correctable.

questions.explanation: A malformed input is a validation error: name the field, state the expected format, and mark it correctable so the agent fixes the argument and re-calls in one step. Rename `process_refund` to `process_refund_not_exchange`.
Block exchange-context refunds with a hook and let the error teach the agent.
Merge refunds and exchanges into one `resolve_return` tool.

questions.explanation: Tool descriptions should state boundaries — what the tool is for and what it is not for, naming the alternative. The agent chooses refunds because nothing signals exchanges are out of scope. B abuses naming to carry documentation. C teaches by failure at customer expense. D merges two flows with different semantics, creating a new selection problem inside one tool.

Add a mandatory reasoning step before every tool call.
Scope tool access by role — split into specialized agents, each carrying only the tools its role needs.
Shorten all tool descriptions so the full list fits in less context.

questions.explanation: Selection reliability degrades as the tool count grows; the correction is scoped tool access — split by role so each agent carries only the handful of tools its job needs. Skip MCP and call Zendesk's REST API from a hook.
Wrap Zendesk's API in your existing backend and expose one mega-tool.

questions.prompt: A platform wrapper catches all tool exceptions and returns `{}` with a success status "to keep conversations smooth." Yesterday the agent told a customer their refund was complete when `process_refund` had actually thrown. What is the design lesson?

choices.text: Wrappers should return `null` rather than `{}` so downstream code can detect the failures.
The agent should verify refunds with a follow-up lookup after every attempt.
The wrapper needs better logging so engineers catch these incidents sooner.
Failures must surface as structured errors, not be disguised as successes.

The fix is structured errors that surface. A trades one sentinel for another — still not an error the agent can reason about. B adds a verification round-trip to compensate for lying infrastructure. Escalate to a human immediately — high negative sentiment indicates a case the bot shouldn't touch.
Escalate if sentiment remains negative after the agent's first empathetic response.
Process the replacement silently without addressing the tone.

Handle issues strictly one at a time, closing each before discussing the next.
Persist each issue's structured data (order ID, amount, status, next action) in a separate context layer, keyed by issue.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: Reports on "the impact of an aging population" consistently cover only healthcare; labor markets, housing, and public pensions never appear. The coordinator's decomposition logs show subtasks like "hospital staffing shortages" and "elder-care costs." What is the fix?

choices.text: Improve the coordinator's decomposition: enumerate the topic's major domains first, then create subtasks against that list with coverage criteria.
Instruct the search agent to broaden every query it receives with additional sectors.
Add a fourth subagent dedicated to domains the others miss.
Have the synthesis agent note in the report which domains received less attention.

questions.explanation: The decomposition is the failure point: the coordinator collapsed a broad topic into one domain's subtasks. Fix decomposition — enumerate the topic's major domains first, then generate subtasks against that enumeration with coverage criteria. B patches queries downstream of bad assignments. C adds a guessing agent. D documents the gap instead of closing it.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. Findings arrive out of order, some overwrite others, and nobody detects missing pieces. Which component should own result collection, and why?

choices.text: The report agent, since it consumes the results anyway.
The shared channel, upgraded with ordering and dedup logic.
The coordinator — aggregation, completeness checks, and error handling belong at the hub.
Each subagent, verifying its own delivery with a read-back check.

questions.explanation: In hub-and-spoke architecture, aggregation belongs to the coordinator: one place for completeness checks, ordering, and error handling before synthesis. A gives the consumer an orchestration job. B rebuilds coordinator responsibilities inside a message bus. D verifies delivery without anyone owning the whole picture.

questions.prompt: After an expensive shared analysis of a 400-document corpus, you want to evaluate two competing report frameworks — thematic versus chronological — each developed independently from that same analysis. What mechanism does the Agent SDK provide?

choices.text: `--resume` the analysis session twice, once per framework.
`fork_session` — two independent branches from the shared analysis baseline, one framework in each.
Run the analysis twice in two fresh sessions, one per framework.
Develop both frameworks alternately within the single session.

questions.explanation: `fork_session` creates independent branches from a shared analysis baseline — each framework develops in isolation without re-paying for the 400-document analysis and without cross-contamination. A resumes one lineage twice into the same history. C re-buys the corpus analysis. D lets each framework bias the other.

Both fixed — consistency simplifies operations.
The digest dynamic and the investigations fixed, since digests have more room for creativity.
The weekly digest as a fixed prompt chain; the ad-hoc investigations with dynamic decomposition.

questions.explanation: Match decomposition to predictability: the six-section weekly digest is a fixed prompt chain; novel ad-hoc investigations need dynamic decomposition that adapts to findings. A adds adaptive overhead to clockwork. B scripts the unscriptable. C assigns each pipeline the wrong pattern.

questions.prompt: Monday's run must gather updates from six independent news domains before synthesis. The coordinator currently delegates them one per turn. What single change most reduces wall-clock time?

choices.text: Have the coordinator emit all six Task tool calls in one response so they run in parallel.
Cache Friday's results and only fetch weekend changes.
Reduce each domain's search depth so sequential runs finish faster.
Move synthesis earlier so it overlaps with the last two searches.

questions.explanation: Independent gathering tasks parallelize by emitting all six Task calls in a single coordinator response. B changes what is fetched, not the serialization. C makes each sequential step cheaper but keeps six round-trips. D starts synthesis before its inputs exist.

questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: A reviewer flags this coordinator code: `if "DONE" in assistant_text: break` — paired with a system prompt instructing the model to "say DONE when research is complete." What is the professional assessment?

choices.text: Acceptable — explicit completion markers are a common convention in agent frameworks.
The marker should be structured (a JSON field) rather than a bare string in prose.
Termination should key off `stop_reason` (`"end_turn"`), not a natural-language marker.
The check is fine but should also require that no tool calls are pending in the response.

questions.explanation: Natural-language completion markers are the classic termination anti-pattern: they fire spuriously (the model discusses "DONE"), get paraphrased away, and duplicate what `stop_reason` already provides reliably. A normalizes the anti-pattern. B structures the wrong mechanism. D patches one failure mode of a signal that shouldn't be the signal.

questions.prompt: Researching an extremely niche topic, the search subagent's query legitimately matches nothing. The tool returns an error, and the coordinator logs "search infrastructure degraded" and switches to a fallback provider — wasting a cycle. What is the correct contract?

choices.text: The tool should return the closest partial matches instead of nothing.
The coordinator should ping a health-check endpoint before interpreting errors.
Empty results and failures can share a response shape if the log message differs.
Zero matches is a successful query with an empty result set; errors are reserved for access failures.

questions.explanation: Zero matches from a valid query is a *successful* search; conflating it with failure caused a pointless failover. Tools must distinguish valid empty results from access failures. A substitutes wrong results for honest emptiness. B adds infrastructure to disambiguate what the response shape should state. C keeps the ambiguity and hides the distinction in logs the agent never sees.

Usage statistics showing typical query lengths.
A warning that search quality varies by topic.

questions.explanation: Descriptions should document input formats, limits, and edge-case behavior — a 256-character truncation is exactly the constraint an agent needs to compose valid queries. A and C are metadata that don't prevent the failure. D is a disclaimer, not a contract.

choices.text: Enhance the description: what it searches, what it returns, and when to prefer it over general web search.
Remove WebSearch from the agent so arxiv_search wins by default.
Add a system prompt rule to always use arxiv_search for anything containing the word "paper."
Lower WebSearch's priority via tool ordering.

questions.explanation: The agent prefers the tool it understands; "Searches arXiv" gives no case for selection. Enhance the description — what it searches, what it returns, when to prefer it over general web search. B removes a tool still needed for non-academic queries. C is keyword-matching brittleness. questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. questions.prompt: The document analysis agent abandons its entire assignment the first time a PDF-parsing call times out, reporting total failure to the coordinator even when 9 of 10 documents parsed fine. What error-handling design is missing?

choices.text: A longer parsing timeout so failures stop happening.
A coordinator-side retry of the whole document analysis task.
Local recovery: retry the failed parse, continue with the rest, and propagate only the unresolved failure with partial results.
Parallel parsing so one timeout doesn't serialize the rest.

questions.explanation: Subagents should recover locally from transient failures (retry the parse) and, failing that, continue the assignment — propagating only the unresolvable failure with partial results. Nine parsed documents is a report, not a total failure. A pretends timeouts can be configured away. B re-runs everything including the nine successes. D addresses throughput, not the give-up-entirely logic.

questions.prompt: While analyzing a corpus, the analysis agent finds two credible papers reporting incompatible efficacy figures. It currently discards the outlier and reports one clean number. What should it do instead?

choices.text: Report the average of the two figures with a note describing the variance.
Hold both papers back from synthesis until a human adjudicates.
Re-run the analysis with instructions to prefer the more recent paper.
Include both values, annotated with source and methodology, and let the coordinator decide reconciliation.

questions.explanation: Conflicting values from credible sources are completed analysis, not noise: include both, annotated with source and methodology, and let the coordinator decide reconciliation before synthesis. A invents a number no source reported, however carefully footnoted. B stalls the pipeline where annotation suffices. C encodes an arbitrary tiebreak (recency) as truth.

questions.prompt: The synthesis agent regularly misdates events and attributes findings to the wrong methodology. Upstream, the analysis agent's outputs are well-written prose summaries. What structural requirement fixes this?

Require the analysis agent to attach metadata — dates, source locations, methodology — to every structured finding.
Have the synthesis agent flag any date it is unsure about.
Use a stronger model for synthesis so it infers metadata more accurately.

A sends synthesis hunting for facts upstream already had. C flags the symptom. D asks a better model to guess better.

Raise the synthesis agent's budget and accept the cost.
Have synthesis summarize its input first, then synthesize the summary.
Have upstream agents return structured key facts, citations, and relevance scores sized for the consumer.

In report review — a final pass that re-checks every claim against sources.
By excluding pilot studies from research entirely.
By having the search agent rank small studies lower.

Run two identical pipelines in parallel and keep whichever finishes.
Agents export structured state as they work; on resume the coordinator loads the manifest and injects prior state.
Schedule runs during the provider's historically most stable hours.

Edit with `replace_all`, then revert the four unwanted changes with four more Edits.
Read the file, then Write it back with the single intended occurrence modified.

`--non-interactive`, which auto-answers prompts with defaults.
`--quiet`, which suppresses interactive input requests.
`-p` (`--print`) — process the prompt, print the result, and exit.

questions.prompt: Developers complain that after each push, the review bot re-posts its full findings list, burying the thread. What re-review design fixes the noise?

choices.text: Feed prior findings into the re-review context; post only new issues, noting which prior ones remain open.
Only run the bot once per PR, on first open.
Have the bot delete its old comments before posting the new full list.
Replace inline comments with a single continuously-edited summary comment at the top of the PR.

questions.explanation: The re-review pattern: prior findings go into context, and the bot reports only new issues plus a note on which prior ones remain unaddressed — no duplicates, threads preserved. B leaves post-push changes unreviewed. C destroys the discussion threads reviewers asked to keep. D abandons the inline-comment requirement entirely.

`claude -p "..." --strict` to enable careful output mode.
`claude -p "..." --output-format json --json-schema findings-schema.json`
`claude -p "..."` with a prompt instruction to "output valid JSON matching our schema."

questions.explanation: Guaranteed field names and types come from `--output-format json` with `--json-schema`: schema-enforced structure for machine parsing. A and D parse unguaranteed output defensively or hopefully. B is an invented flag.

choices.text: "Only flag comments you are highly confident are wrong."
"Flag a comment only when its claimed behavior contradicts what the code actually does."
"Flag at most three comments per pull request."
"Prefer flagging comments on public APIs over internal helpers."

questions.explanation: Effective criteria are specific and categorical: flag only when the comment's claimed behavior contradicts the code. Noise increases token costs, which dominate the tool's budget.
The style category's noise statistically hides the security findings in long lists.
High false-positive categories erode trust in the whole tool — the accurate security findings get ignored too.

questions.explanation: False-positive-heavy categories destroy trust in the whole tool: developers who learn to skim past style noise skim past the accurate security findings too. For clear-cut cases it chooses well, but for ambiguous ones (a real bug that's out of the PR's scope; a severe issue in unchanged code) it picks inconsistently. What most improves these decisions?

A decision matrix in prose mapping issue attributes to tools.
Removing `open_issue` so there are fewer choices.
Making `request_changes` the default for any uncertainty.

questions.explanation: Ambiguous cases are the targeted-few-shot case: examples of exactly these situations, showing the chosen tool *and the reasoning* over plausible alternatives, teach judgment the model generalizes. choices.text: A markdown linter that rejects malformed summaries and triggers regeneration.
Few-shot examples showing complete sample summaries in the exact required table format.
Lowering temperature to reduce formatting creativity.
A stricter prose description of the table with column widths specified.

questions.explanation: Format consistency comes from demonstration: complete sample summaries in the exact required table. Description (D), even stricter, keeps producing drift; that's the observed failure. A regenerates until lucky. C reduces variance around a format the model hasn't internalized.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `tool_choice` is correct?

choices.text: `"auto"` guarantees at least one tool call per response.
`"any"` lets the model call any number of tools, while `"auto"` limits it to one.
`"auto"` may yield text only; `"any"` forces some tool call; `{"type": "tool", "name": ...}` forces a specific one.
Forced tool selection applies to every subsequent turn until reset.

questions.explanation: The correct trio: `"auto"` permits text-only responses; `"any"` mandates some tool call, model's choice; forced selection mandates one named tool. A describes "any." B invents count semantics. D — forcing applies per-request, not until reset.

Free-form "reason for dismissal" text boxes, reviewed monthly.
A `detected_pattern` field in each suggestion identifying the construct that triggered it.

questions.explanation: A structured `detected_pattern` field ties every suggestion to the construct that triggered it, so dismissals aggregate into pattern-level insight — the systematic feedback loop. A and C produce anecdote at low volume. B counts dismissals without capturing what caused them.

questions.prompt: The review bot's finding — "this implementation may not match the approved design" — fails validation because it cites a design document the bot was never given. Will retry-with-error-feedback resolve it?

choices.text: No — the design document was never provided; supply it in context or scope the review to what's available.
Yes — the validation error will make the bot reason more carefully about the design.
Yes, if the retry also raises `max_tokens` for deeper analysis.
No — findings referencing external documents should be auto-deleted.

questions.explanation: The design document was never in the input; no retry recovers information that isn't there. Provide the document, or scope the review to available material. B and C retry harder at reading an absent file. D deletes a category wholesale when the fix is supplying context.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Two jobs are proposed for the Message Batches API: (1) a nightly "explain every lint suppression in the repo" report read weekly; (2) the PR-blocking security gate developers wait on before merging. Evaluate.

choices.text: Both fit — the 50% savings applies to both equally.
Job 1 fits (latency-tolerant, non-blocking); job 2 cannot depend on a no-SLA, up-to-24-hour service.
Neither fits — CI workloads need real-time APIs across the board.
Job 2 fits better, since security scans are heavier and benefit more from discounts.

questions.explanation: Batch fits latency-tolerant, non-blocking work: the nightly report is ideal; a merge-blocking gate cannot ride a no-SLA, up-to-24-hour service. A ignores the blocking constraint. C overcorrects — the report genuinely fits. D prices workloads instead of matching latency requirements.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: Your overnight batch analyzes 300 open PRs. When results return, the poster must attach each analysis to the right PR. How is the mapping maintained?

choices.text: Results return in submission order, so index alignment suffices.
Ask the model to embed the PR number in its own output text.
Submit 300 separate single-request batches so each result is unambiguous.
Set each request's `custom_id` to its PR number at submission and route each result by it.

questions.explanation: `custom_id` is the Batch API's request/response correlation mechanism: set it to the PR number at submission, read it on each result. A relies on ordering the API doesn't promise. B trusts model output for plumbing. C abandons batching's economics to avoid using the feature built for this.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: One pipeline job generates a bug fix and then, in the same session, reviews that fix before auto-merging. Post-incident analysis shows the reviews approve nearly everything, including a fix that broke production. What is the structural correction?

choices.text: Add "assume the fix is wrong until proven otherwise" to the review prompt.
Require two self-review passes before the auto-merge.
Split generation and review: an independent instance reviews the diff without the generator's session context.
Auto-merge only fixes under 20 lines, reviewing larger ones manually.

questions.explanation: Generation and review must be separated: an independent review instance receives the diff without the generator's session context, avoiding the self-approval bias that shipped the bad fix. A and B prompt or repeat a structurally biased review. D limits exposure without fixing the reviewer.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: A 16-file PR gets inconsistent review depth — thorough on early files, thin on later ones — and the bot approved a cross-file API change in one file while flagging its mirror image in another. How should the review be restructured?

choices.text: Reverse file order on a second pass and merge both passes' findings.
Split into per-file passes for local issues plus a dedicated cross-file integration pass.
Cap PRs at 6 files via repository policy.
Increase the review job's `max_tokens` so later files get more budget.

questions.explanation: Declining depth across files plus contradictory verdicts on mirrored code are attention dilution; the restructure is per-file passes for local issues and a separate integration pass for cross-file consistency. A averages two diluted passes. C constrains developers to fit the tool. D — token budget doesn't reallocate attention across a long input.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.scenario_context: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.
questions.prompt: You want findings the bot is demonstrably reliable about to post automatically, while shakier ones queue for human moderation. The bot emits a per-finding confidence score. What makes this routing sound?

choices.text: Validate first: measure accuracy per confidence level against labeled findings, then set the auto-post threshold.
Trust findings at confidence ≥ 9/10; models rarely overstate certainty at the top of the scale.
Route by category instead — security findings to humans, everything else auto-posts.
Auto-post everything but add a "low confidence" label where the score is low.

questions.explanation: Confidence becomes routable only after calibration: measure accuracy at each score level against labeled outcomes and place the threshold where precision meets the bar. B trusts raw self-report at the extreme — where miscalibration concentrates. C discards per-finding signal for category stereotype. D posts everything anyway, labeling the risk instead of routing it. --- *End of Practice Exam 9.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code

Re-clone the repository on the desktop.
Run `/memory` on both machines to see which memory files each session actually loaded.
Run `/compact` on the desktop session to clear interfering context.

questions.explanation: Same repo, different behavior across machines points at configuration loading, and `/memory` shows exactly which memory files each session loaded — diagnose before changing anything. The likely culprit is user-level configuration present on one machine only. A, B, and D change things before establishing what differs.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code

choices.text: In each package's CLAUDE.md, use `@import` to pull in only the standards files relevant to that package.
Concatenate all four files into the root CLAUDE.md.
Copy the relevant files into each package directory.
Reference all four from every package CLAUDE.md, letting Claude judge relevance.

questions.explanation: `@import` lets each package's CLAUDE.md include only the standards files relevant to it — one copy of each standard, selectively composed. B loads everything everywhere. C duplicates and drifts. D loads all four and hopes the model scopes them correctly.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
