choices.text: Freeze the file and require RFC approval for changes.
Move it to a wiki and link from CLAUDE.md.
Auto-generate it nightly from team documentation.
Split it into focused topic files under `.claude/rules/`, each owned by the appropriate team.

questions.explanation: The recommended structure for a contested monolith: topic-specific files under `.claude/rules/`, each owned by the team that owns the topic — smaller diffs, fewer conflicts, clearer ownership. A freezes the pain in place. B removes the content from Claude's view. C generates a monolith instead of splitting it.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: Your database-seeding workflow — 300 lines of steps, fixtures, and cleanup logic — is used about once a week. Universal code conventions are used in every session. Where does each belong?

choices.text: Both in CLAUDE.md, since both matter.
Conventions in CLAUDE.md (always loaded); the seeding workflow as a skill in `.claude/skills/`.
Both in skills, to minimize context cost.
Conventions in a skill; the seeding workflow in CLAUDE.md.

questions.explanation: The dividing line: universal always-applicable content in CLAUDE.md; occasional task-specific workflows as skills loaded on invocation. A pays 300 lines of seeding logic in every session. C makes universal conventions opt-in. D is backwards on both.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: Your `/explore-alternatives` skill generates several competing design sketches. After it runs, the main session's context carries all the rejected sketches, and Claude later resurrects abandoned ideas as if they were current. What frontmatter fixes this?

choices.text: `context: fork` — the exploration runs isolated and only the selected direction returns.
`argument-hint`, so the skill is scoped to one design question.
`allowed-tools`, so the skill can't write the sketches to files.
`paths`, restricting the skill to design documents.

questions.explanation: Exploratory content that shouldn't persist is what `context: fork` isolates: the sketches live in the fork, and only the chosen direction returns. B narrows scope without isolating the residue. C affects file writes, not conversation context. D isn't the mechanism for this.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: Your `/update-changelog` skill needs only to read the git log and edit `CHANGELOG.md`. An incident review found a run where it also executed `git tag` and pushed the tag. What is the structural fix?

choices.text: Add "never create or push tags" to the skill's SKILL.md.
Have developers review each skill run's transcript.
Protect tags server-side so pushes fail.
Set `allowed-tools` to the minimum the skill needs: Read, Edit, and Bash scoped to `git log` only.

questions.explanation: `allowed-tools` scoped to the skill's actual needs — Read, Edit, and Bash limited to `git log` — keeps the changelog function working while making `git tag` and pushes structurally unavailable. A is the advisory approach that already failed. B reviews after the fact. C catches only the push, not the local mutation, and depends on server configuration.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: Your `/fix-issue` skill needs a ticket number to look up the issue before fixing it. Developers regularly invoke it bare and it fabricates an interpretation of "the issue." Which frontmatter option addresses the invocation problem?

choices.text: `context: fork`, so the fabricated interpretations stay isolated.
A SKILL.md instruction to refuse when no ticket is given.
`argument-hint`, prompting the developer for the required ticket number on bare invocation.
`allowed-tools` restricted to read-only until a ticket is provided.

questions.explanation: `argument-hint` prompts for the required parameter when the skill is invoked bare — fixing the invocation gap that causes the fabrication. A isolates the bad output instead of preventing it. B handles the failure politely rather than collecting the input. D misuses tool permissions as input validation.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: End-to-end test specs (`*.e2e.ts`) live next to the features they test, in dozens of directories. They must all follow your Playwright conventions. Which mechanism applies the conventions to exactly those files?

choices.text: A CLAUDE.md in the `tests/` directory, where some of the specs live.
A `.claude/rules/` file with frontmatter `paths: ["**/*.e2e.ts"]`.
The root CLAUDE.md with a section headed "For e2e files only."
A skill that developers run before writing e2e tests.

questions.explanation: Files identified by naming convention and spread across directories are the glob-rule case: `paths: ["**/*.e2e.ts"]` loads the conventions exactly when those files are edited. A covers only one location of many. C loads always and scopes never. D depends on someone remembering.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: You're adding a caching layer. Three integration approaches are viable — sidecar, library, or gateway-level — each with different infrastructure requirements, and the choice constrains several services. How do you start?

choices.text: Direct execution starting with the simplest approach, switching if it fails.
Implement all three behind a feature flag and benchmark.
Prototype whichever approach is fastest to build and decide from that spike.
Enter plan mode: explore the affected services, weigh the three approaches, and settle the design first.

questions.explanation: Multiple viable architectures with cross-service constraints is plan mode's core criterion: explore, compare, and commit to a design before code. A ships the first idea and discovers constraints by failure. B triples the work to avoid a decision. C optimizes for build speed, not fit — the fastest prototype says little about the approach that constrains several services best.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: A user reports that phone numbers with spaces fail validation. The regex lives in one function; the failing input and expected behavior are both known. How do you proceed?

choices.text: Direct execution — a single-function fix with a clear reproduction needs no planning phase.
Plan mode, to consider validation architecture holistically.
An Explore subagent to find all validation patterns first.
A `fork_session` to compare two candidate regexes.

questions.explanation: Single function, known reproduction, clear expected behavior: direct execution. Planning (B), repo-wide exploration (C), and session forking (D) add process where there is no design uncertainty.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: Claude's fixes to your date-parsing utility keep regressing other formats: each fix breaks a previously working case. What iteration structure stops the whack-a-mole?

choices.text: Ask Claude to enumerate all formats before each fix.
Write a test suite first covering all formats and edge cases, then iterate by sharing the failing tests.
Freeze the utility and write a new one alongside it.
Fix formats in order of usage frequency.

questions.explanation: Regressions on previously working cases mean nothing is pinning existing behavior: write the test suite first (all formats, edge cases), then iterate on failing tests. The suite converts whack-a-mole into convergence. A relies on enumeration without enforcement. C abandons instead of stabilizing. D orders the moles without stopping the whacking.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and both plan mode and direct execution.
questions.prompt: You're deep in a productive session; context is nearly full of file dumps from earlier exploration, and you have an hour of implementation left. You want to preserve key decisions but reclaim space. What do you do?

Ask Claude to respond more tersely for the remainder.
Run `/compact` to summarize the conversation, preserving key information while reclaiming space.
Export the transcript and continue in a text editor.

questions.explanation: `/compact` is the mid-session relief valve: summarize the conversation, reduce usage, preserve key information, keep working. A discards the decisions unless you can reconstruct them perfectly. B conserves output, not context. D takes the work out of the tool entirely.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code

Design first from assumptions, verifying afterwards.
Investigate each question in the main session, running `/clear` between questions.
Spawn subagents to investigate each question, returning summaries to the main session.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: Analytics show that 30% of user queries are simple definitions or single facts, yet every query traverses search → analysis → synthesis → report. What should the coordinator do differently?

choices.text: Add a cache in front of the pipeline for repeated questions.
Shorten each stage's prompt so the pipeline is cheaper per query.
Assess each query's complexity and invoke only what it needs — a single search for simple facts.
Route simple queries to a smaller, cheaper model running the same full pipeline.

questions.explanation: Coordinators should match invocation to query complexity: simple factual queries get a single search or a direct answer; the full pipeline is for real research. A helps only repeats. B makes every unnecessary stage cheaper instead of skipping it. D changes who runs the unnecessary pipeline, not whether it runs.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: Reviewing the coordinator wrapper, you find: `for turn in range(8): response = send(...)` with no other exit condition, and users report reports that stop mid-topic. What is the correct redesign?

choices.text: Loop on `stop_reason` — continue on `"tool_use"`, exit on `"end_turn"` — with any bound kept as a backstop.
Raise the range to 20 — telemetry shows 95% of tasks finish by then.
Add a check that breaks early when the response "looks complete."
Let users configure the turn budget per query.

questions.explanation: A bare `range(8)` makes an arbitrary cap the only termination — hence mid-topic truncation. Loop on `stop_reason`, with any bound kept strictly as an emergency backstop. B tunes the wrong mechanism. C adds a "looks complete" heuristic — a second anti-pattern. D makes users configure a bug.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: The report agent produces beautiful reports with invented citations. Investigating, you find its prompt contains the synthesis text but not the claim-source mappings the synthesis agent produced. What is the fix?

choices.text: Instruct the report agent to only cite when certain.
Give the report agent a search tool to find real citations.
Have a post-processor verify and correct the citations.
Pass the claim-source mappings explicitly in the report agent's prompt alongside the synthesis.

questions.explanation: Subagents use only what their prompts contain: the mappings existed upstream but never reached the report agent, so it improvised. Pass the claim-source mappings explicitly with the synthesis. A asks for restraint while withholding the data. B invites fresh, unvetted sourcing. C corrects fabrications after generation instead of preventing them.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.prompt: Five regional market analyses are needed before a global rollup; each is independent. The coordinator currently runs them one per turn, and latency is five times the single-region time. What fixes the latency?

choices.text: Merge the five analyses into one subagent prompt.
Emit five Task tool calls in a single coordinator response so the analyses run in parallel.
Precompute regions on a nightly schedule so requests hit a cache.
Shorten each regional analysis to a summary.

questions.explanation: Independent analyses parallelize via multiple Task calls in one coordinator response — five subagents at once, latency near single-region time. A serializes inside one context. C changes freshness semantics to dodge an orchestration fix. D trades quality for speed unnecessarily.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. questions.prompt: An engineer wired the search agent to hand results directly to the analysis agent and the analysis agent directly to synthesis, bypassing the coordinator "for speed." Since then, failures are impossible to localize and partial results vanish silently. What does the incident illustrate?

choices.text: Subagent chains need distributed tracing infrastructure.
Direct handoffs are fine, but each agent needs retry logic.
The speed gain proves the coordinator was unnecessary overhead.
Hub-and-spoke routing exists for these exact properties: observability, error handling, controlled information flow.

questions.explanation: The lost properties — failure localization, non-vanishing partial results — are exactly what hub-and-spoke routing through the coordinator provides: observability, consistent error handling, controlled information flow. A rebuilds those properties as infrastructure around a broken topology. B patches one symptom. C mistakes the cause of the speedup for proof the coordinator was waste.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A required `pricing` section in the report template, left blank when data is missing.
A refinement loop: the coordinator checks synthesis against required coverage and re-delegates for the gaps.
More search results per query so pricing shows up more often.

questions.explanation: Completeness requires an evaluation loop: the coordinator checks synthesis against required coverage, re-delegates targeted queries for gaps, and re-invokes synthesis. questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. questions.prompt: Policy: the document analysis agent may only load documents from your licensed research library. It has a `load_document` tool that accepts any URL, and prompt instructions restricting it. You need a guarantee. What is it?

choices.text: A hook intercepting `load_document` calls that blocks any URL outside the licensed domains.
A nightly job auditing which URLs were loaded.
A stronger system prompt listing approved domains.
Renaming the tool `load_licensed_document` as a cue.

questions.explanation: A guarantee means interception: a hook validating every `load_document` URL against the licensed domains, blocking and redirecting anything else. B detects violations after the licensing breach. C remains probabilistic. D is a naming hint, not a control.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. choices.text: Longer lists of predefined search strings covering more phrasings.
Delegating research goals and quality criteria, leaving search formulation to the specialist.
A search-string-generation subagent feeding the search agent.
Letting subagents ignore instructions when results look thin.

questions.explanation: Delegation should specify goals and quality criteria, leaving method to the specialist — dictated search strings are procedural micromanagement that breaks on unanticipated topics. A writes more of the brittle thing. C adds an agent to generate the brittle thing. D makes adaptation an act of disobedience.

questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. questions.prompt: `process_source` takes `mode: "summarize" | "extract" | "verify"` and agents keep calling it with the wrong mode for the situation. What is the recommended redesign?

choices.text: Better documentation of the three modes in the description.
A default mode so wrong calls do something reasonable.
A wrapper that infers the mode from the arguments.
Split it into three purpose-specific tools, each with a clear description and contract.

questions.explanation: Mode-switched generic tools invite wrong-mode calls; split into three purpose-specific tools with clear contracts so selection happens at the tool level, where descriptions can differentiate. A documents the confusion. B substitutes silent wrong behavior. C hides the decision in inference.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. questions.prompt: Your toolset includes `search_news` ("Searches for news") and `search_web` ("Searches the web") — and agents use them interchangeably, though one hits a curated news API with date filtering and the other a general engine. What is the first fix?

choices.text: Drop `search_web` since news is the primary use case.
Route by keyword: queries containing "news" go to `search_news`.
Rewrite both descriptions: what each source is, which parameters matter, and when to prefer each.
Merge them into `search_all` with a source parameter.

The continuation request — after appending tool results, the conversation must be sent back to the model.
The Grep result was too large and must be truncated.
A `continue: true` flag on the tool result block.

Start fresh but paste in Friday's final message.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Your invoice extractor prompts for "a JSON response" and parses the text. Failures cluster around markdown fences, apologetic preambles ("Here is the extracted data:"), and occasional mid-output drift where fields wander from the required structure. What eliminates the failure class?

choices.text: A response prefix trick — pre-filling the assistant turn with `{`.
Tool use — an extraction tool whose input schema is the invoice structure, read from the `tool_use` block.
A prompt rule: "no prose, no fences, JSON only."
A tolerant parser that strips fences and leading prose.

questions.explanation: Tool use eliminates the failure class: the extraction tool's input schema guarantees structure — no fences, no preambles, and no mid-output drift, because the schema is enforced. A (prefill) suppresses preambles and opening fences but guarantees nothing about the rest of the output — the drift failures survive. C is an instruction, already being violated. D is an arms race with formatting variety.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. questions.prompt: Receipts often genuinely lack a due date, but `due_date` is required in your schema — and audits found the model quietly inserting a date 30 days after the purchase date. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Keep it required but add "never invent dates" to the prompt.
Post-validate that due dates appear verbatim in the source text.
Default the field server-side to 30 days, making the model's behavior official.
Make `due_date` optional/nullable and instruct the model to return null when the document has none.

questions.explanation: A required field the source may not contain pressures the model to fabricate; make `due_date` nullable and instruct null when absent. A keeps the pressure and adds a plea. B catches some fabrications after the fact (and fails on reformatted dates). C institutionalizes the fabrication.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction

choices.text: Add `"other"` to the enum with a companion detail field capturing the actual method.

Make the field free text and classify downstream.
Reject documents with unrecognized payment methods.

questions.explanation: The extensible-category pattern: `"other"` plus a detail field capturing the actual method — novel categories are represented faithfully, and the enum stays machine-readable. `tool_choice: "any"` — a tool call is guaranteed and the model picks the matching schema.
Three pipeline lanes with a rules-based classifier in front.

questions.prompt: Contracts occasionally arrive with a stated term whose end date precedes its start date (drafting or OCR errors). Downstream date math silently produces negative durations. What extraction design surfaces the problem?

Extract both dates as stated and set a `conflict_detected` boolean when the ordering is impossible.
Reject any contract whose dates are out of order.
Extract only the start date, deriving the end from the stated term length.

The field should be removed from the schema.

A model update shipped at the same time; the examples were irrelevant.
Few-shot examples teach the underlying judgment, which the model generalizes to novel layouts.

Batch for both — the discount is too large to pass up.

questions.explanation: The archive is the Batch API's ideal customer: enormous, latency-tolerant, half price. Onboarding has a customer waiting — synchronous. A forfeits major savings. C parks live customers behind a no-SLA queue. D is backwards on one of the two.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Your contract guarantees extraction results within 36 hours of document receipt. Batch processing takes up to 24 hours. Documents arrive continuously. Which accumulation window keeps the guarantee?

choices.text: 8 hours — worst case 8 + 24 = 32 hours, within the guarantee.
24 hours — one daily batch is operationally cleanest.
16 hours, since batches usually complete in far less than 24.
48 hours with an expedite lane for old documents.

questions.explanation: The guarantee must hold in the worst case: 8-hour accumulation + 24-hour processing = 32 ≤ 36 with margin. B gives 48 worst case. C's 16 + 24 = 40 breaches the SLA, and "usually faster" isn't a guarantee. D starts beyond the SLA and patches with an expedite lane.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Legal has approved extracting 10,000 archived medical consent forms with a new prompt. The batch budget is fixed. What do you do before submitting the full batch?

choices.text: Submit the full batch immediately; failures can be resubmitted within budget.
Submit the batch at half temperature to be safe.
Split into two 5,000-form batches and correct between them.
Refine and verify the prompt on a representative sample via the synchronous API first.

questions.explanation: With a fixed budget, first-pass success is everything: refine the prompt on a representative sample synchronously, verify, then submit the batch. A spends the budget discovering flaws at full scale. B tweaks a parameter instead of validating the prompt. C still burns half the budget on the unvalidated version.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Your extraction step ends with "double-check your extraction against the document" — and reports itself accurate. Auditors keep finding wrong values the self-check approved. What is the structural lesson?

choices.text: The self-check needs a rubric listing common error types.
The self-check should run twice, with disagreements escalated.
Verification should run as an independent instance, comparing output to source without the extractor's context.
Self-checks work if you also request a confidence score.

questions.explanation: A model verifying its own extraction retains the reasoning that produced the errors — self-checks approve their own mistakes. Verification must be an independent instance comparing output to source without the extractor's context. A gives the biased checker a rubric. B repeats the biased check. D scores it.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: Your dashboard proudly shows 96% extraction accuracy. An operations manager mentions that handwritten intake forms "seem to always be wrong." You segment the data: typed forms 99%, handwritten 61%. What is the lesson?

choices.text: Handwritten forms should be excluded from the accuracy metric.
Aggregate metrics mask segment failures — validate accuracy by document type and field before it justifies decisions.
The dashboard should show median accuracy instead of mean.
96% is accurate as an overall number, so no process change is needed.

questions.explanation: 96% aggregate coexisting with 61% on handwritten forms is exactly how aggregate metrics mask segment failures: validate by document type and field before the number justifies anything, and remediate the failing segment. A hides the problem from the metric. C changes the statistic, not the blindness. D accepts a segment that's wrong 4 times in 10.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: After automating high-confidence extractions, you need an ongoing mechanism to catch error patterns the confidence model doesn't know about yet. What is it?

choices.text: Quarterly re-validation against the original benchmark set.
Alerting when confidence scores drift statistically.
Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions for continuous human review.
A user-facing "report an error" button on downstream systems.

questions.explanation: Novel error patterns in the automated stream are caught by stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions with ongoing human review — measuring true error rates where no one otherwise looks. A can't contain patterns that didn't exist at benchmark time. B watches the scores, not the truth. D makes customers the QA layer.

questions.scenario: Scenario D: Structured Data Extraction
questions.scenario_context: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.prompt: The model emits per-field confidence scores, and you plan to auto-accept above a threshold. A colleague proposes 0.9 "because it's high." What is the defensible way to choose?

choices.text: Calibrate against a labeled validation set: measure accuracy at each score level and set thresholds where it meets the requirement.
Adopt 0.9 but review the first month's auto-accepts.
Pick 0.95, splitting the difference between the proposal and maximum caution.
Average the last quarter's scores and use that as the threshold.

questions.explanation: Thresholds come from calibration: measure actual accuracy at each confidence level against labeled data, and set the cutoff (per field type if performance differs) where accuracy meets requirements. B and C are round numbers with different amounts of caution — neither is a measurement. D averages scores into a threshold with no connection to accuracy. --- *End of Practice Exam 10.*

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: Every contributor must follow the same repository-wide naming and error-handling conventions in every Claude Code session. The guidance changes with the repository and should be reviewed in pull requests. Where should it live?

choices.text: In each contributor's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
In an on-demand project skill named `/standards`.
In the repository's project-level `CLAUDE.md`.
In an inline prompt copied into each new session.

questions.explanation: Shared, durable, always-applied repository guidance belongs in the committed project `CLAUDE.md`. User memory is personal, a skill is on demand, and repeated inline prompts are not reliably shared.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: Security conventions apply to every file named `*Controller.ts`, which appears under many unrelated packages. The conventions should load only when Claude edits those files. Which mechanism fits?

choices.text: A `.claude/rules/` file with a `paths: ["**/*Controller.ts"]` glob.
A `CLAUDE.md` in the first package containing a controller.
A root `CLAUDE.md` section that asks Claude to infer when the rule matters.
A slash command developers invoke before changing controllers.

questions.explanation: A path-scoped rule follows matching controller files across unrelated directories and loads only for those files. Directory memory misses scattered locations, root memory loads too broadly, and a command is not automatic.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: A team-wide dependency audit is run only before quarterly releases. It produces lengthy exploratory output that should not remain in the implementation conversation. How should it be packaged?

choices.text: As several hundred always-loaded lines in the root `CLAUDE.md`.
As a user-level command installed separately by every contributor.
As a path rule that activates whenever any dependency file is read.
As a project skill configured with `context: fork`.

questions.explanation: An occasional reusable workflow belongs in a skill, and `context: fork` keeps its verbose exploration out of the main conversation. The other placements either load it constantly, make it personal, or activate it for unrelated file work.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: A deployment tool may run only when its arguments contain both an approved change-ticket ID and the current maintenance-window identifier. Prompt reminders have already been bypassed. What should enforce the rule?

choices.text: A stronger warning in `CLAUDE.md`.
A `PreToolUse` hook that validates the tool arguments and blocks invalid calls.
A path-scoped rule for deployment manifests.
A custom command that prints the policy and requires the operator to confirm both values before deployment.

questions.explanation: The rule depends on live tool arguments and must be deterministic, so a `PreToolUse` hook should validate and block before execution. Documentation and commands remain advisory; a file-path rule cannot inspect the required operational state.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: You created a personal `/rewrite-commit` command with an experimental style that should not affect teammates or be committed to the project. Where should it be stored?

choices.text: `.claude/commands/rewrite-commit.md` in the repository so every teammate receives the experiment.
`~/.claude/commands/rewrite-commit.md` in your user configuration.
The project `CLAUDE.md` under a personal heading.
`.mcp.json` as a prompt definition.

questions.explanation: User-scoped commands are personal and are not distributed through the repository. A project command would affect teammates, while `CLAUDE.md` and MCP configuration are different mechanisms.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: During one debugging task, Claude needs the exact contents of `docs/legacy-auth-flow.md`. The file is unlikely to matter again after the task. What is the most appropriate way to provide it?

choices.text: Add its full contents permanently to the root `CLAUDE.md`.
Turn the document into an MCP server.
Create a path rule that loads whenever any source file is edited.
Reference it with `@docs/legacy-auth-flow.md` in the current prompt.

questions.explanation: An `@` reference supplies a known relevant file to the current task without permanently consuming future context. The other choices make one-time context durable or introduce unrelated infrastructure.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: Everything under `services/payments/` follows one cohesive set of conventions, while no other subtree uses them. The conventions should apply automatically throughout that subtree. What is the simplest placement?

choices.text: A `CLAUDE.md` inside `services/payments/`.
A personal skill in `~/.claude/skills/`.
A root slash command that developers must remember to invoke.
An MCP resource containing the conventions.

questions.explanation: A directory-level `CLAUDE.md` is the natural automatic scope for one cohesive subtree. Skills require invocation, and commands or MCP resources do not provide inherited directory guidance.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: After every file edit, the team must run the formatter and immediately return any formatting failure to Claude, regardless of whether Claude remembered to run it. Which mechanism provides that behavior?

choices.text: A formatting paragraph in `CLAUDE.md` and an instruction that Claude invoke it after every edit.
A `PreToolUse` hook on Read operations.
A `PostToolUse` hook matched to file edits.
An `@` reference to the formatter configuration.

questions.explanation: `PostToolUse` runs after the edit and can invoke the formatter and return failures to Claude every time. A prose instruction is probabilistic, PreToolUse is the wrong event, and an `@` reference does not execute checks.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: Claude's CSV converter mishandles quoted commas. Repeating “support all valid CSV” has not helped. Which feedback is most likely to produce a reliable correction?

choices.text: Increase the reasoning budget without showing the failure.
Ask for a completely different implementation with no constraints and compare it manually against a few successful CSV files.
Add the issue permanently to user-level memory.
Provide the failing input, the current output, the exact expected output, and the relevant regression test.

questions.explanation: A concrete failing input, observed output, expected output, and regression test give Claude an exact correction target and preserve the fix. More effort without evidence and permanent memory do not clarify the transformation.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: You are designing an unfamiliar cache invalidation layer and have not decided how freshness, failure recovery, or multi-region writes should behave. Which refinement technique should come before implementation?

choices.text: Ask Claude to interview you about unresolved design constraints and failure modes.
Generate the simplest cache, let production incidents reveal requirements, and document whatever behavior emerges as product policy.
Put “use best practices” in `CLAUDE.md` and start direct execution.
Ask multiple agents to implement alternatives before clarifying acceptance criteria.

questions.explanation: The interview pattern surfaces missing product and failure-mode decisions before code hardens accidental assumptions. Implementing first or multiplying implementations cannot resolve requirements that have not been decided.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: A refactor has two interacting API changes that share a compatibility constraint, plus an unrelated spelling error. How should you present the feedback during iteration?

choices.text: Send all three one at a time so each response can be reviewed and merged before the next issue is discussed.
Send all three together because batching is always more efficient.
Describe the interacting API changes together with their shared constraint, and handle the independent spelling fix separately.
Add every issue to `CLAUDE.md` so later sessions can decide the order.

questions.explanation: Interacting issues should be presented together with their shared constraints, while independent issues can be iterated separately. Universal “always batch” or “always sequence” rules ignore dependency structure.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: You need to find every source file whose contents reference `LegacyTokenValidator`, regardless of filename. Which built-in tool is the best starting point?

choices.text: Glob.
Grep.
Write.
Edit.

questions.explanation: Grep searches file contents for symbol references. Glob searches paths, while Write and Edit mutate files rather than discover usages.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: An unfamiliar service has thousands of files. You need to understand how requests reach `authorizePayment` without flooding the context window. What is the strongest exploration strategy?

choices.text: Search for the symbol and likely entry points, Read only the matching files, then follow relevant imports incrementally.
Read every file under the service before forming any hypothesis.
Glob only for filenames containing `payment`, infer the call flow from names, and use import order as a proxy for runtime behavior.
Run the entire test suite repeatedly and infer architecture from pass/fail output.

questions.explanation: Targeted search followed by selective Read and import tracing builds understanding incrementally without filling context. Reading everything wastes the window, and names or test output alone do not establish the call path.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: Yesterday's named investigation session contains an accurate repository map, and no relevant files have changed. You want to continue the same work today. What should you do?

choices.text: Start a blank session and reconstruct everything from scratch.
Fork the session even though no divergent approach is needed.
Copy only the last assistant response into a new conversation.
Resume the named session with `--resume <session-name>`.

questions.explanation: Named resumption is appropriate when prior context and tool results remain valid and the goal is unchanged. Forking is for divergence, and starting over discards reliable work.

questions.scenario: Scenario A: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.scenario_context: Your platform team uses Claude Code across a monorepo. Teams want reusable context without bloating every session, deterministic enforcement for operational controls, and repeatable ways to refine code safely.
questions.prompt: A named session contains useful architectural conclusions, but a major framework upgrade rewrote most analyzed files. What is the most reliable continuation?

choices.text: Resume unchanged because the conversation still contains the old tool results, and rely on the transcript to identify which files still matter.
Fork the stale session and trust both branches equally.
Start fresh with a structured summary of durable conclusions, identify changed areas, and re-read the affected files.
Discard both the durable conclusions and all repository context.

questions.explanation: Major file changes make old tool results stale, so a fresh session seeded with durable conclusions and targeted re-reading is safer than resuming or forking stale evidence. Discarding durable architecture facts is unnecessary.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: Every engineer should receive the same internal issue-tracker MCP server definition from version control, but each engineer has a different access token. What configuration is correct?

choices.text: Put the server and literal shared token in the root `CLAUDE.md`, then tell every engineer to copy the token into a local file before starting Claude Code.
Commit the server definition in project `.mcp.json` and reference an environment variable for the token.
Ask every engineer to create an unrelated personal skill.
Store the server only in one maintainer's `~/.claude.json`.

questions.explanation: Project `.mcp.json` distributes shared tooling, while environment expansion supplies per-user credentials without committing secrets. User scope is not shared, and neither skills nor `CLAUDE.md` configure the server.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: One developer is evaluating an unstable local MCP server that nobody else should see yet. Where should the definition live?

choices.text: In project `.mcp.json`, commented as experimental.
In the root `CLAUDE.md` so teammates can ignore it.
In `.claude/rules/` with a path that matches only the developer's files.
In that developer's user-scoped `~/.claude.json`.

questions.explanation: Personal or experimental servers belong in user-scoped `~/.claude.json`. Committing an unstable server exposes it to the team even if comments or path rules try to limit it.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: Claude Code connects to three configured MCP servers. A teammate proposes writing a router that activates exactly one server for each request. What should you explain?

choices.text: Tools from all connected servers are discovered at connection time and can be available simultaneously; selection is driven by their contracts and context.
Project servers disable user-scoped servers whenever both are configured.
Claude Code can discover only the first server listed in `.mcp.json` and requires manual reconnection whenever a tool from another server is needed.
MCP resources, rather than tools, select which server becomes active.

questions.explanation: Tools from connected MCP servers are discovered together and made available to the agent; clear contracts and context guide selection. There is no required one-active-server router or first-server-only rule.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: A committed `.mcp.json` currently contains a plaintext production token. What is the correct credential pattern?

choices.text: Base64-encode the token in the same file.
Move the token into a comment so Claude does not read it.
Replace it with environment-variable expansion such as `${INTERNAL_MCP_TOKEN}`.
Put the token in a project slash command.

questions.explanation: Environment-variable expansion keeps the secret outside version control while leaving the server definition shareable. Encoding, comments, and commands do not secure a committed credential.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: The team needs a standard Jira integration, and a well-maintained community MCP server already meets the requirements. When is a custom server justified instead?

choices.text: Only when team-specific behavior or interfaces are not provided by an appropriate existing server.
Whenever an integration will be shared by more than one developer, so its definition remains consistent across machines and repositories.
Whenever authentication uses an environment variable.
Always, because community servers cannot be project-scoped.

questions.explanation: Existing maintained servers are preferred for standard integrations; custom work is warranted for team-specific contracts or behavior not otherwise available. Scope and authentication do not by themselves require a custom server.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: Agents repeatedly call `list_services` and `list_tables` just to discover what internal data exists before choosing a real operation. What MCP feature should expose those catalogs efficiently?

choices.text: A `PostToolUse` hook.
A forced write tool.
MCP resources describing the available services and schemas.
A larger user-level `CLAUDE.md` containing copied live data.

questions.explanation: MCP resources expose catalogs and reference structures without repeated exploratory tool calls. Hooks intercept events, and copying live catalogs into memory creates stale, bloated context.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: You need an inventory of files named `Dockerfile`, `Dockerfile.dev`, or `service.Dockerfile` across the repository. Which built-in tool should start the search?

choices.text: Read every service root.
Grep for the text `FROM`.
Edit the build configuration.
Glob using filename patterns.

questions.explanation: Glob is designed for matching file paths and naming variants. Grep searches contents; reading every root is slower and less precise.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: Glob found four candidate configuration files. You now need the complete surrounding structure of one 120-line file before deciding where a setting is inherited. What should you use?

choices.text: Grep for a single key and ignore the rest of the file.
Read the selected file.
Write a replacement configuration.
Bash-delete the other candidates.

questions.explanation: Once candidates are narrowed, Read supplies the selected file's full local context. A single Grep match can hide inheritance structure, and mutation is premature.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: A production log contains the exact message `permission cache exhausted`, and you need to locate where that text is emitted. Which tool is most direct?

choices.text: Glob for files with `cache` in their names.
Read the whole repository sequentially.
Grep for the exact message.
Edit likely logging files until the message changes.

questions.explanation: An exact log string is a content-search problem, so Grep is direct. Filename guesses and exhaustive reads are weaker; Edit should follow diagnosis, not replace it.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: You must trace how a CLI command reaches a database adapter in an unfamiliar repository. Which sequence best manages context?

choices.text: Read every Python file, then search after the context is full and infer the database route from whichever file was read last.
Locate command registration with Grep/Glob, Read the matches, and follow only the relevant imports and calls.
Infer the route from directory names and skip file contents.
Ask a generic coding question without repository evidence.

questions.explanation: Incremental discovery narrows candidates before reading and follows only evidence-bearing relationships. Reading everything exhausts context, while inference without file evidence is unreliable.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: Claude confuses `search_source_code` with `search_runbooks`. Both descriptions currently say “search company content.” What is the best first correction?

choices.text: Force `search_source_code` for every query containing the word “error.”
Put both operations behind a third generic `search` tool.
Give the agent more tools and allow it to call them all before choosing which result should drive the task.
Rewrite each description with distinct use cases, accepted inputs, outputs, examples, boundaries, and when to prefer the other tool.

questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the model's primary selection signal and should differentiate purpose, formats, outputs, examples, edges, and neighboring tools. Forced keyword routing, generic consolidation, and more tools preserve the ambiguity.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: `analyze_content` handles web snippets while `analyze_document` handles uploaded files, but their names and descriptions overlap. What redesign most directly improves selection?

choices.text: Rename the first to a web-specific operation and make both contracts explicitly source-specific.
Keep the overlap, add “choose carefully” to the system prompt, and require Claude to explain its choice after the selected tool has already run.
Randomize between the tools and compare outputs later.
Force both tools on every item.

questions.explanation: Source-specific names and contracts move the distinction into the interface the model selects. Warnings, randomness, and always calling both do not remove overlapping semantics.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: Detailed tool descriptions look correct, yet a system prompt says “for any investigation, always begin with the archive tool.” Claude keeps ignoring a better live-search tool. What should you inspect?

choices.text: Whether the archive tool's JSON schema has alphabetized properties and whether its server connected before the live-search server.
Keyword-sensitive prompt instructions that override or bias normal tool selection.
Whether the tools appear in different MCP servers.
Whether the response token limit is high enough.

questions.explanation: System-prompt wording can create keyword associations that overpower good descriptions. Property ordering, server placement, and response length do not explain the mandated archive preference.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: A source-control MCP tool times out. The agent must know whether to retry and what operation failed. What should the tool return?

choices.text: A successful empty list so the workflow continues.
The text “something went wrong” without an error flag, plus a `CLAUDE.md` suggestion that Claude decide whether the string represents data or failure.
`isError` plus a transient category, retryability, attempted operation, safe description, and suggested next action.
Only the provider's raw stack trace.

questions.explanation: Structured error type, retryability, attempted action, and next steps let the agent choose a recovery path. Empty success hides failure, generic text is not actionable, and raw traces are unsafe and incomplete.

questions.scenario: Scenario B: Developer Productivity with Claude
questions.scenario_context: You are standardizing codebase-exploration tools and MCP integrations for a distributed engineering organization. Shared services must work after a clone, while experiments and credentials remain personal.
questions.prompt: A code search completes successfully and finds no references. How should the tool represent this outcome?

choices.text: As a retryable transient error because the result is empty.
As a permission error so the coordinator investigates access.
As a business-rule failure requiring human escalation.
As a successful empty result, distinct from any tool failure.

questions.explanation: No matches is a valid successful query result and must remain distinct from access or operational failures. Mislabeling it prompts wasteful retries or unnecessary escalation.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A compliance review always checks the same four known controls, while an incident investigation must branch based on each new log or dependency discovered. Which design is appropriate?

choices.text: Dynamic decomposition for both because all agent work should branch.
One large prompt for both to avoid coordination overhead.
A fixed chain for both so the step count is predictable and auditability takes priority over evidence discovered during the investigation.
A fixed chain for the repeatable control review and dynamic decomposition for the investigation.

questions.explanation: Known repeatable stages suit a fixed chain, while evidence-driven incident work needs adaptive decomposition. One decomposition style is not optimal for both predictable and open-ended work.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: The request is “add comprehensive tests to this unknown legacy service.” What should the coordinator do first?

choices.text: Generate one test file for every source file immediately.
Map the service, identify high-impact behavior and dependencies, then create subtasks that adapt to what the map reveals.
Apply the same fixed list of unit-test prompts used for every repository and rerun it unchanged whenever a test exposes a new dependency.
Delegate only to a test-writer and prohibit further exploration.

questions.explanation: An unknown legacy system must first be mapped so high-impact behavior and dependencies can drive the testing plan. Immediate file-by-file generation is a fixed guess and can miss integration risk.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A simple factual query needs one authoritative source, but the coordinator always invokes search, document analysis, statistics, synthesis, and report agents. What is the best change?

choices.text: Keep the pipeline but shorten every agent's response so latency and cost remain predictable for every query.
Cache every specialist's last answer.
Let the coordinator select only the specialists justified by the query and intermediate findings.
Replace all specialists with one unrestricted agent.

questions.explanation: The coordinator should scale delegation to query complexity and what is discovered. Making an unnecessary full pipeline cheaper or caching irrelevant work does not remove it.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A broad market study omits regional regulation because the coordinator decomposed it only by product feature. How should decomposition be improved?

choices.text: Partition the full scope across complementary dimensions or source types, then verify coverage before synthesis.
Ask the synthesis agent to invent a regulatory section from general knowledge and label it as an informed architectural estimate.
Make every existing subtask longer without changing scope.
Remove the coverage requirement to match the available research.

questions.explanation: Broad work needs complementary scope partitioning and a coverage check so no major dimension vanishes. Longer reports cannot recover an unassigned region, and synthesis must not fabricate it.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: An open-ended performance investigation has not yet established which component is slow. What is the strongest initial subtask?

choices.text: Rewrite the database layer because it is commonly slow, even if later measurements implicate a different component.
Ask every specialist to optimize its favorite component.
Measure and map the request path first, then generate prioritized subtasks from the observed bottlenecks.
Execute a fixed sequence of generic optimizations.

questions.explanation: Measurement and mapping identify actual bottlenecks, after which subtasks can adapt to evidence. Generic or preference-based optimization starts with unsupported assumptions.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: Forty files need the same predictable local checklist, followed by one cross-file compatibility review. Which decomposition best preserves depth?

choices.text: Run focused per-file passes and then a separate integration pass.
Use an open-ended dynamic investigation for every file even though the stages are known.
Put all files in one prompt and ask Claude to divide attention evenly.
Skip the integration pass because every local result passed.

questions.explanation: Predictable local checks benefit from focused per-file passes, and a separate integration pass catches cross-file behavior. One mega-prompt dilutes attention, while skipping integration leaves an explicit gap.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A dependency audit discovers midway that two services share a generated client, invalidating several planned subtasks. What should the coordinator do?

choices.text: Finish the original task list before acknowledging the dependency so the plan remains comparable with prior audit runs and reports.
Revise the plan and generate replacement subtasks that account for the shared client.
Restart the entire investigation without preserving valid findings.
Hide the discovery from specialists so assignments remain stable.

questions.explanation: Adaptive plans change when a newly discovered dependency invalidates prior assumptions, preserving still-valid findings while replacing affected work. Blind completion and wholesale restart are both wasteful.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: Which coordinator behavior most clearly distinguishes adaptive decomposition from a fixed workflow?

choices.text: It uses the same specialists in a different order each run while preserving the predefined task list and completion conditions.
It runs all predefined steps in parallel.
It asks for longer reports when evidence is thin.
It creates or revises subtasks in response to intermediate discoveries and remaining coverage gaps.

questions.explanation: Creating and revising subtasks from intermediate findings is the defining adaptive behavior. Reordering or parallelizing a fixed list does not change what work is generated.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: Initial synthesis is strong but lacks evidence for one geography. What should an iterative coordinator do?

choices.text: Identify the gap, delegate a targeted follow-up search, then resynthesize with the new evidence.
Add a generic disclaimer and stop despite the recoverable gap.
Restart every completed subtask from scratch.
Ask the synthesis agent to fill the section without sources and cite the originally assigned material despite its missing geographic coverage.

questions.explanation: Iterative orchestration evaluates synthesis, identifies a specific gap, commissions targeted evidence, and resynthesizes. Disclaiming or inventing content skips a recoverable refinement step.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A specialist repeatedly maps “active users” to total registered accounts. Which feedback is most useful?

choices.text: Tell it to think harder about metrics.
Raise the maximum output length.
Replace the agent without describing the observed failure and ask the replacement to infer the intended definition from previous reports.
Provide representative inputs, the incorrect mappings, the desired mappings, and a precise definition of “active.”

questions.explanation: Examples of the failure and desired mapping plus an exact definition teach the disputed boundary. Generic effort, length, or agent replacement supplies no corrective evidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: Three findings arise from the same mistaken date-window assumption and will interact if fixed separately. How should the coordinator request refinement?

choices.text: Send each issue in isolation and withhold the shared assumption so every specialist can optimize its correction independently.
Batch the related issues in one detailed request that explains their common dependency.
Fix only the easiest finding and ignore the rest.
Add the errors to permanent user memory.

questions.explanation: Related failures caused by one assumption should be evaluated together so the fix is coherent. Isolating them hides the interaction; permanent memory is not an issue tracker.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: You resume a research session after editing three previously analyzed parsers. Most other context remains valid. What should you tell the agent?

choices.text: Nothing; resumption automatically detects every filesystem change.
Re-read the entire repository because targeted recovery is impossible.
Name the changed files and request targeted re-analysis while retaining unaffected findings.
Trust the old parser outputs because named resumption snapshots the current filesystem before the next answer.

questions.explanation: A resumed agent must be told what changed so it can refresh affected evidence without repeating valid exploration. Session history does not automatically know filesystem changes.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: You want two independent research strategies to begin from the same accepted source map without contaminating one another. What mechanism fits?

choices.text: Resume the same session in two terminals.
Copy only the user prompt into two blank sessions.
Run both strategies sequentially in one conversation.
Use `fork_session` to branch from the shared baseline.

questions.explanation: `fork_session` preserves the accepted baseline while isolating divergent reasoning. Concurrent resume shares the same branch, blank sessions lose context, and sequential work contaminates the comparison.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A research agent has `search_news` and `search_academic`, but the latter is almost never chosen even for peer-reviewed-evidence requests. What should its description add?

choices.text: A promise that it is always better than every other tool and an instruction to prefer it whenever the user requests credible evidence.
Its indexed sources, accepted query/date inputs, output metadata, example academic requests, and explicit contrast with news search.
Internal implementation details unrelated to selection.
A requirement that both tools run for every query.

questions.explanation: Selection improves when the academic tool says what it indexes, how to query it, what it returns, and when it wins over news search. Boasts, implementation trivia, and mandatory dual calls are not useful boundaries.

questions.scenario: Scenario C: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.scenario_context: Your research coordinator handles requests ranging from routine comparisons to open-ended investigations. It must choose decomposition strategies based on the work rather than blindly running a fixed pipeline.
questions.prompt: A search specialist sees a transient timeout that succeeds on a safe local retry. What error-handling structure best protects coordinator context?

choices.text: Let the specialist recover locally; propagate only unresolved failure context, attempts, and partial results.
Propagate every first failure immediately, let the coordinator retry it, and preserve a full transcript of every attempt in the main context.
Hide all failures, including permanent ones, from the coordinator.
Terminate every subagent when any tool reports an error.

questions.explanation: Specialists should recover locally from safe transient failures and spare coordinator context; unresolved errors should include attempts and usable partial results. Immediate propagation and total suppression are both brittle.
